en: In the first chapter,
the first section,
[salutation] to the one whose self consists of infinite vision, knowledge, power, and bliss.
Faith in the principles or general knowledge is *darśana*.
Homage to the Arhat, the Protector who has established the ford of Dharma through compassion. (1) [Racita]

In order to cultivate the seed of enlightenment for the wise through the practice of reality, so that they may attain the qualities of a Jina after death— enlightenment being its seed, which is rightness— a commentary on the sūtras of our own Jaina doctrine is here composed. (2)

Now, if these sūtras of the Jaina doctrine belong to you, then what were the [sūtras] before you, and to whom did they belong? You have asked this quite trivially; you should also inquire as to what the sūtras of grammar and other sciences were prior even to Pāṇini, Piṅgala, Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and the rest, and to whom they belonged! These sciences are indeed beginningless; they appear ever new through the desire to express them either in brief or in detail, and thus they are said to have various authors.

Have you not heard that "the world has never been otherwise than it is"? Or rather, consider the *Tattvārtha-sūtras*, composed by the foremost of teachers (*Vācakamukhya*) and serving as the crest-jewels of all scriptures—whose work are they?

If this is so, why not simply compose a treatise (*prakaraṇa*) like Akalaṅka, Dharmakīrti, and others? What is the point of this vanity of claiming to be a "Sūtra-author"? Do not speak thus; for people have diverse tastes, and therefore there is no worldly or royal decree to restrain one's own desire. Thus, this [objection] is of little consequence.
Through a futile attachment,

the Teacher composed this treatise consisting of words which are collections of phonemes, sūtras which are collections of words, chapters (*prakaraṇa*) which are collections of sūtras, daily lessons (*āhnika*) which are collections of chapters, and five books (*adhyāya*) which are collections of daily lessons.
And in order to state the subject matter— which is a necessary factor for the engagement of a discerning person— he [offers] this first sūtra:
Now, the Investigation of the Means of Valid Cognition (*Pramāṇamīmāṃsā*).

Because the word "now" (*atha*) signifies the commencement of a topic, and because it denotes the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which is the subject under discussion and being introduced by this treatise, discerning persons are both informed of the intended purport of the entire treatise and incited to engage with it.

Alternatively, the word *atha* has the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*); the meaning is that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be investigated immediately after the treatises on grammar, poetics, and prosody.
By this, he indicates that these works share a single author with the present treatise, such as grammar and the others.

Furthermore, when the word *atha* is used in the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*), its mere hearing—just like the sight of a flower garland or a water-pot being brought for another purpose—also serves as an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*).

When there is an auspicious rite (*maṅgala*), the accomplishment of the treatise occurs without delay due to the destruction of obstacles and impediments, and it ensures that the audience lives long; however, although the author of the aphorisms (*sūtrakāra*) performed an auspicious rite such as a salutation to the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*), he did not include it [in the text] because he desired brevity—
thus [it is stated] in the *Vyākhyāna* (the *Tattvārthasūtra-vyākhyā*).
O venerable ones, the listeners of this scripture [should attend] to this recitation of the praise and names at its beginning.

That by which the reality of an object (*vastutattva*) is measured—that is, determined through the complete exclusion of doubt and other such obstacles—is *pramāṇa* (the means of valid cognition), being the most effective instrument for the production of valid knowledge (*pramā*). The investigation (*mīmāṃsā*) of that [means] consists of a thorough examination in the form of its enunciation (*uddeśa*) and so forth.
For the operation of a treatise (*śāstra*) is threefold: enunciation, definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and critical examination (*parīkṣā*).
In this context, *uddeśa* (enunciation) is the mere mention of a name, as in this very sūtra.
*Lakṣaṇa* (definition) is the statement of the unique characteristics (*asādhāraṇadharma*) of that which has been enunciated;
it is twofold: general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristic (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
The general definition [of perception] has just been stated in the immediately preceding sūtra;
the specific definition is: "clear direct perception" (1.1.4).
13. Thus, since differentiation (*vibhāga*) is merely an auxiliary to the definition of the particular (*viśeṣa*), it is not stated separately.
Investigation (*parīkṣā*) is the examination, according to reason, of that which has been defined, as to whether it is thus and not otherwise; as in the third aphorism.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," error (*viparyaya*) and non-apprehension (*anadhyavasāya*) are also understood.
"Classification" (*vibhāga*) is the statement of distinctions by way of number, such as: "Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect cognition (*parokṣa*)."

1.1.9–10 [The Sūtra states: "Because [the self] is not perceived when the body is present, it follows that the self does not exist. [The Bhāṣya explains: This argument is not valid. For even though the self is not perceived when the body is present, its existence is established by inference. Just as fire, though not perceived when fuel is present, exists because its effects are observed, so too the self exists because its effects—such as desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition—are observed. Furthermore, the self is inferred from the fact that the body, which is composed of the elements, cannot itself possess desire and the like; therefore, there must be another entity distinct from the body that possesses these qualities. Thus, the non-perception of the self when the body is present does not prove its non-existence. Alternatively, the Sūtra may be interpreted as follows: "Because [the self] is not perceived when the body is absent, it follows that the self does not exist. To this, the Bhāṣya replies: This is also not a valid proof. For even though the self is not perceived when the body is absent, its existence is established by inference. Just as fire exists even when fuel is absent [in the form of latent potential], so too the self exists even when the body is absent [in the state of liberation]. Moreover, since the body is composed of the elements, it lacks the capacity for desire and the like; therefore, there must be an entity other than the body that possesses these qualities. Consequently, the non-perception of the self when the body is absent does not prove its non-existence. Thus, the argument is refuted.
— Let it be; "lakṣaṇatā" means a limb, a constituent part, that is to say, a cause—
thus [it is stated] in the third sūtra.
Furthermore, the word *mīmāṃsā* denotes an investigation that is worthy of honor;

therefore, it is not only the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone that is undertaken here, but also that of the *nayās* (standpoints), which constitute a part thereof and whose paths have been purified by the refutation of fallacious standpoints (*durnaya*). As it is said: "The comprehension [of reality] is achieved through both *pramāṇas* and *nayās*" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 1.6).
Thus, O chief of speakers, when liberation— which is the crowning jewel among all human goals and which includes both its means and its adversaries—
is investigated in this manner, it becomes truly honored;
for an investigation into the means of valid cognition alone, if it results merely in the refutation of opposing views, would be nothing more than a verbal quarrel.
If, however, that were intended, then it would simply have been written as "Now, the examination of the means of valid cognition" (*atha pramāṇaparīkṣā*) [as found at Pramāṇaparīkṣā, p. 1].

Therefore, this is established: the Teacher employed the term "investigation" (*mīmāṃsā*) with the intention of explaining liberation along with its means and its counter-arguments, as well as the path of objects of knowledge purified by the means of valid cognition and the viewpoints (*naya*).
Those by whom the path of the means of valid cognition has been purified [to reveal] that reality is manifold in nature—

for the sake of their realization, and not for the sake of verbal disputation— is the engagement with the scripture, which is accompanied by the means consisting of right knowledge, vision, and conduct.
“Samsara is the counter-position”—
this error of the commentator Akalaṅka appears to have come down from the very root;
in reality, however, the *Pramāṇaparīkṣā* was not composed by Akalaṅka, but by Vidyānanda— Editor’s Note.
Regarding that liberation which has as its nature a path consisting of manifold aspects (anekāntātmaka),
he states the general definition of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "Valid cognition is the definitive determination of a real object."

"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is the designation of the subject (*lakṣya*); the remainder is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). For the purpose of a definition is the prescription of that which is not yet established by restating that which is already well-known. In this context, since "valid cognition" is established as the subject (*dharmin*) without dispute, its property (*dharma*), namely the nature of being a definitive determination of a correct object, is here prescribed.

Here, "because of being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatvāt*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). Nor is it untenable for the subject (*dharmin*) itself to function as the reason; for when the subject is a particular, its universal can serve as the reason, just as in the case: "This smoke possesses fire, because it is smoke, like previously perceived smoke.

Nor is there a lack of probative force in the absence of an external example, since the probandum is established through internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) alone, as will be shown in such cases as: "The living body possesses a self, because it possesses breath and so forth."
In the case of a subject (*dharmin*) in its specific form— for example, "the perception of a jar under dispute is of the nature of a correct determination of an object, because it is a perception"—
an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not a constituent part of the inference. 1.2.
Thus, in that Sūtra, the definition of *nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is given as "knowledge free from doubt, indecision, and non-conceptuality.

By the term *nirṇaya*, there is a negation of the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for both that which is not of the nature of knowledge— such as sense-organ contact— and that which, though of the nature of knowledge, is of the form of doubt and so forth.

Although the cognition produced by the first contact of the sense organ with the object is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) and lacks determinative judgment (*anadhyavasāya*), the term "non-conceptual" (*avikalpaka*) is nevertheless employed here specifically to refute the Buddhist position—
[the reading *°lpatva* is supported by the Ḍe manuscript].

From the word "ādi" (and so forth), it is understood that there is an operation of the knower (*jñātṛ-vyāpāra*), and that there is an object (*artha*)—characterized as that which is to be abandoned, accepted, or disregarded—because it is sought after: for what is to be abandoned is sought for the purpose of abandoning it, what is to be accepted for the purpose of accepting it, and what is to be disregarded for the purpose of disregarding it.

Furthermore, that which is to be disregarded does not fall within the category of the acceptable simply because it is not acceptable; for if it were so, it would follow that it must instead fall within the category of the abandonable, since it is not something to be abandoned.
Furthermore, the object that has been consecrated (the *mūrdhābhiṣikta-artha*) is indeed one to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*), because it is sought after only by yogis.

For people such as ourselves, too, there is a vast amount of matter to be disregarded among things to be rejected or accepted; therefore, this "ascertainment of the object" (*arthasya nirṇayaḥ*) cannot be disregarded. Here, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), because the object is pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) by the act of being ascertained.

And the inclusion of the term *artha* is for the purpose of excluding one's own determination (*svanirṇaya*), because we shall explain that although it exists, it is not a defining characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*).
[The suffix *ṇyat* is applied] because of being sought (*arthyamānatvāt*),
according to Pāṇini 3.1.97 and the *Haima-śabdānuśāsana* 5.3.20.
90 Thus, he is fit for that.

The term *samyak* signifies "non-erroneous" (*aviparīta*) and is indeclinable; alternatively, it is a form derived from the root *sam-añc*. It serves as an adjective qualifying "determination" (*nirṇaya*), because it is appropriate to qualify that very determination by means of its connection with correctness or incorrectness. The object (*artha*), however, is neither inherently correct nor incorrect; thus, since there is an absence of both possibility and deviation [in the object itself], it need not be qualified. Therefore, by the qualification "the determination of an object that is correct," error (*viparyaya*) is excluded.

Therefore, this general definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is free from the defects of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), under-extension (*avyāpti*), and impossibility (*asambhava*). That [definition], however, is determined— Tātparya-ṭīkā.
Indeed, a qualification is meaningful when there is the possibility of [the definition applying to] insentient things (*jaḍa*) and when there is ambiguity;

for the elders have stated that self-determination, like the determination of the object, is a characteristic of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is said: "Valid cognition is that which illuminates both itself and the other" (Nyāyāvatāra 1), and "Valid cognition is knowledge whose nature consists in the ascertainment of its own object" (Tattvārthaślokavārttika 1.10).

10.77 And thus, it is not the case that this [consciousness] does not exist, because— just like the agent and the object in such cases as "I know the jar"— consciousness itself also appears [in cognition].
Furthermore, for one who does not perceive the apprehension [of an object], the perception of the object itself is not established;

nor is it possible for that apprehension to be perceived by another cognition, because that [second] cognition, being itself unperceived, lacks the direct perception required to apprehend the apprehension under discussion.
And if one were to postulate yet another apprehension, there would be an infinite regress.

Because the object is perceived through the perception of that [cognition], there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). By this, the perception of that [object] even through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—namely, that the existence of the object would not be possible if cognition did not exist—is refuted; for since that [presumptive testimony] too functions as a cognizer, it cannot function as a cognizer if it is itself unknown.
If its cognition were derived from another presumptive testimony, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and the fault of mutual dependence, so the defeat remains as it was.
Therefore, because cognition appears not only as directed toward an object but also as directed toward itself, it possesses the nature of self-determination.

Now, one might argue that if experience were itself an object of experience, it would follow—like a jar or other objects—that it is not an experience; do not speak thus. For just as the knower is experienced as a knower, experience is experienced precisely as experience.

Nor is being an object of experience a defect in experience; for it is an experience in relation to an object, whereas it is an object of experience in relation to itself. There is no contradiction here, just as one person can be both a son and a father in relation to his own father and son respectively.
Nor is there a contradiction in an action operating upon itself, for no contradiction can be established regarding a matter that is established by direct experience (*anubhava*).

Furthermore, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is established through inference as well. To explain: cognition manifests an object only while it itself is being manifested, because it is a manifestor, like a lamp.

If it is argued that the status of being a manifestor is unestablished because consciousness is itself something to be manifested, we say no; for its status as a manifestor is logically consistent by way of dispelling ignorance and so forth.

Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) regarding the eyes and other [senses], because they are illuminators only insofar as they possess the nature of functional sense-faculties (bhāvendriya), and since functional sense-faculties have the very nature of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), there is no deviation.
Likewise, consciousness is self-luminous (svaprakāśa) because it is the cognition of an object; for that which is not self-luminous is not the cognition of an object, just like a jar.

Likewise, whatever is knowledge does not depend on the operation of another for its own self-awareness, just as the final cognition in a series of cognitions apprehending different objects—which precedes a cognition apprehending yet another object—is independent. And since the cognition under dispute, namely the cognition of color and so forth, is itself knowledge, consciousness does not require another of its own sub-class for its self-manifestation, because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a jar. If it is argued: "Consciousness is manifested by another, because it is a real entity, like a jar," we say no; this argument is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). For it is not because a jar is a real entity that it is manifested by another, but rather because it is distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*).
Therefore, having raised the objection that "one's own ascertainment (svanirṇaya) should also be a defining characteristic of valid cognition," he says:
"One's own ascertainment consists in the nature of certainty."
The perception of a person's own determination [is impossible] due to the fault of infinite regress.
The linguistic convention "this has an object" is not [established] through the perception of the cognition itself,
but rather through the perception of the object.

In the case of the cognition of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), if another presumptive testimony is required for the sake of knowing that [first] presumptive testimony, then yet another presumptive testimony must be postulated, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, if the knowledge of one presumptive testimony depends upon another presumptive testimony, then there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Because it is an object—
thus, there is no [need for] the removal of doubt and so forth regarding ignorance and the like.
The cognition whose object is the jar has an operation that does not depend on another cognition.
Kevalānvayi inference is another type of cognition;
although it is a self-determining [cognition], it is not a defining characteristic [of valid knowledge], because it occurs even in the case of invalid cognition.
"Even though it exists"—this is how he approves of what was stated by the opponent;

the meaning is this: it is not the case that everything simply because it "exists" must be stated as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa), but rather that a property (dharma) which excludes [the probandum] from the heterologous instances (vipakṣa) [is required].
Self-determination, however, exists even in non-valid cognitions such as doubt and the like; for there is no cognition whatsoever that is not self-cognized.
Therefore, we did not state "self-determination" as a defining characteristic [of valid cognition], but rather it was proposed by the elders for the sake of examination—thus there is no fault.
The definition must be stated—[the opponent] says:
"But surely, by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines an object already determined, one would be grinding what has already been ground;
and thus, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even successive cognitions (*dhārāvāhijñāna*) which grasp what has already been grasped would possess validity."

Therefore, let the definition be "the determination of a previously unknown object," as they have said: "Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is knowledge whose nature is the ascertainment of its own previously unknown object" (Parīkṣāmukha 1.1).
Regarding that, he says: "In that case, [it would follow that] the cognition of a previously unknown object... and so forth.
— of the knowledge [arising] from the *vāhika* (conveying) [process],
of one's own [self], and of the unprecedented object; likewise, of the unprecedented— Ḍe.

Regarding the word "your" (*tvaditi*), the Prābhākara Bhaṭṭas maintain that even a cognition that apprehends what has already been apprehended is not invalid, just like one that apprehends what is yet to be apprehended.

This is the meaning: would the charge of "grasping what has already been grasped" (*gṛhītagrāhitva*) be refuted with respect to the substance (*dravya*), or with respect to the mode (*paryāya*)? In that regard, even for serial cognitions (*dhārāvāhijñāna*), the state of grasping what has already been grasped is not possible from the perspective of the modes, because modes are momentary (*kṣaṇika*); so how could a qualification be employed to exclude that [charge]? Now, suppose it were with respect to the substance; that too is incorrect, because since the substance is eternal, there is no difference between its state of having been grasped and its state of being about to be grasped, as it is a single entity.

Furthermore, based on what specific distinction would validity belong to that which apprehends what is yet to be apprehended (*grahīṣyamāṇagrāhin*), and not to that which apprehends what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhin*)? Moreover, even though *avagraha*, *īhā*, and so forth apprehend what has already been apprehended, their validity is indeed accepted, and it is not the case that they have different objects; for if that were so, because there would be no striving (*īhana*) for what was merely grasped (*avagṛhīta*), and no ascertainment (*niścaya*) for what was merely striven for (*īhita*), an inconsistency would result. Nor can it be said that these possess "the quality of having a new object" (*apūrvārthatva*) due to the determination of a previously unapprehended particular with respect to successive stages (*paryāya*); for if that were so, as has already been stated, nothing at all would ever possess the quality of apprehending what has already been apprehended.
The meaning is: "for the purpose of excluding a cognition that apprehends an object already apprehended" (dīyate). — Ḍe.
Furthermore, for memory—which is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—its very nature consists in its apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).

Even by those who maintain that memory lacks validity (*aprāmāṇya*), it is stated that the reason is precisely its non-arising from the object (*anarthajatva*), and not its apprehending what has already been apprehended. As it is said: "The invalidity of memory is not caused by its apprehending what has already been apprehended; rather, the cause of its invalidity is its being produced without an [external] object" (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 23).
The nature of recollection is not invalidity caused by its grasping what has already been grasped.
"Furthermore, the cause of its invalidity is its being produced by what is not a [valid] object" (Nyāyamañjarī, p.

23). Now, he states the definitions of doubt (*saṃśaya*), non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), and error (*viparyaya*), which are excluded from the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
"Doubt is a cognition that touches upon both alternatives, but neither [of them exclusively]."

The term "both" (*ubhaya*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*), because doubt also exists when there is contact with the initial limit (*ādikoṭi*). (Note: *ādikoṭisaṃsparśe* is the reading in manuscript D.)

Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is that cognition which, regarding an object that possesses neither of two natures, has the habit of examining both extremes and in whose presence the self, as it were, lies down entirely; for example, when in the dark one perceives an object with an upward shape from a distance, and in the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to confirm or refute it, there arises the notion: "Is it a post (*sthāṇu*) or a person (*puruṣa*)?

The inclusion of the term "neither" (*anubhayatra*) is for the purpose of excluding doubt even in the case of an object possessing both forms where both alternatives are touched upon, such as: "The jar both exists and does not exist," or "The self is both eternal and non-eternal," and so forth.
Non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) is the non-specification of particulars;

it is a cognition devoid of the reflection upon unique properties (*asādhāraṇadharma*) due to distance, darkness, and so forth. Because its nature is that of non-certainty, it is called non-determination, as in: "What is this?"

Furthermore, even that non-conceptual [cognition] occurring in the first moment, which others accept as a valid means of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), is indeed a mere non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*), because there is an absence of the delineation of particulars (*viśeṣollekha*) therein as well.
Therefore, the notion "that very thing is in what is not that" is a misconception (*viparyaya*).

That cognition which appears with respect to a real object devoid of that [apparent] form, yet occurs as the thought "this is that very thing," is an error because it is of the nature of a misconception (*viparyāsa*). For example: due to a disorder of the humors (*dhātu*), there is the cognition of bitterness and so forth regarding substances that are sweet and so forth; due to defects such as cataracts (*timira*), there is the cognition of two moons and so forth even when there is only one moon; due to traveling in a boat, there is the cognition of moving trees even though they are not moving; and due to rapid rotation, there is the cognition of a wheel even in a firebrand (*alāta*) which is not a wheel.
Thus, the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is concluded.
In the case of a substance such as a firebrand (*ulmuka*) and so forth.

Now, let it be granted that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the characteristics previously stated; however, is its validity (*prāmāṇya*) ascertained intrinsically (*svataḥ*) or extrinsically (*parataḥ*)? It cannot be intrinsic, for since that [cognition] is self-cognized, it would apprehend itself merely as "cognition" (*jñāna*), but not as having the validity characterized by correctness (*samyaktva*). Moreover, mere "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) is common even to fallacious cognitions (*pramāṇābhāsa*).
Furthermore, if validity were intrinsic, it would follow that there would be no disagreement among anyone regarding it.

Nor [is validity established] from another [source]. For would that other [source] be accepted as a cognition whose object is the object of the former, or as one appearing as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), or as the perception of an object necessarily concomitant with the object of that [first cognition]? And since all of these, having their own validity unascertained, remain unsettled, how could they establish the initial impelling cognition? Or, if its validity were intrinsic (*svataḥ*), what fault would there be in the impelling cognition such that it too would not possess it? Furthermore, it has already been stated that validity is not known intrinsically; yet, fearing the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding extrinsic validity (*parataḥ*), he says:
"The means of valid cognition... (*pramāṇam*).
For that—

namely water and so forth— is the object (*gocara*) or domain of that first cognition; and that which is the object of the second cognition, whose object is that [first cognition], is fire and so forth, as well as smoke and so forth, which are invariably concomitant with it.
Regarding the initial operative cognition—[the Ḍeśika says]:
its validity is intrinsic;
the ascertainment of that validity is either intrinsic or extrinsic.

8. The Chapter on the Noble Ones (*Āryavarga*) 1. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will never find peace. 2. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will indeed find peace. 3. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will fall away from the good. 4. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will indeed attain the good. 5. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will go to a state of suffering. 6. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will go to a state of happiness. 7. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will be overcome by Māra. 8. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will transcend Māra. 9. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will be led away by others. 10. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will lead others. 11. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will be bound by the fetters. 12. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will be released from the fetters. 13. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will be subject to birth and death. 14. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will be free from birth and death. 15. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will wander in saṃsāra. 16. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will put an end to saṃsāra. 17. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will suffer in the hells. 18. "But one who has seen the noble ones, who associates with them, and who understands their Dharma, will not suffer in the hells. 19. "One who has not seen the noble ones, who does not associate with them, and who does not understand their Dharma, will be reborn in the animal realm. 20. The ascertainment of validity is in some cases intrinsic (*svataḥ*), as in the case of the cognition of one's own palm when one has reached a state of familiarity, or in a perceptual cognition where the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) appears, such as bathing, drinking, immersion, or the cessation of thirst. For in these instances, there is no desire for further examination on the part of discerning persons. To illustrate: there is the cognition of water; then, one afflicted by burning heat and thirst engages in activity toward it; then its attainment; then the acts of bathing, drinking, and so forth; and finally, the cessation of the burning heat and thirst. By this much alone, the knower achieves his goal; he does not further examine even the cognition of that cessation of burning heat and thirst. Thus, its validity is intrinsic.

In inference, however, in every instance, its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), because all suspicion of error has been entirely dispelled, owing to its arising from an infallible logical mark (*liṅga*). There is no cognition in the form of a mark without a mark, nor is there a mark without the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*); thus, for a cognition transformed by the apprehension of a mark, the determination of its validity is never extrinsic (*parataḥ*), as is the case with perception when it is in an unpracticed state.

For that [cognition] does not have its validity ascertained through another cognition that apprehends the same object and is non-deviant from it, nor through another cognition that manifests purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), nor through the perception of an object necessarily concomitant with it;
and since their validity is ascertained intrinsically (*svataḥ*), there is no room for the difficulty of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). (Ḍe edition: *tadekadeśaviṣaya-*)

In the case of other cognitions that corroborate the same object, [corroboration is required]; however, regarding verbal testimony (*śabda*) concerning perceptible objects, because it is difficult to ascertain the non-deviation from the object, the determination of its validity is dependent on corroboration and the like. But regarding imperceptible objects, having ascertained the validity of those statements that convey perceptible matters—such as eclipses, lost items, or stolen goods—through corroboration, one may then determine the validity even without further corroboration simply by virtue of being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). Thus, everything concerning sentences is logically consistent.
The Naiyāyikas maintain that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of the apprehension of an object.

In this regard, if being the "cause" of the apprehension of an object refers merely to being a general instrumental factor (*nimitta*), then that would be common to all causal factors (*kāraka*); consequently, it would follow that even the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and so forth, would be considered means of valid cognition.

If, on the other hand, by the word "cause" one intends the instrument (*karaṇa*) as distinct from the agent, the object, and the rest, then it is logical that this [cause] is cognition (*jñāna*) itself, and not the contact of the sense organs (*indriya-sannikarṣa*) and so forth. For that in whose presence the object becomes apprehended is the instrument for that apprehension.

Furthermore, that [valid cognition] does not occur when there is an absence of knowledge, even though the causal complex such as the contact of the sense-faculties is present; for it is held that the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and its fruit must be immediate. If that which has a mediated fruit were also considered an instrument, then even the eating of curd and the like would result in being [classified as] an instrument.
Therefore, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) does not belong to anything other than knowledge; elsewhere it is used figuratively.
Thus, the object is characterized by knowledge.

Regarding the statement, "The cause for the apprehension of that [object] is the apprehension of the object; the means (*sādhana*) for correct experience is *pramāṇa*" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3), although the inclusion of the term "means" (*sādhana*) here establishes that the instrument (*karaṇa*)— rather than the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)— is the *pramāṇa*, nevertheless, because it possesses the quality of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) due to its immediate connection with the result, cognition (*jñāna*) alone must be accepted as the *pramāṇa*.
The Buddhists maintain that "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge" (Pramāṇavārttika 2.1).
Even in that case, if the cognition is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), then it is not capable of producing conventional linguistic activity (*vyavahāra*).

And you maintain that this is the definition of conventional valid cognition (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*); how then is its validity established? If its validity is derived from a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising at a later time which is capable of producing practical activity (*vyavahāra*), then there is the fallacy of "borrowed ornaments" (*yācitakamaṇḍananyāya*). It would be better to simply accept the validity of the conceptual construction itself as the cause of practical activity; for in this way, the labor of an infinite regress (*paramparā-pariśrama*) is avoided.

If conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇya*), how could the conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) caused by it be non-erroneous? Furthermore, if one were to accept its correspondence (*saṃvāda*) by unifying the perceived object and the object of conceptual construction—just as in the case of the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia—then that correspondence would be merely figurative (*upacarita*).
Therefore, for one who desires the definition of a valid means of knowledge to be non-figurative non-erroneousness, ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) must be accepted as a valid means of knowledge.
"Avikalpaka" (non-conceptual) refers to that whose purpose is a conventional usage based on association;

Having stated the general definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and having examined it, the author, desiring to state the specific definitions, says the following for the purpose of demonstrating its classification, since it is impossible to state those [definitions] without first providing a classification:
Valid cognition is twofold (sūtra 9).

In the Sāmānyalakṣaṇa-sūtra, the mention of "valid cognition" was interrupted by the examination [of its nature], and thus it was not explicitly referred to there; rather, valid cognition was stated directly [in this sūtra].
It is of two kinds, of exactly two types, because the result of a division is to establish a limit.

By this, those who maintain views on fewer or more means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are refuted: the Cārvākas hold that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition; the Vaiśeṣikas hold that perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition; the Sāṅkhyas hold that it is those same three; the Naiyāyikas hold there are four, including comparison (*upamāna*); the Prābhākaras hold there are five, including presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); and the Bhāṭṭas hold there are six, including non-existence (*abhāva*).
This refutation will be explained later.

In that case, does the word "tat" [in the sūtra] imply a twofold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the same way as the Buddhists say: "The means of valid cognition are perception and inference"? (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.3)
"Is it as stated in Nyāyabindu 1.3, or otherwise? To this he says:
Perceptible and imperceptible.
— *parokṣaṃ ca paro* — Ḍe, Mu, Saṃmū.

The *akṣa* is the living soul (*jīva*), so called because it "eats" (*aśnute*) or "perceives" (*akṣṇoti*), that is, it pervades all substances, locations, times, and states; or it is the sense organ, so called because it "eats" its respective object. The prefix *prati* has the sense of "towards" or "reaching. That knowledge which is "towards the *akṣa*"—meaning dependent upon it—or which is "towards the *akṣas*" (the senses), meaning it arises by depending upon the senses, is *pratyakṣa*, whose definition will be stated hereafter.

It is called *parokṣa* because it exists beyond the senses (*akṣebhyaḥ parataḥ*) and because it is manifested by means of something other than the senses and so forth (*pareṇendriyādinā ucyate*). It is precisely that which will have its definition stated later;
the word "and" (*ca*) is intended to demonstrate that the two [perception and inference] possess equal force regarding their respective objects.
By this, the claim made by some—that perception is the eldest among all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is refuted.

If it is argued that perception is the eldest [of the means of knowledge] because the other means of knowledge are preceded by it, we say no; for even perception is observed to be preceded by another means of knowledge, since the perception of an object such as fire arises for one who has already acted after having understood that object through a logical mark (liṅga) or from the instruction of a reliable person (āpta).
[The sense organ is the instrument of perception—Tātparya.]
The materialists (Lokāyatikas) maintain that there is no means of valid cognition other than direct perception;
regarding this, he says:

The establishment of the distinction between valid and invalid means of cognition, the establishment of the cognition of another’s mind, and the negation of supersensible objects are all established through the exclusion of other [means] once one is established; these cannot be established without inference and the other means of valid cognition.

For the Cārvāka, having observed that some individual instances of cognition are non-deviant due to their correspondence and others are deviant due to their lack of correspondence, must necessarily establish the status of validity or invalidity for other such instances of cognition at a later time.

However, perception—which arises by the power of a present object and is devoid of reflection upon what precedes or follows it—is incapable of discerning the cause that establishes the validity or invalidity of those individual instances of cognition occurring at prior and subsequent times.
Furthermore, he is not capable of establishing the validity or invalidity of even those individual cognitions that are within the scope of his own experience for the sake of another person.

Therefore, one should resort to another means of knowledge included within the category of the "parokṣa" (indirect), namely inference (*anumāna*), which establishes the validity or invalidity of present individual cognitions by way of their similarity to previously observed individual cognitions and communicates this to another.
Moreover, one who attempts to communicate a matter that is not sought after would be neither a worldly person nor an investigator; he would be disregarded like a madman.

Furthermore, there is no apprehension of the mental states of others through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); and even if those states were understood by observing specific outward behaviors, the validity of indirect means of knowledge (*parokṣa*) would be established—even against one's will—for the one who denies it.
Moreover, the negation of the next world (*paraloka*) and such cannot be accomplished by direct perception alone, because its scope is restricted solely to that which is immediately present.

Furthermore, he does not rest in ease by failing to refute the existence of the next world and so forth, yet he does not accept other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, his position is like the whimpering of a child.

Moreover, since even perception possesses validity only because it is non-deviant from its object, why is that same non-deviation from the object not accepted for the indirect (*parokṣa*) [cognition] as well, which emerges through the medium of signs (*liṅga*) and words that are invariably connected to their objects? If it is argued that indirect cognition lacks validity because it is seen to be deviant, then perception would also follow as being invalid everywhere, since it is observed to be invalid due to defects such as cataracts (*timira*). Thus, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of invalidity in all cases.
If it is argued that this is a fallacy of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*), this applies equally to the other case as well, except for [your] partiality.
Dharmakīrti also said this—here [in the text]: ḍe.

The existence of other means of valid cognition [than perception] is established because the general character of both valid and non-valid cognitions is understood through another cognition, and because there is the negation of certain [other] things; furthermore,
even in the case of perception, its status as a means of valid cognition exists because it does not occur when the object is absent.
"—the two are equal in being the cause [of that effect], since their nature is dependent upon it.

(2) Thus, even though they accept the aforementioned number [of means of valid cognition], the Buddhists maintain that inference alone is the means for objects beyond the senses (*parokṣārtha*); this is incorrect, because verbal testimony (*śabda*) and other means are also valid cognitions, and it is impossible to subsume them within inference.
However, there is no fault in the inclusion of other means of valid cognition within a single all-encompassing means of valid cognition;

for just as sensory perception, mental perception, self-awareness, and yogic cognition are included under direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too are recollection, recognition, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony included under indirect perception (*parokṣa*), since their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not different.
Furthermore, the specific definitions of recollection and the others will be stated in their respective places.

Thus, it will be explained that comparison (*upamāna*), which is indirect, is included within recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is included within inference (*anumāna*).

As for that which is not even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no purpose whatsoever in its being either included or excluded [within other categories], just as in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*).
How is this [negation] invalid? We reply: because it lacks an object.
If one asks, "How so?"—it is because an entity consists of both existence and non-existence; therefore, negation lacks an object.

There is no entity that consists solely of existence (*bhāva*), because that would entail the consequence of the universe being of a single uniform nature; nor is there one that consists solely of non-existence (*abhāva*), because that would entail the consequence of it being formless. Rather, an entity consists of both existence and non-existence, because it exists by its own nature and does not exist by the nature of another, and because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function in exactly that way. To illustrate: perception (*pratyakṣa*), for instance, determines an object through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—such as "this is indeed the ground, it is not a jar"—and thereby excludes any further object consisting solely of non-existence. Thus, relying upon what object could there be a means of valid cognition characterized as "non-existence"?

Thus, even indirect means of valid cognition (*parokṣapramāṇa*) are indeed inclined toward grasping objects in the form of both existence and non-existence; otherwise, the apprehension of their respective unmixed objects would be impossible. As it has been said: "For this very determination that 'it is this' which occurs regarding an existent thing does not occur without being followed by the cognition of the non-existence of other things" (*Ślokavārttika*, *Abhāva* chapter).
Thus,
the jar and so forth do not exist— Ḍe.

"For this very thing is what constitutes the determination regarding an entity; it does not occur without being followed by the cognition of the absence of other things. (Ślokavārttika, Abhāva, verse 15). Now, let it be that an object has the nature of both existence and non-existence; what is lost for us? For we too have established exactly that.

Since only the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) falls within the scope of the means of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*) because it is in contact with the sense faculties, whereas the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) is not so, it falls within the scope of the means of non-perception (*abhāvapramāṇa*); how then could it be without an object? As it has been said: "This cognition that 'it does not exist' is certainly not produced by the sense faculty; for the sense faculty is capable of contact only with the positive aspect.
Having apprehended the existence of the object and having recollected its counter-positive,
a mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the senses.
As stated in the *Ślokavārttika*, Abhāvapariccheda, verses 18 and 27:
"First of all, this cognition that 'it does not exist' is not produced by the sense faculty."

For the sense organ possesses the capacity for conjunction only with an existing entity. Having apprehended the presence of the object and having remembered the counter-positive, the mental cognition of non-existence arises without dependence on the senses. (Ślokavārttika, Abhāvapariccheda, verses 18 and 27)

Now, if the aspect of non-existence is not distinct from the aspect of existence, how can it be that perception does not apprehend it? Or, if they are distinct, since the ground is perceived by perception as being devoid of the absence of a jar and so forth, it follows that the jar and so forth are themselves apprehended, because the non-apprehension of their absence is inseparable from the apprehension of their presence. Furthermore, even the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), which operates subsequently, would not be capable of displacing them [the jars]. Otherwise, because one would be apprehending a mixture where there is no mixture, perception would be erroneous. [End of Ḍe manuscript]
And there is also the apprehension of non-existence—
otherwise, it would be a mere conceptual construct (saṅkīrṇa)— for this [non-existence] is insubstantial because it consists in the cessation of the five means of valid cognition.
Therefore, how could that which is of the nature of non-cognition (*ajñāna*) be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Consequently, since the aspect of existence (*bhāvāṃśa*), which is in some way non-different from the aspect of non-existence (*abhāvāṃśa*), is determined by a means of valid cognition such as perception, the aspect of non-existence is indeed apprehended. Thus, because there is no object distinct from that [apprehended existence], non-existence is without an object;
and so it is established that it is not a means of valid cognition.
12—Because of the absence of [any other] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is [the word of the Buddha]. Tā. [notes: *dinābhāvāṃ* is corrected to *dinābhāvāt*].
Division—
having stated the division, he states the definition of the particular: "The clear [cognition] is perception."

Since the specific definition is prescribed by way of restating the general definition, "the determination of the true object" (samyagarthanirṇayaḥ) is the restatement of the general definition of valid cognition (pramāṇa), while "distinct" (viśadaḥ) is the specific definition prescribed for well-known perception (pratyakṣa);
and thus, perception is the subject (dharmin).
The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "consisting of a clear and correct determination of an object" (*viśadasamyagarthanirṇayātmaka*);
the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is direct perception" (*pratyakṣatvāt*).
That which does not consist of a clear and correct determination of an object is not direct perception, as for example, the indirect (*parokṣa*); this is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

If it is argued that there is the fault of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*) when the subject (*dharmin*) itself is the reason (*hetu*), we say no; for while the specific subject is the locus, the generality of the subject (*dharmisāmānya*) serves as the reason, and since that generality is grounded in the particular, concomitance with the particulars is possible.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that the capacity to produce knowledge arises from the power of exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*), even in the absence of presence in similar instances (*sapakṣavṛtti*).
Now, what is this so-called "clarity" (*vaiśadya*)? If it is the apprehension of its own object, then that is unimpaired even in the case of indirect cognition (*parokṣa*).
Now, as for clarity (*sphuṭatva*): suspecting that this too is common to all cognitions because they are self-cognized (*svasaṃviditatva*), he says:

[from the *Uṇādi* list] "from the roots *dukṣu*, *ru*, *kuṃk* in the sense of 'sound'—[the suffix] *gaṇa*"; and according to *Uṇādi* rule II.26, 27, 28: "after *sthā* and *kṣu*, with the augment *ū*, [the suffix] *ṇa*" (185), we have *kṣūṇam*, meaning "an offense."
Clarity (*vaiśadya*) is either the manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantayā*) independent of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*),

or it is the independence from that which is other than the present means of valid cognition— namely, cognitions based on words, logical marks (*liṅga*), and so forth; such independence constitutes clarity.

Perception does not, like verbal testimony or inference, depend upon another means of knowledge—such as the cognition of a word or a logical mark—for its own production; this is one definition of clarity (*vaiśadya*).

Furthermore, there is another definition: "manifestation as 'this-ness' (*idantayā*). Manifestation as "this-ness," that is, manifestation directed toward a specific particular (*viśeṣa*), which constitutes the correct determination of an object, is also clarity.
The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to indicate that this is an alternative definition.
Śabdānu°—Ḍe.

Now, keeping in mind the twofold division of perception (pratyakṣa) based on the distinction between the primary (mukhya) and the conventional (sāṃvyavahārika), he states the definition of the primary [perception]:
When all obscurations have dissolved in every way, the manifestation of the true nature of consciousness is the primary state of "aloneness" (*kevala*);
the word "that" (*tat*) is used for the purpose of referring back to what has been directly perceived, otherwise it would be connected immediately with the preceding term "clarity" (*vaiśadya*).

When the destructive karmas (*ghātikarmans*), such as the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and others, have been entirely destroyed through the power of meditation characterized by one-pointedness (*ekatvavitarka*) and non-discursive reflection (*avicāra*)—which is the culmination of the excellence attained by practicing with reverence toward the Three Jewels for a long time and without interruption—then there occurs the manifestation of the very nature of the self, which is of the essence of consciousness (meaning, of the essence of light), simply by the removal of its veils. This manifested nature is the primary, principal, and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of all cognitions, just as the face is [the primary part] of the body.
And that [perception] is well known in the scriptures as "pure" (*kevala*) because it is devoid of assistance from the senses and so forth, because its object is everything, and because it is unique;
this is the supreme degree of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Regarding the [karmas] such as knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya) and so forth—if it be asked how the self’s nature of luminosity (*prakāśasvabhāvatā*) is established, we reply as follows: the self has the nature of luminosity because its nature is non-doubtful (*asaṃdigdhasvabhāvatva*). Whatever does not have the nature of luminosity is not of a non-doubtful nature, just like a jar; yet the self is not like that. Indeed, no one doubts, "Am I or am I not?"—thus the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Likewise, the self has the nature of luminosity because it is a knower (*boddhṛtva*). Whatever does not have the nature of luminosity is not a knower, just like a jar; and the self is certainly not a non-knower.

Likewise, that which is the agent of a particular action is not the object of that action; for example, Caitra, who is the agent of the action of going, is not its object; and the self is the agent of the action of cognition.

Now, if the self (*ātman*) has luminosity as its intrinsic nature (*prakāśasvabhāvatva*), how can there be obscuration? Or, if there were obscuration, would it not follow that there is perpetual obscuration? It is not so; for even though its nature is luminous, obscuration is possible through the veiling karmas (*jñānāvaraṇīya-karman*) and so forth, just as the moon, the sun, and other such bodies are obscured by dust, mist, and masses of clouds. And just as with the moon and sun, their dissolution occurs through means such as meditation and contemplation (*dhyāna-bhāvanā*), which are like powerful winds. (As in the case of the moon and others—[the commentary reads] "like powerful winds"—Tā.)
Regarding the phrase "and of dissolution":

[the opponent objects,] "Surely, if [the obscuration] were beginningless, its dissolution could not occur through a means; it is not so, for even the impurity of gold, though beginningless, is observed to dissolve through alkaline treatment, clay, heating in a crucible, and so forth. In the same way, the dissolution of even beginningless karma—such as that which obscures knowledge—is logically possible through the practice of the Three Jewels, which serve as its antidote.

Nor should it be asked how there can be an obscuration of the formless Self; for we observe the obscuration of the power of consciousness, though it is formless, by intoxicants, aphrodisiacs, *kodrava* grain, and the like."
Now, would the self undergo modification through the veiling factors and their opposites, or not?
And what follows from this?
Does rain and sun affect the sky, or do they produce their effects upon the skin?

If it is argued that "if [the self] were like a hide, it would be impermanent; if it were like space, it would yield no fruit," we say: no. For this objection applies only to the position of absolute, unchanging permanence (*kūṭasthanityatā*). We maintain, however, that the self is *pariṇāminitya* (changeably eternal), because its nature consists in a persistence accompanied by the arising and ceasing of successive states (*paryāya*). This is because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is entirely absent in the positions of absolute permanence or momentariness, as it has been said: "Causal efficiency is not possible in the positions of absolute permanence or momentariness, since it is considered the defining characteristic of entities through either succession or simultaneity."
Laghīyastrayālaṃkāra 2.1,
thus [ends section] 15.
What effect do rain and sun have upon the sky? Their fruit is found in leather.
If the Self were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like the sky, it would be devoid of fruit—[the form that persists through both states].

Causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is not possible for either the eternal or the momentary positions, since it is considered the defining characteristic of entities by virtue of occurring either successively or simultaneously. (Laghīyastraya 2.1) Now, the determination of the objects of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for establishing either primary perception or that which possesses it;
for perception, whose operation is restricted to objects such as form and so forth, is not capable of engaging with an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

Nor is there inference, because its nature consists in being produced by the force of a relationship between a mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) that has been perceived through perception.

If scripture is established as being preceded by supersensuous knowledge, then that [knowledge] is its proof; this results in a circular argument, for it cannot be established without that scripture, nor can that scripture exist without it—
Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, Verse 142.
But there exists no non-human (apauruṣeya) means of proving that [Veda]; for it is said:
"He indeed is without hands or feet, yet He is the grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears;
He knows the universe, for there is no knower of Him; they call Him the foremost, the Great Person."

Anticipating the objection that a certain passage such as *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* 3.19 is merely an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) and not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since validity is admitted only for injunctions (*vidhi*) and there is no occasion here for other means of knowledge, he says:
The support produced by the power [arising] from the differentiation of objects—Tā. edition; *viṣayavinirbheda-balopajanita-dharaṇa-āśrayam*—Ḍe. and Mu. editions.
It cannot be established through that scripture, nor is there scripture without it. (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, verse 142):
"For he has neither hands nor feet, yet he is a grasper; he sees without eyes and hears without ears.
(The reading *apādau hyama* is found in the Tātparyaṭīkā.)
In this context, "the swift one" (*javana*) alone is correct, because that very term has been explained by Śaṅkara:
"He knows the universe, for there is no knower of him; they call him the foremost, the great Puruṣa. (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.19). [The word *vedyam* appears in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad.]
The establishment of that [omniscience] follows from the establishment of the ultimate limit of excellence in wisdom and so forth.

(16) The excellence of wisdom—the gradation of its degrees—must rest upon some point, because it is an excellence, like the excellence of magnitude; by means of this inference, the establishment of unsurpassed wisdom results in the establishment of that absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*), since the establishment of absolute knowledge consists in the establishment of that [unsurpassed wisdom].

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [it is meant that] subtle, concealed, and distant objects are perceptible to someone, because they are objects of knowledge (*prameya*), like a jar; and their existence is established by the fact that otherwise the non-contradiction of astrological knowledge would be inexplicable. As it has been said: "If there were no cognition of an object that is entirely beyond the senses for men, then from where could the non-contradiction of astrological knowledge come? If it comes from scripture, then there must be another means of proof. (Siddhiviniścaya, p. 413A)

Moreover— "For it is verbal testimony (*codanā*) alone that makes known an object that is past, present, future, subtle, concealed, remote, or of such a kind; no other sense organ does so"— Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.2.

By saying this, it is clearly intended that some person must possess complete knowledge of the past and other objects; otherwise, for whom would the Veda communicate an object pertaining to the three periods of time?

For in communicating it, the Veda accepts as its qualified recipient only one who knows the reality of the three periods of time. Thus he says: "To whom would the Veda communicate the reality of the three periods of time, if man were not likewise [endowed with it], being exclusively and eternally shrouded by an imperishable veil?"

*Siddhiviniścaya*, folio 414A: Thus, because the communication of objects pertaining to the three times would otherwise be impossible, there is established the existence of supersensuous, exclusive knowledge (*kevalajñāna*). To whom could the Veda communicate reality that pertains to the three times, if it does not know it as such due to the absolute presence of imperishable obstructions? *Siddhiviniścaya*, folio 414A.

Furthermore, it is scripture alone—possessing corroboration established through perception and inference—that serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of one who perceives supersensuous objects.

For that very subject matter of scripture, namely *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects), is also the subject matter of perception and the other means of knowledge; thus there is corroboration. To illustrate: everything exists in its own nature (*svarūpa*) and does not exist in the nature of others (*pararūpa*).
Otherwise, either everything would exist [absolutely] or even its own nature would be impossible.

Thus, by this method, the scripture, while establishing the doctrine of manifold aspects (*syādvāda*) as proven by valid means of knowledge, also establishes the omniscience of the Arhat; as it is said: "By the power of whose right faith we perceive the state of the Supreme Self in those such as you—salutations to that teaching of yours which destroys the bonds of evil latent impressions" (Ayogavyavacchedikā 21).

Although perception, being sensory in nature, does not have supersensory knowledge as its object, nevertheless, the yogic perception born from the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is indeed the knower of both external objects and itself; thus, its existence is established even through direct perception.
Everything exists by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*) and does not exist by way of another's nature (*pararūpa*);
otherwise, there would be either the existence of everything or the impossibility of even one's own nature.
By the power of whose right conviction we recognize the state of the Supreme Self in those such as you—
homage be to that teaching of yours for the destruction of the noose of evil tendencies. (Ayogavyavacchedikā 21)
— *janmakayogi*— Ḍe., Mu.

Now, regarding omniscience: since it is stated that "for the Lord of the World, non-obstructed knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and dharma—this fourfold set are co-existent from the beginning," let such omniscience belong to [deities] like Īśvara; however, for any human being, even one possessed of learning and conduct, it is impossible. As Kumārila says: "Moreover, because they have the Vedas as their bodies, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara..."

"Let them be omniscient at will; what does omniscience matter to a human? (Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 3208). Ah! You sinner who denies omniscience, you wicked speaker! Do you insult the God of Gods under the pretext of a figurative statement disparaging humanity?

Indeed, those who—having accumulated a mass of merit through previous births and having experienced incomparable happiness in celestial existences—desiring to uplift the entire world of living beings submerged in the mire of suffering, descended to the human world; who, even while in the hells, were like showers of nectar providing a momentary seat of happiness; whose birth-festivals were celebrated by the hosts of all the lords of gods whose thrones shook simultaneously at the moment of their birth; who were served by throngs of gods acting as their servants in a spirit of competitive devotion; who, casting away like a blade of grass the immense glory of sovereignty that came to them of its own accord; who behaved with equal indifference toward grass, jewels, enemies, and friends; who, by their own power, quelled calamities such as epidemics afflicting the world; who, having burnt away their destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*) with the fire of pure meditation (*śukla-dhyāna*), manifested the power of *kevala-jñāna* which illuminates the nature of all existence and non-existence and shatters the spread of delusion over the entire world of living beings; who, occupying the site of the *samavasaraṇa* constructed by gods and demons, established the ford of Dharma through speech transformed into every individual language; who, after enjoying the fortune of being a Lord of the Tirtha endowed with the thirty-four excellences, attained the Supreme Brahman—the eternal bliss consisting of liberation from all karma—it is they whom you seek to disparage by teaching common attributes such as "humanity," just as one might attempt to equate Mount Sumeru with a clod of earth by classifying both as "earthly"!

Furthermore, what sovereignty over all knowledge can there be for those such as Brahmā and others, whose conduct is spoiled by incessant dalliance with the limbs of women, who bear a multitude of various weapons, whose mental restraint depends upon rosaries and the like, and who are defiled by passion, hatred, and delusion? As we stated in our hymn: "The affliction of sovereignty over others is in vain for the gods, who are forcibly conquered by intoxication, pride, the god of love, anger, greed, and arrogance.
(25) Thus ends the section on non-connection.

Moreover, if Brahmā and the others are free from the impurities of defects such as passion and possess forms consisting of eternal knowledge and bliss, then we do not dispute with such beings; for we have said: "At whatever time, in whatever manner, and whoever you may be—by whatever name—you who are free from the stain of defects, if you are that one Lord, O Blessed One, salutations be to You. (Ayoga-31)
Only the falsity of those accounts found in the Śruti, Smṛti, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas concerning deities such as Brahmā and others would be established;
thus, the attainment of knowledge of supersensible objects has been explained through these means of valid cognition for the sake of practitioners.
For that Lord of the World, there is unimpeded knowledge and dispassion,
as well as unobstructed sovereignty and righteousness— this fourfold set is innate to him.

Furthermore, even if Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—on account of having the Veda as their body—should indeed be omniscient, what [omniscience] is there for a human being? (Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 3208). Excessive rain, drought, rats, locusts, parrots, one's own army, and the enemy's army—these seven are known as calamities (*īti*).
—mu— Ṭīkā:
Death (maraṇa) is pestilence (mārī);
these are the [eight] extraordinary qualities (atiśaya). And their bodies possess a form and fragrance arising from them that is free from disease and devoid of even a drop of sweat.
The breath has the fragrance of a lotus, and the blood and flesh are white like a stream of cow's milk and free from any foul odor;
the manner of eating and excreting is invisible— these four extraordinary qualities arise simultaneously.

In a field even the size of a single *yojana*, there is the presence of millions upon millions of humans, gods, and animals; his speech conforms to the languages of the human, animal, and divine worlds, and it reaches a distance of one *yojana*.
And upon the back of his crown is a beautiful halo, its splendor rivaling the orb of the sun;
and within two hundred yojanas from its tip, there are no afflictions, hostilities, plagues, excessive rain, or drought.
Famine and fear from foreign armies or one's own subjects may occur; these eleven are born from the destruction of karma.
In the sky appear the Wheel of Dharma, yak-tail whisks, a footstool, and a radiant lion throne.
The three parasols, the jewel-encrusted banner, and the golden lotuses at his footfalls;
the triple rampart, the beautiful four-facedness, the sacred tree at the shrine, and the thorns with their heads turned downward.
The trees resounded with the deep boom of kettledrums, the wind blew favorably, and birds circled to the right;
there was a rain of scented water and a shower of flowers of many colors, while the hair, beards, and nails did not grow.
Even from the lowest state, ten million classes of immortals [reside] at his side;
these are the seasons and the objects of the senses, which are favorable to him.
Nineteen divine [verses] and thirty-four combined make fifty-three.
(Abhidhāna 1.8)

Furthermore, their bodies emit a fragrance of form and scent that is free from disease; their breath is devoid of drops of sweat and possesses the aroma of a lotus; and their blood and flesh are as white as a stream of cow’s milk and are indeed free from any foul odor.
The manner of taking food and excreting waste, invisibility—these four excellences arise simultaneously;

even while remaining within a single *yojana* of the field, there is the capacity to produce millions upon millions of humans, gods, and animals. His speech is intelligible in the languages of humans, animals, and the world of gods, and it reaches a distance of one *yojana*.
And upon the back of his crown, there is a beautiful halo (bhāmaṇḍala) that mimics the splendor of the sun’s orb.

Within two hundred and fifty *gavyūtis*, there shall be no disease, hostility, calamities, pestilence, excessive rain, drought, famine, or fear from foreign or domestic armies; these eleven [misfortunes] do not arise from the destruction of karma.
In the sky appear the Wheel of Dharma, yak-tail whisks, a lion throne together with its footstool,
three radiant parasols, a banner made of jewels, and golden lotuses at every step.
There is a beautiful triple-rampart, the presence of four faces, a sacred tree (caityadruma), and thorns with their points turned downward.
The sound of drums and kettledrums resounded loudly; the wind blew favorably; birds circled to the right;

there was a rain of fragrant water and a shower of many-colored flowers; and the hair on his head, beard, and nails did not grow, even as millions of hosts of gods from the four classes remained close at hand.
The favorability of the seasons and the objects of the senses—these nineteen, together with the thirty-four divine [qualities], amount to fifty-three when combined. (Abhidhāna 1.56–63; Mu-Ṭīkā:
by means of intoxication, pride, passion, anger, greed, and arrogance...)
O noble one, for the gods who have been utterly defeated by greed, the illness of sovereignty over others is truly in vain.
At whatever time and in whatever manner, whoever you are, you remain that very person, regardless of whatever name you may bear.
O Blessed One, if you alone are free from the impurity of defects, then homage be to you! (Yogabindu 31) And because there is no sublater [of this].
The phrase "its establishment [is proven] like pleasure and so forth, because there is no well-ascertained sublation" is to be connected [to the argument].
To explain: whatever might serve as a sublation of omniscience (kevalajñāna) must be either perception (pratyakṣa) or another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).

It cannot be perception first of all, because that is restricted to affirmation alone—[for] it is only that which is connected [with the senses] and present that is grasped by the eye and other [senses].
Because he himself has stated [this] in *Ślokavārttika* 4.84, it is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇopapanna*).

That which is connected and present is apprehended by the eye and other [senses] (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 4, verse 84). Now, if it is argued that perception is not the sublater [of the non-existent] while it is operating, but rather when it has ceased; then, if it is a sublater by virtue of having a specific place and time as its object, we agree. But if it is by virtue of having all places and times as its object, then that is not possible without the direct perception of all places, times, and assemblies of persons; thus, our desired conclusion is established.

Furthermore, neither Jaimini nor anyone else can possibly be a direct perceiver of all places and so forth, because they possess a nature of being a sentient being (*sattva*) and a person (*puruṣa*), just like an ordinary man on the street. If it is argued that, because wisdom possesses degrees of excellence, its ultimate perfection is also inferred [to exist], then why is a seer of all objects not likewise inferred from that very same [fact]? Moreover, if you do not accept non-perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding your own position, how could you rely upon it as a means of valid cognition for the non-existence of an omniscient being? There is no distinction between the two cases.
If, while turning back,
there is the direct realization— O Maheśvara.

Nor is it possible for inference to subvert that [omniscience], because inference does not function without the apprehension of a subject (*dharmin*), and if the subject is apprehended, inference simply fails to arise since it is subverted by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it. Now, if you claim that the following inference is what subverts it—"The person under dispute is not omniscient, because he is a speaker, or because he is a human being, like a man on the street"—that is incorrect. For if the reason (*hetu*) is "being a speaker of objects perceived through valid cognition," then it is contradictory (*viruddha*), because such a capacity for speech exists only in one who is omniscient.

If, on the other hand, the reason is "the state of being a speaker of unreal objects," then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because those who speak of objects contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are accepted as non-omniscient.

However, mere "speakership" (*vaktṛtva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the heterologue (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful; for one does not observe a decrease in speakership as knowledge increases, but rather observes that excellence in speakership belongs precisely to one who possesses excellence in knowledge.
By this, "humanity" (*puruṣatva*) is also refuted.
If "humanity" (puruṣatva) is not tainted by passion and the like, then it is contradictory, because humanity endowed with qualities such as knowledge and dispassion is impossible without omniscience.
If, however, humanity is tainted by passion and the like, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
But humanity in its general sense has a doubtful exclusion from the counter-example (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika), and thus it is not a subverting proof.

Nor can scripture be a subverter of that [omniscience], because such scripture—being non-human (apauruṣeya)—is impossible; or, even if it were possible, since no such subverting scripture is observed, how could a scripture originating from an omniscient being itself be its subverter? Enough of this excessive digression.
*Upajñā* means initial knowledge—Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 6.9;
Commentary: Not only is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) primary, but there is also another kind; thus he says:

Regarding the degrees of that [knowledge], the two sūtras— the eighteenth and the nineteenth— beginning with "the mind-reading [knowledge] and the [omniscient knowledge] are the limits" (tattāratamye'vadhimanaḥparyāyau ca), are seen written as a single sūtra without the mark of separation in the Tā-mū manuscript.

When all obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) have dissolved entirely, there is absolute [perception]. Regarding the gradation of that dissolution of obscurations—that is, the specific degrees of the subsidence and destruction of obscurations (*āvaraṇakṣayopaśama*)—there arise, caused by those [degrees], *avadhi* (limited perception) and *avadhijñāna* (limited knowledge), as well as *manaḥparyāya* (mind-reading) and *manaḥparyāyajñāna* (knowledge of the modes of mind).
