These are primary forms of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) independent of the sense organs. In this context, it is called *avadhi* because "it is delimited" (*avadhīyate*). This delimitation (*maryādā*) concerns material objects, according to the scriptural statement: "The domain of *avadhi* consists of material substances" (*tattvārtha-sūtra* 1.28). Furthermore, the knowledge characterized by *avadhi* is also termed *avadhi*.

That [movement] is twofold: conditioned by existence (*bhava-pratyaya*) and conditioned by qualities (*guṇa-pratyaya*). Among these, the former is the movement through the sky of gods and hell-beings, like that of birds; the latter is the movement of humans and animals.

The modes (*paryāya*) of the mind (*manas*), which is of the nature of a substance, are specific transformations corresponding to thought; knowledge having those [modes] as its object is "knowledge of mental modes" (*manaḥparyāya*). However, the knowledge of external objects being thought about—which exists because such mental modes would otherwise be inexplicable—is purely inferential and is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of mental modes. As they say: "One knows the external by means of inference" (*Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, Gāthā 814). Thus [ends the section]. 18.

Now, since both [clairvoyance] and mental perception have material substances as their object and are produced by the subsidence-cum-destruction of karmic matter, one might ask: what is the distinction between them? To this he says:
"Their difference arises from the distinctions of purity, field, owner, and object.

Even though there is some degree of similarity between them, there is a distinction between limited knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*) and mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyāya-jñāna*) due to differences such as purity;

therein, mind-reading knowledge is purer than limited knowledge. For those mental substances that a possessor of limited knowledge knows, a possessor of mind-reading knowledge knows to be even more pure.

There is also a distinction between these two based on their field (*kṣetra*): avadhi-knowledge occurs within a range starting from an incalculable fraction of an *aṅgula* up to the entire world, whereas manaḥparyāya-knowledge occurs only within the human realm (*manuṣyakṣetra*). There is also a distinction based on their possessor (*svāmikṛta*): avadhi-knowledge occurs in those who are restrained (*saṃyata*), unrestrained (*asaṃyata*), and partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*) across all states of existence (*gati*); manaḥparyāya-knowledge, however, occurs only in a restrained human being of superior conduct (*prakṛṣṭacāritra*) during the spiritual stages (*guṇasthānaka*) beginning with the "negligent" (*pramatta*) and ending with the "extinguished passions" (*kṣīṇakaṣāya*).
Even there, it belongs to one whose transformation is increasing, and not to another; and even among those who have attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), it belongs to some, but not to all.

And regarding that which is determined by its object: the restriction of the object for *avadhi* (clairvoyance) is to all modes (*paryāya*) of substances possessing form (*rūpavat*), whereas for *manaḥparyāya* (telepathy), it is to an infinite fraction of those;
thus concludes the primary direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Regarding the definition of the mind,
he now describes the conventional [perception]:
that which is caused by the sense organs and the mind, consisting of avagraha (apprehension), īhā (speculation), avāya (perceptual judgment), and dhāraṇā (retention), is conventional perception.

The twenty faculties, beginning with the sense of touch, whose definitions will be stated later, and the mind (*manas*) which is their cause or instrument— this is the qualification of "correct determination of the object" (*samyagarthanirṇaya*), because it follows the general definition; thus, correct determination of the object has the faculties and the mind as its cause.
Having stated the cause, he describes its essential nature: "Consisting of apprehension (avagraha), speculation (īhā), perceptual judgment (avāya), and retention (dhāraṇā).
Apprehension and the others have their definitions to be stated later; that which has these as its essence is "consisting of apprehension, speculation, perceptual judgment, and retention.

The inclusion of the term "essence" (ātman) is for the purpose of demonstrating that although apprehension and the others arise in a sequence, there is no absolute difference between them, but rather they constitute a single entity because each preceding stage transforms into the form of each succeeding one.

Correct worldly activity consisting of engagement and withdrawal is "conventional" (*saṃvyavahāra*); that which has this as its purpose is "conventional" (*sāṃvyavahārika*) perception. It should be understood that the status of being caused by the sense organs and the mind applies both collectively and individually: that which arises through the predominance of the sense organs and the support of the mind is "sense-born" (*indriyajam*).
Since it arises from the mind itself while depending upon purity, it is indeed caused by the mind (*manonimitta*).

One might ask: "Is there not another kind of perception in the form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), so why is it not mentioned? This need not be said; for the self-awareness of sense-born cognition is included within sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*); the awareness of pleasure and so forth not born of the senses is included within mental perception (*manaḥ-pratyakṣa*); and the self-awareness of yogic perception is included within yogic perception. Furthermore, since the self-awareness of memory and other such states is purely mental, there is no other distinct perception called "self-awareness"; thus, it is not mentioned separately.
Sensory cognition— [omitted]—
the self-cognition of pleasure and so forth— [omitted].
It has been stated separately—

[in the Ḍeśika-mukha] it is said "the senses"— thus he defines the senses: the senses, which are the skin, tongue, nose, eyes, and ears, are characterized by the apprehension of touch, taste, smell, form, and sound, and they are divided into the categories of substantial (dravya) and existential (bhāva).
The two sūtras ending with "twenty-one faculties" and ending with "divisions" are seen together in the Saṃmūrchita manuscript.

Those whose characteristics are the apprehension of touch and so forth are, respectively, the sense-faculties such as the tactile; for instance, the perception of touch and so forth is preceded by an instrument because it is an action, like the act of cutting.
In this context, the sense organs (*indriya*) are so called because they were created by the action (*karman*) of Indra;

that is, they are either signs of the self (*ātman*), Indra, due to being caused by the emergence of name-karma (*nāma-karman*), or else the sense organs are the instruments for the perception of objects by the self, which—being defiled by karma—is itself incapable of perceiving objects.
[Objection: If that is the case, then the self’s cognition of objects arising from the sense organs as its sign would be inferential (*ānumānika*).
And likewise, if the indicative mark (*liṅga*) were not cognized, inference would not arise;

yet if that [mark] were cognized through inference, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is not so; for since the functional sense-organ (*bhāvendriya*) is self-cognized (*svasaṃvidita*), there is no room for an infinite regress.

Alternatively, the "senses" (*indriya*) are the marks of the "Indra," which is the Self (*ātman*), because they lead to the cognition of the Self; or else, because it is observed that an instrument—such as an axe and the like—is presided over by an agent.
And these are distinguished by way of substance (*dravya*) and state (*bhāva*);

therein, the substantial sense organs (*dravyendriya*) have as their cause the rising (*udaya*) of name-karma (*nāmakarma*), whereas the functional sense organs (*bhāvendriya*) have as their cause the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the obscuration of those [senses] and of energy-obscuring karma (*vīryāntarāya*).
This very set of five aphorisms [is as follows]: "The sense organ of touch has the characteristic of grasping touch; the sense organ of taste has the characteristic of grasping taste," and so forth.

The tactile sense (*sparśana*) is mentioned first because it exists in all transmigrating beings and because it pervades the body; thereafter, the gustatory, olfactory, visual, and auditory senses are mentioned in sequence because they each have progressively fewer living beings as their objects.

Among these, the tactile sense arises from the destruction-cum-subsidence (*kṣayopaśama*) of its specific obscuration in earth, water, fire, air, and plants—those immobile (*sthāvara*) living beings who possess the obscuration of the remaining senses.
Regarding them, it is said: "Earth is declared to possess consciousness" (Daśavaikālika Sūtra 4.1).

The proof [of this] comes from such authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) as well as from inference (*anumāna*): "Knowledge reaches its ultimate minimum in some self, because its specific qualities are subject to diminution, like dimension (*parimāṇa*). That wherein that diminution reaches its limit consists of immobile beings with a single sense-organ.
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a diminution of knowledge even in the absence of the tactile sense-organ, as in the case of ashes and the like."

For in that case, there is simply an absence of knowledge, not merely its diminution. Therefore, just as measurement—starting from the magnitude of space and having its specific qualities diminished until it reaches the ultimate minimum in an atom—is so too is knowledge; starting from omniscience (*kevalajñāna*), its specific qualities are diminished until it is utterly diminished in one-sensed beings.
Furthermore, the establishment of the individual living nature (*jīvatva*) of earth and the other elements will be explained later.
As for the two senses of touch and taste, they are found in mobile beings such as worms, *apādikās*, *nūpurakas*, earthworms, conchs, mother-of-pearl oysters, *śambūkās*, leeches, and so forth.

The sense organs of touch, taste, and smell belong to [creatures such as] ants, termites, earthworms, kunthu-insects, tubaraka-insects, cucumber-seeds, cotton-seeds, centipedes, ayenaka-insects, grass-leaves, wood-carriers, and so forth;
the sense organs of touch, taste, smell, and sight belong to bees, wasps, honey-bees, flies, small insects, gadflies, mosquitoes, scorpions, nandyāvarta-insects, moths, butterflies, and so forth;
these, together with the sense of hearing, belong to fish, snakes, serpents, birds, quadrupeds born of animal wombs, and to all hell-beings, humans, and gods.
Rohiṇikā-apecikā—Ḍe;
tubarakā—Tā;
tumburaka—Mu.
Tripuṣa—ḍe;
bījaka-karpāsa—tā;
vaṭhara—ḍe.
[Commentary on] *pustitrikā*: [The variant reading is] *pustikā*.

Now, the Sāṅkhyas maintain that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals—characterized by speaking, grasping, walking, excretion, and sexual pleasure—are also sense organs (*indriya*). Therefore, how can there be only five sense organs? No; for here, only those which are causes of specific types of cognition (*jñāna-viśeṣa*) are intended as sense organs. If one were to conceive of them as sense organs merely because they are the instrumental causes of specific types of activity (*ceṣṭā-viśeṣa*), it would follow that there is an infinite number of sense organs, since specific activities are infinite. Therefore, based on the enumeration of the individual instances, there are only five sense organs.

The causes are indeed the sense-faculties; and between them there may be non-difference from the perspective of substantiality (*dravyārthādeśāt*), but there may be difference from the perspective of modalities (*paryāyārthādeśāt*). For if there were the absolute position of non-difference, it would follow that taste and other objects would be perceived by the sense of touch, just as touch is.

Furthermore, the postulation of additional sense-faculties would be redundant; moreover, if one faculty were either complete or defective, it would follow that all others would likewise be complete or defective.

Even under the doctrine of absolute difference (*bhedakānta*), it follows that they could not collectively produce a single cognition in one place, just like the sense-faculties belonging to different mental continua (*santāna*).
If it is argued that the mind (*manas*) is their producer, we say no; for the mind, when independent of the sense-faculties, lacks the capacity to produce such a cognition.

If it is argued that the mind (*manas*) is the producer of mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) in dependence upon the sense-faculties (*indriya*), then it must be asked: why does [the mind] not produce [synthesis] in dependence upon the sense-faculties belonging to another continuum (*santānāntara*)? If it is replied that this is because of a lack of proximity (*pratyāsatti*), then one must ask: what constitutes proximity here, other than identity with the same substance (*ekadravyatādātmya*)? Furthermore, any other kind of proximity is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
By this, the absolute positions of difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*) between those [faculties] and the self (*ātman*) are refuted.

If there were an absolute non-difference between the self and the instruments, it would follow that the self is the instrument, or that the instruments are the agent, or that both possess the nature of both, because there would be no distinction between them. Alternatively, if there were an absolute difference between them, the self would lack the status of an instrument, or the opposite would occur—just as with the instruments of another continuum. Since this is established by experience and there is no subverting evidence, one must resort to non-absolutism (anekānta), because the object [of cognition] is not different from the means of its cognition.
Because it would follow that there is an absence of the capacity to produce a cognition that synthesizes them into a unity—*Tattvārthaślokavārttika*, p.

327, vya.—it is likewise logical that even the material sense organs (*dravyendriya*) possess a non-absolutist nature (*anekānta*) by way of both difference and non-difference from one another and from the matter-substances (*pudgaladravya*) that constitute them; for, from the perspective of the substance-aspect (*dravyārthādeśa*), their non-difference is established, while from the perspective of the mode-aspect (*paryāyārthādeśa*), their difference is established.

In this way, it should be understood that the sense objects, such as touch and the rest, possess the nature of both difference and non-difference by virtue of being substances and modes; for they are perceived in exactly that manner without contradiction.

Thus, neither substance alone nor mode alone is the object of the senses; rather, one should see that touch and the others function both as the instrument of action (*karmasādhana*) and as the state of being (*bhāvasādhana*).
It has been stated that there are distinctions between substantial and functional [senses]; he defines them in order: "The substantial sense-organ consists of matter (pudgala) with a fixed form. (22)
In the Tā-mū manuscript, the twenty-second and twenty-third sūtras are seen as a single unit;
the singular form "dravyendriyam" (the material sense organ) is used by resorting to the genus (*jāti*).

Those *pudgalas* which possess fixed, specific external and internal forms—that is, specific configurations—and which are subject to the properties of filling and diminishing, and which possess touch, taste, smell, and color, are [the sense organs]. For instance, in the case of the ear and other senses, that entire collection of *pudgalas*—whether external, such as the ear-canal, or internal, having the shape of a *kadamba* bud—is the "substantial sense organ" (*dravyendriya*), because it consists of the substance of *pudgalas*.
Alternatively, the word "substance" (*dravya*) may be used in a secondary sense, as in the expression "the teacher who grinds charcoal" (*dravyācārya*).

The material sense organ (*dravyendriya*) is secondary, because even when it is present and active, and even when the collection of auxiliary conditions such as light is present, the perception of touch and so forth is not established without the functional sense organ (*bhāvendriya*);
The functional sense-faculty (bhāvendriya) consists of acquisition (labdhi) and utilization (upayoga).
Acquisition is the attainment; it is a specific state of the subsidence-cum-destruction (kṣayopaśama) of the knowledge-obscuring karma (jñānāvaraṇa-karma).

That specific modification (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of the self (*ātman*), caused by the proximity of which the self functions toward the production of the physical sense-organ (*dravyendriya-nirvṛtti*), is *upayoga*;
here too, the singular number in the term "sensory faculty as disposition" (*bhāvendriyam*) is used by resorting to the genus (*jāti*).
The word *bhāva* is intended to signify that which is not subordinate (*anupasarjana*).

Just as the "existent Indra" (bhāvendra) is called such because he possesses the quality of being Indra by virtue of being endowed with the nature of Indra—thereby possessing the status of Indra in a non-figurative sense—so too the "existent sense-faculty" (bhāvendriya) is that which possesses the status of being a sense-faculty in a non-figurative sense, by virtue of being endowed with the qualities of possessing the characteristics of a sense-faculty and so forth. [The soul (ātman) arises] from the accumulation [of these].
(Variant readings: *dhānād vātmā* / *dhānād dhyātmā*)
Regarding the meaning of "predominance":

first, the sense-faculty (*indriya*), which has the nature of attainment (*labdhi*), acquires the state of being a functional sense-faculty (*bhāvendriyatā*) by conferring upon the self the capacity for the cognition of its own object;

for it is not possible for that which lacks such capacity to produce that cognition, just as [space cannot produce it], and this very capacity for the cognition of its own object is what constitutes attainment.
Furthermore, the nature of cognition (*upayoga*) consists in its activity (*vyāpāra*) with respect to the awareness of its own object;

for sensory perception, such as touch, is not capable of manifesting touch and so forth if it were devoid of activity, since that would imply that even those in deep sleep and similar states could manifest such objects.
(Sparśādi-tā.)

If it is argued that since consciousness (*saṃvedana*), being occupied with the manifestation of its own object, functions as the result (*phala*), it cannot logically be the sense organ (*indriya*); we say no. This is because the property of the cause persists in its effect;

for the fact that fire is illuminating does not contradict the fact that its effect, the lamp, is also illuminating. Furthermore, we do not maintain that the sense organ possesses the status of a result by the very same nature through which it is a sense organ, such that there would be a contradiction.

For its status as a sense-faculty (*indriya*) consists in its nature as the most effective means (*sādhakatama-svabhāva*), and its status as a result (*phala*) consists in its being of the nature of an action (*kriyā-rūpatā*).

Just as in the case of a lamp, which illuminates by means of its luminous nature—wherein the luminous essence is the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the most effective means, the action itself is the result, and it is also the agent (*kartṛ*) due to its independence—all of this is not difficult to find within the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*); so enough with this digression.
It has been stated that [the self] has the mind as its cause; he now defines the mind: "The mind is that which grasps all objects.

Not all objects are apprehended by the sense of touch and the others in the same restricted manner as their respective objects, such as touch; rather, that by which all objects are apprehended is the mind (*manas*). It is called "non-sense" (*anindriya*) or "not-a-sense" (*noindriya*). If it were simply called "the mind that apprehends all objects," there would be the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) of this definition to the Self (*ātman*) as well; therefore, it is specified as "apprehension" (*grahaṇa*) in order to demonstrate its status as an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Since the Self is the agent (*kartṛ*), there is no over-extension. Furthermore, the fact that the mind apprehends all objects is indeed well-established.
As for the statement by the chief of expounders that "the heard" refers to the reality of the non-sensory [self],
in the passage beginning with "the heard," there is indeed a designation of the object by means of the subject.
And "hearing" (śruta) is an indicative mark for "cognition" (mati); therefore, the meaning is that whatever is the object of mati and śruta is the object of the mind (manas).

Since the statement of the Vācaka [Umāsvāti] says, "The basis of mati and śruta is in substances, but not in all their modes" (Tattvārthasūtra 1.27), it follows that mati and śruta have everything as their object; thus, the fact that the mind also has everything as its object is established.
The commentary on all substances—regarding the *Tattvārtha*:
the mind (*manas*) is also of two kinds, like the five senses, due to the distinction between substance and state (*bhāva*).
Among these, the substance-mind (*dravya-manas*) consists of *pudgala* substances transformed into the state of mind-ness (*manastva*).

The mental mode (*bhāvamanaḥ*), however, is the attainment (*labdhi*) consisting of the subsidence and destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the karma that obscures it; it is a specific activity of the self directed toward the apprehension of objects.
(24) And the mind (*manas*) is also [an internal sense organ]—Indra-ḍe.
Is it not the case that this which is stated—namely, "having the sense-faculties and the mind as its cause"—is far too limited?

For there are other causes for visual cognition as well, such as the object and light. As they say: "Cognition arises from form, light, mental attention, and the eye, just as fire arises from a gem, sunbeams, and cow dung."
To this, he says:
[visual consciousness] is produced and arises from form, light, mental attention, and the eye.

Consciousness [arises] from the jewel, the rays of the sun, and cow dung, just as fire [arises from them]; neither the object nor the light is the cause of cognition, because they are not distinct from it.

An external object and light are not the direct causes of visual cognition; however, their status as indirect causes—like those of space, time, and so forth—is not precluded. This is because they are accepted as contributing to the causal complex of the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of knowledge-obscuring karma (*jñānāvaraṇa*) by way of remote assistance, and as assisting the eye like collyrium and other such aids. Why, then, are they not direct causes? He says: "Because of non-exclusion" (*avyatirekāt*), that is, due to the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

For it is not only positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—characterized by the presence [of the effect] when that [cause] is present—that is the basis for determining the relation of cause and effect; rather, there must also be negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), characterized by the absence [of the effect] when that [cause] is absent.

Furthermore, this [object] does not exist as a causal factor for either the object or the illumination; for we observe that in cases such as a mirage in the desert, there is cognition of water even in the absence of water, and that cats and other animals perceive objects located in places covered by dense masses of darkness even in the absence of light.
Moreover, when yogis grasp objects past and future, how could the object serve as a cause?
If it were a cause, then because it would possess existence through its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), its status as past or future would be lost.
Regarding the term *vilupta* and the question "for what purpose is it concealed":

the illuminator's status as an illuminator does not consist merely in its obtaining its own existence (*ātmalābha*) from the object to be illuminated; for we observe that a lamp and the like function as illuminators even when they have not arisen from objects such as jars.
Furthermore, how can that which is accepted as eternal, namely the knowledge of the Lord (Īśvara), be said to be "produced by an object"?

For even for people like us, if one accepts that only that which is the producer [of a cognition] is its object, then it would follow that valid cognitions such as memory and recognition would lack validity.

Moreover, for those who hold the view that an object is strictly momentary and is both the producer and the object of cognition, the relationship of apprehended and apprehender is impossible because the cognition and the object—which stand in the relation of produced and producer—exist at different times.

Now, if it is held that there is no relationship of apprehended and apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) between cognition and its object other than the relationship of produced and producer (*janyajanakabhāva*), like a pair of tongs and a glowing iron ball—if it is asked how an object at a different time can be apprehended, those who know the logic reply: "The wise know that the very state of being a cause, which is capable of imparting its form to the cognition, is what constitutes apprehensibility" (*Pramāṇavārttika* 3.247). If that is so, then it is in no way possible for the cognition of an omniscient one to have a present object as its domain, because a present moment is not a producer, and that which is not a producer cannot be apprehended.

Furthermore, since self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not produced from its own nature, it must be considered how it can possess the status of a grasper (*grāhaka*), or how its own nature can possess the status of the grasped (*grāhya*).

Therefore, just as between a lamp and its illumination and a jar produced by their respective causal complexes, the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is possible for cognition and its object; thus it is established that objects and light do not have cognition as their cause. [End of Prakaraṇapañcikā] — Tattvabindu.
Regarding the phrase "it is apprehended":

if it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be apprehended, those who know the principles of logic understand that its very status as an object of cognition consists in its capacity to impart its form to the cognition; [Pramāṇavārttika 3.247].
Omniscient one—Ḍe;
therefore, of the two [states] arising from one's own power—Ḍe; the manifestation—Ḍe.

[Objection: But if cognition is not produced by an object, how is the restriction of cognition to specific objects (pratikarmavyavasthā) established? For that [restriction] is possible only through being produced by the object and having its form (tadutpatti-tadākāratā); otherwise, since cognition that is neither produced nor possesses the form of the object would be indistinguishable with respect to all objects. [Response: It is not so; for even without being produced by it, the illumination of a specific object is possible through fitness (yogyatā) alone, characterized by the subsidence and destruction of obstructions (āvaraṇakṣayopaśama).

Furthermore, even regarding its arising from that [object], a capacity must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, even when all objects are in proximity, how could this distinction be accounted for—namely, that a particular cognition arises from only a specific object?

As for the theory of "having the form of that," it is untenable if it means the transfer of the object's form, because that would entail the absurd consequence that the object itself is devoid of form.

Moreover, what kind of similarity could there be between an insentient, material object and an immaterial cognition? Therefore, one must accept that [the cognition] consists in a transformation resulting from the apprehension of the specific features of the object.
Therefore, the claim that "it connects this [cognition] with the object, for it cannot do so except by taking on the form of the object" (Pramāṇavārttika 3.305) is trivial;
for that very [form] is what is accepted as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
— [and] subsequently—
O Goddess, [the cognition] connects this [object] with its meaning, for it does not do so apart from the nature of the object (pramāṇavārttika 3.305).
Furthermore, these two [the sense organ and the object] could be the cause of apprehension either separately or together.

If [the cause] were separate [from the effect], then the first moment of the potsherd would follow as the perceiver of the final moment of the jar, or the moon in the water would be the perceiver of the moon in the sky, because of its arising from that and its having that form.
If, on the other hand, it were combined [with the effect], then the subsequent moment of the jar would result in being the perceiver of the preceding moment of the jar.

If it is argued that "these two—being of the nature of cognition and being the cause of apprehension—are the grounds for perception," then it follows that a cognition of the same class would perceive its immediately preceding cognition.
Therefore, we see no cause for apprehension other than suitability (*yogyatā*).
Since it was stated that [perception] consists of *avagraha*, *īhā*, *avāya*, and *dhāraṇā*, he now defines *avagraha* and the others:
In the conjunction of the sense-organ and the object, the apprehension of the object immediately following perception is *avagraha* (perception).

(26) The sense-organ (*akṣa*) is the faculty, consisting of both substantial and functional forms; the object (*artha*) is that which consists of substance and its modifications (*paryāya*). Their "conjunction" (*yoga*) is their relationship, characterized by a state of fitness [for cognition] based on being situated at a distance that is neither too far nor too near, nor obstructed by space and so forth.

For that [distinction] between the object and the subject is fixed; as it is said: "One hears sound when touched, but one sees form even when untouched" (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 5), and so forth. When there is that conjunction of the sense-organ and the object, "seeing" is the apprehension of an entity whose specific qualities have not yet been delineated.
The phrase "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*) is intended to indicate the sequence [of the stages of cognition].

By this, it is stated that perception (*darśana*) is transformed into apprehension (*avagraha*); for there is no arising of anything from what is absolutely non-existent, nor is there absolute destruction of what exists. Thus, perception itself undergoes a subsequent transformation: it becomes the grasping of an object (*artha*) which consists of substance and its modes (*paryāya*) and is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Because the general definition [of valid cognition] as "the correct determination of an object" (*samyagarthanirṇaya*) applies here, apprehension (*avagraha*) is a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*), and not merely indeterminate perception.
"One perceives sound as something touched, but form, however, one sees as something untouched. (Āvaśyaka-niryukti 5).
The nature of transformational causality (*pāriṇāmika-kāraṇatā*) has been stated [here], unlike that of the Buddhists.

And this is not a mental conceptualization (*vikalpa*), because it depends upon the presence of the eye and other [senses], and because it cannot be set aside by analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*).
For a mental conceptualization is ceased by analytical discernment, but this is not so; therefore, it is not a conceptualization.
Ihā is the desire for specific details regarding an object that has been grasped through the contemplation of contradictory meanings, because it cannot yet be rejected.
27—*Viśeṣaka*:

When there is a doubt regarding an object apprehended by the sense of hearing, such as "Is this sound from a conch (*śāṅkha*) or from a horn (*śārṅga*)?", the specific qualities of sweetness and so forth, which are the properties of a conch, are perceived, and not the properties of hardness and so forth, which belong to a horn. Here, "mental activity" (*mati-ceṣṭā*) consists of the investigation of such specific characteristics through the method of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, here in the interval between avagraha (perception) and īhā (speculation), even when the object has been practiced, there certainly exists doubt-knowledge; however, due to its rapid occurrence, it is not perceived.
Yet it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the nature of being a definitive determination of the true object. — Śaṅkha-ṭīkā.

Now, it will be stated that there is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called *ūha*, which consists of a specific type of indirect valid cognition (*parokṣapramāṇa*); what, then, is the difference between that and *īhā*?

It is said in reply: *Ūha* has the three periods of time as its object and is expert in grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans; relying upon this, the cognizer becomes like a yogi at the time of grasping the pervasion—so say the experts in Nyāya.
*Īhā*, however, has a present object as its domain and is a variety of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, there is no redundancy.

Although *īhā* is called "endeavor" (*ceṣṭā*), it is nevertheless essentially of the nature of cognition because it belongs to a conscious being; thus, it is logical that it is a variety of perception.

Nor should its status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) be doubted on the grounds that it is not of the nature of a definitive judgment (*nirṇaya*); for it is indeed of the nature of a judgment regarding its own object. Otherwise, if [mere] non-similarity to other judgments were to render them non-judgments, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even other definitive judgments would themselves fail to be judgments.
Because it is a definitive determination regarding its own object—[the Ṭīkā states: "Apoha is the definitive determination of a specific intended object.
When an object has been grasped through *īhā*, the ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*) of its specific quality in the form "this sound is indeed from a conch, not from a horn" is *avāya*.
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the cause of memory. 28.

The cause of memory—which consists of the recollection of the past—is the transformative cause (pariṇāmikāraṇa), that is to say, the mental impression (saṃskāra). Retention (dhāraṇā) is the persistence of knowledge for a period of time that may be countable or uncountable;
however, the three [stages] beginning with apprehension (avagraha) last only for the duration of an internal muhūrta.

Since the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) consists of a specific form of direct perception, its nature as cognition (*jñānatva*) is to be inferred; it is not, however, as others claim, that this impression called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) is something distinct from cognition.

For if it were of the nature of non-cognition, it could not produce a memory which is of the nature of cognition; indeed, one existence does not enter into another existence. Furthermore, if it were of the nature of non-cognition, it would not be a property of the self (*ātma-dharma*), because that which is a property of consciousness cannot be insentient.

The Vaiśeṣikas: But did not the elders also teach *dhāraṇā* as non-lapse (*avicyuti*), as the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "Non-lapse is *dhāraṇā*, according to the *Viśeṣāvaśyaka-bhāṣya*, verse 180"? How then do you define *dhāraṇā* solely as the cause of memory?
True; there is indeed a *dhāraṇā* called non-lapse, but since it is included within *avāya* (judgment), it was not mentioned separately.
Indeed, it is precisely this very *avāya* (ascertainment), when it is extremely prolonged, that is called *dhāraṇā* (retention) because it is non-lapse;
or rather, non-lapse is subsumed under *dhāraṇā* itself because it is the cause of memory.
For memory does not arise from mere *avāya* devoid of non-lapse, since we do not observe that ascertainment—such as the touch of grass while walking—which lacks repeated cultivation, produces memory.

Therefore, there is no fault in the fact that the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) of non-lapse and non-obscuration, which are the causes of memory, are included within this [category of] non-obscuration (*anavaina*).

Although memory is also stated in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) to be a specific variety of retention (*dhāraṇā*), it is not mentioned here because it belongs to the category of indirect means of valid cognition (*parokṣapramāṇa*); thus everything is clear.
Retention (*dhāraṇā*) is a specific variety of that [perception].
—*davicyutivira*—Ḍe.
Furthermore, here one should understand that even though the stages beginning with *avagraha* (perception) occur sequentially, they are in some sense one;
for the imposition of contradictory attributes (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is the obstacle to the realization of oneness.
Nor does he adopt an adversarial stance toward an object established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
For indeed, it is experienced that a single consciousness (caitanya) is seized by various contradictory manifestations such as joy and dejection;

and even by those who fear the imposition of contradictory attributes (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), how is it that the Buddhists accept a single "cognition-canvas" (jñānacitrapaṭī)—which is the crest-jewel of the delineation of both singular and multiple forms—or how do the Naiyāyikas and others accept a single variegated color?

The Naiyāyikas, however, [define] perception as: "Perception is that knowledge which arises from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and of a determinate nature" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4).
Thus they state the definition of perception (pratyakṣa) according to Nyāyasūtra 1.1.4.

In this regard, turning away from the interpretations provided by earlier teachers, this point has been established by those possessed of number-knowledge (saṅkhyāvat), headed by Trilocana and Vācaspati, as follows: "Perception is cognition produced by the contact of a sense-organ with its object that is non-erroneous"—this alone is the definition of perception.

For, by supplying the word "from" (*yataḥ*) and because of the constant syntactic connection between "that which" (*yat*) and "it" (*tat*), that from which cognition characterized by the aforementioned qualifiers arises is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), whether it be of the nature of cognition or not of the nature of cognition.
And regarding this knowledge which has arisen as a result, there are two modes: the non-conceptual and the conceptual.

To state that both of these possess the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is this statement of their distinction: "inexpressible" and "of the nature of ascertainment"—thus [it is said]. (Pra.)—Ḍe.
— either a small portion or both of those— ḍe.

In this regard, it is improper to disregard the validity of cognition—which possesses both [subjective and objective] forms—and instead laboriously supply the word "from" (*yataḥ*) to establish the validity of contact (*sannikarṣa*) and so forth, which are of the nature of non-cognition.

For how can contacts and the like, being of the nature of non-cognition, be the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the determination of an object? Because there is deviation: even when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, the apprehension of the object may not occur;
whereas it occurs only when cognition exists. Indeed, that which is the most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and it must have its result immediately following it.

If "proximity" (*sannikarṣa*) is a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is distinct from "fitness" (*yogyatā*), then it does not exist between the eye and its object, because the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*).
For it is observed that an object, even when obstructed by glass, clouds, crystal, or similar media, is still perceived by the eye.

If you argue that the eye must reach its object because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like an axe or similar tools, then your argument is fallacious due to the counter-example of a magnet, which attracts iron even though it is not in physical contact with it.

Nor can a contact such as "conjunction of the conjoined" (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*) be postulated there, because it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); [this applies] to an object such as glass, a film of clouds, or a crystal.
— By proximity, [it is] distinguished—
[from] — the vicinity of the body and so forth—
... the Buddhists, however, [define] perception as being free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous (Nyāyabindu 1.4).
Thus they have stated the definition:

"Cognition that is devoid of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—that is, [cognition] whose appearance is capable of association with verbal expression" (Nyāyabindu 1.5–6). This is what is meant by "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*).

Furthermore, this definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable because it is useless for practical activity (*vyavahāra*). For indeed, investigators apply themselves to the examination of the definition of a means of valid cognition so that, having ascertained an object from this [cognition], those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) might not encounter disappointment when engaging with an object capable of such action. And if it were useless for practical activity, their labor would be fruitless, like examining whether a crow has eyes or not.

But since conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is undertaken on the basis of the conceptual cognition that arises subsequent to the non-conceptual [perception], it would be better to accept the validity of that [conceptual cognition] alone; what is the use of a non-conceptual [perception] that is like a mere tuft of hair (*śikhaṇḍin*)?
[The reading *tathāpoḍham* is explained as follows: *rahitaṃ tathāpoḍham* (separated from that, thus excluded).
[Variant readings: *rahitaṃ tayāpoḍham*—ḍe; *rahitaṃ tayāpoḍham*—mu.]
The investigation into the sitting and sleeping habits of crows—this is the same as [the following]: "How many teeth does a crow have? How many palas is a ram's testicle?
How many hairs are there on a donkey?"—this is the deliberation of fools. (Mu-Ṭi)
Śikhaṇḍin— A certain princess named Ambā, who had been rejected by Bhīṣma after he was chosen at her svayaṃvara, attained manhood through ascetic penance and lived under the name Śikhaṇḍin;
because he had previously been a woman, he became an object of reproach.
Then, having placed him at the forefront in the battle of Bhārata, Arjuna slew Bhīṣma;
and Śikhaṇḍin, too, was subsequently killed by Aśvatthāman— [Mu-ṭīkā].

The followers of Jaimini, however, under the guise of [denying that perception] is a means for knowing *dharma*, state the definition of perception by way of restating [an established fact]: "When there is contact with an existing object, the arising of cognition in a person's sense organs is perception; it is not a means [for knowing *dharma*], because it is the apprehension of what is present" (Jaiminisūtra 1.1.4). As they say: "If this were so, then even the definition would necessarily be merely repetitive."
And they explain [it] as follows in *Ślokavārttika* 4.39: "Perception is the cognition that arises in the person when there is contact of the sense-faculties."
If this were so, then even a restatement (anuvāda) would possess the characteristic [of perception]. Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 4.39—
*anuvādatvaṃ* (as corrected from *vādatvaṃ* in the manuscript)—
here there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because it would follow that even the arising of a doubtful or erroneous cognition would be perceptual when there is contact with the sense-faculties.

Now, if "contact with the existent" (*satsamprayoga*) is explained as "contact with that which exists," then only those delusions that are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*)—arising independently of an object—would be excluded, but not doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), which do have an objective basis. Alternatively, if "contact with the existent" is taken as a locative absolute (*sati saptamī*), then the position of the locative of the subject (*pakṣasaptamī*) is not abandoned; and for the purpose of excluding doubt and error, the prefix *sam-* in the word "contact" (*samprayoga*) is interpreted, as it has been said: "The word *sam* signifies 'correctly' (*samyak*) and serves to exclude improper contact."
"Because it is defective, the connection with mother-of-pearl is excluded by the perception of silver" (*Ślokavārttika*, Sūtra 4.38–39).

Nevertheless, since the correctness of the application (*prayoga-samyaktva*) is beyond the senses and thus not apprehended through perception, its cognition must be said to arise from its effect (*kārya*);
and that effect is knowledge (*jñāna*). Yet, that [knowledge], being unqualified, is not sufficient for the cognition of the correctness of the application.
Furthermore, there is no other word here intended to qualify that [object],

such as "contact with existing things" (*satāṃ saṃprayogaḥ*), which would be better for the sake of excluding cognition without an objective support (*nirālambana-vijñāna*). However, the word "sati" (in the locative) is redundant because its meaning is already conveyed by the locative case ending itself—
[as in the term] *saṃyoge*.

The prefix *sam-* [in *samyak*] serves to exclude improper application regarding the correct meaning; because it is defective, the connection with mother-of-pearl is excluded from the perception of silver. (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 4.38–39) [The reading is *satā sampra-* in the Ḍe manuscript.]

"Furthermore, when there is contact with that [object], the arising of cognition in a person through the sense organs is true perception (*sat-pratyakṣa*). When there is contact of the sense organs with that which is the object of a cognition, the arising of cognition in a person is true perception; however, that cognition which has a different object when there is contact with something else is not perception.
(Śābarabhāṣya 1.1.4)

Thus, they say that by reversing the order of *tat* and *satoḥ*, the definition becomes faultless; however, even for them, this is merely a strained interpretation, because the deviation [of the definition] with respect to doubtful cognition (*saṃśayajñāna*) has not been eliminated.
For in that case, there is indeed a contact of the sense organs with whatever object the cognition has;

and although the doubtful cognition has both things as its objects, nevertheless the sense organ is still in contact with one of those two. Furthermore, because doubt involves a reflective awareness of both, the cognition produced by the eye when it is in contact with one of them necessarily has that [other] object as well. Thus, there is no avoidance of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
Furthermore, there would be the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) because visual cognition lacks the quality of being born from sense-organ contact;
for it has already been stated that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*).
Therefore, by that very [reasoning]—[the reading *sampra* is supported by the *mu-pā* manuscript].
Regarding that [verse], the elder Sāṅkhyas maintain: "The non-conceptual functioning of the ears and other [senses] toward all objects is perception.
Here, since the ears and other [senses] are insentient, their functioning is even more so; therefore, how can it possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
If it is argued that consciousness is admitted [to exist] due to its association with volition (*cetanā*), then it is more appropriate to admit the validity of consciousness alone;
moreover, there is no validity in that which is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*)—this is trivial. (Variant reading: *avikalpatve*)—De.
Iśvarakṛṣṇa states that the definition of perception is "the ascertainment of each respective object" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 5).

However, that too is not a valid definition because it is over-extensive (*vyabhicāritva*), as it applies to inference as well. If it is argued that the prefix *prati-* denotes "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*)—and thus perception is defined as the ascertainment of an object by way of such facing toward it—that too is equivalent to the case of inference, since there is a cognition by way of facing toward [the object] in such cases as "this mountain possesses fire," just as in "this is a jar."

Now, if it is argued that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) directed toward its object that is distinct from inference and the like, then the definition of perception need not even be formulated, since it is established simply by its distinction from the definitions of verbal testimony and inference. [The opponent replies: "But [perception] is directly experienced. Therefore, since the definitions of others are flawed, this very definition—"Perception is clear [cognition]"—is faultless.

Since reality is fully encompassed within the fourfold scheme consisting of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object (*viṣaya*), the result (*phala*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*), the definition of the means of knowledge is incomplete without the definitions of the object and the others; thus, he defines the object. (In the Tā.
manuscript, it can also be read as "vidheṣu").
The object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the real entity (*vastu*) consisting of substance and modes.

Since perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the subject under discussion, its object and other characteristics ought to be defined first; however, the term "of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasya*) is used to include valid cognition in general. This is because it is appropriate to state the definitions of the objects and other features of the other means of knowledge right here as well, since there is no distinction between them, and furthermore, this approach provides economy of expression. Thus is the purpose [of the general term].

Furthermore, from the designation of "genus" (*jāti*), the object or domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest—is a reality consisting of substance and mode (*dravya-paryāya-ātmaka*).

"Substance" (*dravya*) is that which flows toward or undergoes various modes; it is characterized by persistence (*dhrauvya*) and is, in other words, the "vertical universal" (*ūrdhvatā-sāmānya*), which is apprehended through the continuous cognition of the underlying continuity persisting through preceding and succeeding transformations.
The modes (*paryāya*) are those whose nature is to arise and perish; they are the transformations (*vivarta*).

That which has these as its modes and its own essence (*ātman*)—that is the reality (*vastu*) consisting of substance and modes (*dravyaparyāyātmaka*); the meaning is that it is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). As the foremost of speakers [Umāsvāti] stated: "That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is real" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.29). This is also found in the teaching of the Great Sage: "It either arises, or perishes, or persists."
— the connection of the meanings and categories— ḍe;

therein, by the inclusion of substance and mode (*dravya-paryāya*), there is the exclusion of the objects postulated by those who maintain the doctrines of absolute substance (*dravya-ekānta*) and absolute mode (*paryāya-ekānta*).
By the inclusion of the term "self" (ātman), there is the exclusion of the objects accepted by the Kāṇādas and the Jaugas, who maintain that substance and its modes are absolutely distinct;
as the venerable Siddhasena said: "Although the treatise was composed by Ulūka according to both systems of logic, it is nonetheless false."
"Because they are preeminent in their respective domains, they are independent of one another. (Sanmatitarka 3.49) [Note:
*annanira*—Mu.;
*aṇuṇṇanira*—Ḍe.]

How could two independent perspectives [be possible], when the object of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely that which consists of both substance and mode (*paryāya*), and not merely substance, nor merely mode, nor both as independent entities? To this he says:
"Because of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*)."
The thirty-first and thirty-second sūtras are seen written together in the Saṃmūrchana manuscript without a dividing mark—[Commentary]:

the meaning is that "capacity" (sāmarthyāt) refers to the accomplishment of action characterized by the rejection or acquisition of an object; for only a reality consisting of substance and modification is capable of purposeful action (arthakriyā).
31 — *kriyārthasama* — [The commentary] says: "If it is indeed thus, then what follows? — *ḍe*. He states: "Then what? — *iti āha*.
Because the entity possesses the characteristic of height (or because of the nature of the entity)— Saṃmūrchana 32.

That which has as its characteristic (lakṣaṇa) the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya)—that is, the uncommon form—is "that-characteristic" (tallakṣaṇa); the state of being that is "the reality thereof" (tattva).
From what [does this follow]?
From the nature of a real entity (vastu) that exists in the ultimate sense (paramārthasat).

The meaning is this: everyone who seeks purposeful action (arthakriyā) investigates a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), thinking, "Perhaps by ascertaining from this [cognition] that the object of cognition (prameya) is capable of purposeful action, I may achieve my goal," and not out of mere habit. If the object within the scope of that means of valid cognition were not capable of purposeful action, then one would not care to examine that means of valid cognition;
as it has been said:
Regarding the cultivation of the investigation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
as they have said:
"What is the use of investigations for those seeking that [reality] regarding something incapable of causal efficiency?"

"What is the use of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch for a woman in love? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.215). In that regard, an object that is a single, unitary substance does not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). For how could that which is of a stable, unitary nature—neither fallen away nor arisen—perform causal efficiency, whether successively or simultaneously? Since there is no possibility of another mode [of action] other than these two, which are mutually exclusive, it cannot act successively. For if it were capable, it would necessarily have to perform all actions occurring at a later time right at the time of the first action, since it is impossible for a capable thing to delay its action. Alternatively, if it delays its action, it follows that it lacks capability.

If it is argued that even though it is capable, it produces this or that effect only upon the presence of its respective auxiliary causes; then its capability does not belong to it at all, because its operation depends on other auxiliaries. Have you not heard the rule: "That which is dependent is incapable" (Pātañjala Mahābhāṣya 3.1.8)?

If it is argued that the entity does not depend on the auxiliaries themselves, but rather depends on them because the effect cannot exist when the auxiliaries are absent; then, is that entity incapable?
If it is capable, why does it wait dejectedly for the face of the auxiliaries instead of producing [the effect] immediately?

Is it not the case that even a capable seed produces a sprout only when accompanied by auxiliaries such as soil and water, and not otherwise? In that case, is some assistance rendered to it by those auxiliaries, or not?
If it does not [exist], why does it not remain as before?
If it is to be assisted, then it must be explained whether that assistance produced by them is distinct or non-distinct from it.
In the case of non-difference, that very same thing is being produced; thus, for one who desires gain, the destruction of the very root has occurred.
If [the two] are distinct, how can that [action] be a benefit to it? Why not [be a benefit] to the Vindhya or the Himalaya as well?
If you say, "Because of its connection with it, this [benefit] belongs to it," then what is the connection between the beneficiary and the benefactor?
It is not conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because conjunction exists only between two substances (*dravya*).

Nor is inherence (samavāya) [the cause of restriction], because, since it lacks both proximity and distance, it is uniform everywhere; thus, it is not logical for it to possess a relation restricted to specific relata. If that were the case, one would have to admit that it provides an assistance (upakāra) produced by that [relation]. But if that were so, the dilemma regarding whether this assistance is distinct or non-distinct from the inherence remains exactly as before. If the assistance is non-different from the inherence, then the inherence itself would be what is produced. If, however, it is different, then once again the inherence does not possess a relation restricted to specific relata.

If it is argued that the cause for the specific restriction of inherence (*samavāya*)—which consists in its relation to restricted relata—is the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṇyabhāva*); [we reply that] this too lacks the causality for such restriction in the absence of a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*). But if there is such a benefit, then the same dilemma recurs by way of the alternatives of difference or non-difference;
therefore, an entity that is absolutely eternal does not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) sequentially.
In the case of capacity, the effects such as the seed and the earth [arise] from the other— [the Supreme]. (Ḍe.)
"It should be performed"—
[this refers to] the [rite] performed with a fixed relationship to Mount Indhyādri.
Regarding the nature of inherence (*samavāya*) as a relation:

when two related entities—the seed and its benefit—are fixed in their relationship, the relation between these two is inherence; this constitutes the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
Nor can it be by way of non-succession;

for it is not a matter of common experience that a single entity performs all its actions simultaneously throughout every fraction of time. Even if one were to grant this, what would it do in the second moment?

Alternatively, if there is activity, the fault inherent in the position of succession follows; if there is no activity, because it does not perform any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the consequence is its lack of substantial reality (*avastutva*). Thus, since purposeful action—whether successive or simultaneous—is pervaded by [the property of] being either successive or simultaneous, when that pervader is absent, the pervaded (purposeful action) is excluded by the force of the non-perception of the pervader. This [absence of purposeful action] in turn excludes its own pervaded, which is existence (*sattva*); therefore, the absolute monism of substance (*dravyaikānta*) is non-existent.
By the word "kalā," parts (*aṃśāḥ*) are meant.
Indeed, the passage beginning with "for [it is] actions occurring at different times" must be repeated:
that capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), being a pervader (*vyāpaka*), when it ceases, causes its own pervaded (*svavyāpya*), existence (*sattva*), to cease.

Even an entity that is exclusively of a momentary nature (*paryāyaikāntarūpa*) and perishes every instant is not capable of causal efficiency through succession, because succession—whether spatial or temporal—is simply non-existent for such a thing.
For it is precisely that which remains stable which is said to possess spatial and temporal succession— that is, pervasion across various places and times—
and this does not exist for that which is subject to absolute destruction,
as they have said:
Whatever exists in a particular place exists only there; whatever exists at a particular time exists only then. In this world, there is no spatial or temporal pervasion among entities;
[therefore,] the genitive case is used for the agent.

Furthermore, in the doctrine of absolute modalism, a sequence of preceding and succeeding moments cannot occur even with reference to a continuum (*santāna*), because the continuum is not a real entity;
and even if it were a real entity, if it were momentary, it would possess no distinction whatsoever from the moments themselves.
Now, if there were non-momentariness, the doctrine of the absolute identity of the modes (*paryāyaikāntavāda*) would be well-established! As they say—[the text is corrupt here]—as it was stated:
[the text is corrupt here].

"Moreover, if you maintain that there exists an entity called 'continuum' (saṃtāna) which is eternal and ultimately real, then rise up, O monk! Your hopes have borne fruit; this doctrine of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) is now at an end. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 464).—*tava āśā*—Ḍe. edition.
Nor is causal efficiency possible through non-succession in the case of a momentary entity.

For if that single moment of form (*rūpa*) were to produce simultaneously multiple moments of taste (*rasa*) and so forth, it would have to do so either by means of a single nature or by means of multiple natures. If it produced them by means of a single nature, then those [moments of taste] would be one, because they would be produced by a single nature. If, on the other hand, it produces them by means of multiple natures—some as material causes (*upādāna*) and some as cooperative conditions (*sahakārin*)—then are those natures identical with its own self or not identical with its own self?
If they are not identical with its nature (*anātmabhūta*), then its own-nature (*svabhāva*) is lost.
If, on the other hand, they are identical with it, then it would follow that it is manifold and its own-natures are one.

Now, if it is maintained that there is no difference in own-nature because that which is the material cause (*upādānabhāva*) in one instance is the very same thing that is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāribhāva*) in another, then let there be no difference in own-nature for an eternal entity of uniform form that produces various effects sequentially, nor let there be a confusion of its effects.

If it is argued that this is not so because successive effects do not arise from a non-successive cause; [we reply: since there is a contradiction between a single partless cause and multiple effects produced by multiple causes simultaneously, let there be no non-successive causal efficiency even for momentary things. Thus, through the exclusion of both succession and non-succession—which are the pervaders—the pervaded "causal efficiency" (arthakriyā) is also excluded.

And when that is excluded, "existence" (sattva) is also excluded by the force of the non-perception of the pervader. Therefore, the extreme view of succession (paryāyaikānta) is non-existent, as in the case of a citron fruit and the like.
Regarding the simultaneous [production] of many [effects]:
even for that which is eternal and of a single nature, a passage such as "in succession" and so forth is not tenable;
for in your view, there does not exist one part consisting of the material cause (*upādāna*) and another part consisting of the auxiliary conditions (*sahakārī*).
—[This was] composed by Meṇāka.

—The followers of Kaṇāda, however, accept both substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*). They hold that earth and the other elements, which serve as the substrata for qualities and so forth, are substances; whereas qualities and the like, because they are dependent upon [a substratum], are modes.

Furthermore, some of these are momentary, some exist as long as the substance exists, and some are eternal. Thus, because they merely accept a subject (*dharmin*) and its attributes (*dharma*) as being entirely distinct from one another, they are not proponents of a correct object of cognition.
For instance: if existence (*sattva*) were absolutely distinct from substance (*dravya*), then substance would be non-existent;

if it is argued that substance exists because of its connection with existence (*sattāyogāt sattvam asty eva*), [we reply: even if there is a connection with existence, how can that which is non-existent possess existence? If it is argued that for things already existent, the connection with existence is fruitless and that entities possess existence by their very nature (*svarūpasattva*), then what is the use of connecting them with "existence" (*sattā*) like a crest-ornament?

If it is argued that before its connection with existence (*sattā*), an entity is neither existent nor non-existent, but becomes existent through its relation to *sattā*, this is a mere verbal claim; for there is no third alternative possible that is distinct from both existence and non-existence. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "an entity is the connection with existence," these three do not appear as a triad.
If the connection between the entity and existence were identity (*tādātmya*), that is contradicted by your own non-acceptance [of such a relation].

For this very reason, there is no conjunction (*saṃyoga*); as for inherence (*samavāya*), since it is non-dependent, everything would be connected with everything, or else nothing would be connected with anything—thus [the same applies] to substances, qualities, and actions with respect to their generic properties (*dravyatva*, etc.), to a substance with respect to its own substancehood, qualities, actions, universals, and particulars, and to earth, water, fire, and air with respect to their specificities (*pṛthivītva*, etc.). Furthermore, regarding the connection of substances such as space (*ākāśa*) with their own qualities, everything must be stated according to the circumstances, because an absolute distinction between things makes any kind of relationship impossible. Thus, even in the system of Ulūka (the Vaiśeṣika), the determination of objects is unstable—both [of these views] being accepted [as untenable]. (Notes: *abhyupā* refers to the reading *abhyupagatau* in the Derge edition.)
Cognition and so forth,
as well as the color-forms of jars and so forth, and the color-forms of water and so forth, [are not eternal], because the color-forms of the atoms of water and so forth are eternal.
— because it is sublated by the very fact that [the opponent] does not accept [the existence of] distinct categories of objects (padārtha)— thus, Ḍe. states.
For conjunction belongs only to two substances; as for [qualities] such as color and [actions] such as motion, they are related to something else— Sambandhatātparya-muktāvalī.

Is it not the case that even if a thing consists of both substance (*dravya*) and mode (*paryāya*), the same difficulty remains? To explain: the proponents of *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness) accept a theory of difference and non-difference in some respect (*kathaṃcid-bhedābheda-vāda*), avoiding absolute difference or absolute identity between substance and mode. Yet this is not tenable due to faults such as contradiction—for instance, like blue and non-blue, two things consisting of affirmation and negation cannot coexist in a single entity (1). If it is argued that there is difference in one form and non-difference in another, then, since the locus of difference would be one thing and the locus of non-difference another, there would be a lack of common substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) (2).

1. Those two natures, depending upon which there is difference and depending upon which there is non-difference, are themselves both different and non-different; otherwise, the consequence of extremist doctrine (*ekāntavāda*) would follow, and if that were so, there would be infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

2. By whichever form there is difference, by that [form] there is both difference and non-difference; and by whichever [form] there is non-difference, by that [form] there is both non-difference and difference; thus there is confusion (*saṅkara*).
3. By whichever form there is difference, by that there is non-difference; and by whichever there is non-difference, by that there is difference; thus there is mutual perversion (*vyatikara*).
Furthermore, since a thing that consists of both difference and non-difference cannot be determined through a distinct form, there is doubt (6);
and from that, there is non-comprehension (7); thus, there is no establishment of the object (8).
This is not so; for contradiction is impossible regarding an object that is being perceived.
It is determined that "X is the opposite of Y" when X is not perceived in the presence of Y;
however, when a thing is being perceived, what room is there for even a scent of contradiction?
Even in the case of blue and non-blue, if they are perceived in one and the same place, then there is no contradiction.

In the case of a single cognition of a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭī*), since the Buddhists do not admit a contradiction between blue and non-blue, and the Naiyāyikas admit a single variegated color, and since in the case of a single cloth or similar object one perceives contradictory properties such as moving and stationary, red and non-red, covered and uncovered, and so forth—what room is there for suspicion of contradiction here?
By this, the fault of "different substrates" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is also refuted; for, according to the reasoning previously stated, those two [properties] are perceived as having a single substrate.

As for the objection of infinite regress that was raised, that too was put forward by one who is ignorant of the doctrine of the Proponents of Non-absolutism (Anekāntavādins). For according to their view, in an entity consisting of substance and mode, substance and mode themselves constitute the difference, since it is precisely these two that are denoted by the term "difference. Non-difference, on the other hand, exists in the form of substance; thus, substance itself is non-difference, because an entity possesses both a unitary and a manifold nature. Furthermore, the objections regarding confusion (*saṅkara*) and mutual exclusion (*vyatikara*) have been refuted by the example of variegated cognition and the illustration of the universal-particular relationship.
Now, if it is argued that such an appearance therein constitutes a state of mental composure (*samādhāna*), let that same [appearance] belong to the opponent as well, since appearance is impartial.
Furthermore, once an object has been determined, even doubt is not tenable, because doubt consists of a wavering apprehension and is difficult to reconcile with unwavering apprehension;
and to claim that there is no apprehension of an object already apprehended is sheer audacity.

Since even non-apprehension is not established because it is designated by apprehension, non-existence is therefore not proven; thus, the entity consists of substance and modes, which does not contradict what is seen or accepted regarding the forms of difference and non-difference.
[Regarding] the forms of difference and non-difference.
Confusion (*saṅkara*) is the simultaneous occurrence of both natures;
perversion (*vyatikara*) is the mutual entering into each other's domains.
Refuting the example of "shadow" cited by the opponent, he says:

*yoga* refers to withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth; one who knows or studies that is a *yauga*. [According to] Hemacandra’s Śabdānuśāsana 6.4.59: "One who knows or studies that [is called by the suffix -ika]."
117 Thus, because it is admitted that a single entity possessing variegated form has the status of a whole (avayavin).

Indeed, even if a single entity consists of both substance and modes, how can there be such a thing as causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for a single cognition of a cloth that possesses one form yet is intermingled with manifold forms?

For that [capacity] is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity; therefore, let it be excluded from the absolute nature of substance as well as from the absolute nature of both [substance and mode], just as it is from the absolute nature of modes.

Indeed, it can be argued that an entity consisting of both [substance and mode] is not capable of performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) successively, because what is already capable cannot be delayed.
Nor is dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) logical, because since the substance is unchangeable, it is independent of any assistance provided by auxiliaries.

Furthermore, because the modes (*paryāya*) are momentary, they do not wait for the time of preceding or succeeding effects; nor can [the substance] act without succession, for if it were to perform all its effects simultaneously and then cease acting, it would be non-existent due to its failure to perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). On the other hand, if it continues to act, the fault inherent in the position of succession applies. Moreover, whatever fault exists in the theories of substance alone or modes alone, that same fault applies equally to the theory of both together, according to the saying: "How could that which is a fault for each individually not exist when both are present? Thus he says:

If time consists of both substance and modification, and each of these exists individually in the first and second bodies [of the Jina] respectively, why would that same fault not apply when both are present together?

The validity of its causal efficiency is established through transformation characterized by the relinquishing of a prior form, the assuming of a subsequent form, and the persistence [of the continuum]—[this occurs] moment by moment. (Source: Saṃmatitarka-mahā-ṭīkā)

—The activity of this [entity] is established through its persistence, which is characterized by the avoidance and acceptance of the preceding and succeeding forms (ākāra) or modifications (vivarta) respectively; and that very persistence is its transformation (pariṇāma). By means of this, causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is possible for this entity, which consists of both substance (dravya) and mode (paryāya).

The meaning is this: a real entity is neither of the nature of substance alone, nor of the nature of mode alone, nor of the nature of both; for if it were so, the defects inherent in those respective positions would arise. Rather, the entity is a distinct category (jātyantara), variegated (śabala) in nature, consisting of persistence, origination, and destruction.

Therefore, for an entity that performs various causal efficiencies (*arthakriyā*)—either successively or simultaneously—in proximity to its respective auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), which relies on a succession of assistance provided by those auxiliaries, and whose nature is neither agitated nor complacent regarding the distinction or non-distinction of these assistances; for such an entity, which is not terrified by the stain of doubt concerning the defects inherent in either [monistic] position, there is no cessation of causal efficiency through the force of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), nor is there a cessation of existence (*sattva*), which is pervaded by that [efficiency]. Thus it is established that the object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a reality consisting of both substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*), having the form of independent substance and modification.
Independent Substance-Modification Form.
The relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary at the beginning [of the process] is like that of one fleeing in all directions out of fear— Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 3.30.
Succession and non-succession are pervasive of those two;
[the author] states the result of this very existence— De.

"The fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the manifestation of the object" (verse 34). The term "of the means of valid cognition" carries over [from the previous verse]. The fruit of the means of valid cognition is the manifestation of the object—that is, the awareness of the object. For every cognizer is indeed a seeker of objects; therefore, it is logical that the awareness of the object alone is the fruit.
But in that case, the means of valid cognition itself would be stated as the result. If you say "yes," then there would be no distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result.
What follows from that?

If the means of valid cognition and its result were identical, the defect inherent in the positions of existence and non-existence would arise: that which is non-existent cannot be an instrument, and that which is existent cannot be a result.
True; this fault exists in the case of birth, not in the case of determination, as they say:
"In this context, the word 'object' (artha) denotes a thing capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyākṣama)."
For that which lacks a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
there is no causality for what is non-existent, nor can an existent cause possess the nature of its effect;
for according to your own position, the means of valid cognition is non-different from its effect.
Furthermore, because the result (*phala*) is that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it would follow that it is non-existent;
and since that which is non-existent cannot be an instrument (*karaṇa*), for it is only that which is already established that is accepted [as such].

Likewise, if there were no difference between the result and the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then because the means of valid cognition exists, the result too would have to exist; yet that which already exists cannot be a result, for it is only that which is to be accomplished that is admitted to be a result.
"Thus, there would be a fault in [the theory of] birth, but the established order (*vyavasthā*) does not partake of that fault.
(34) He demonstrates this very established order: "Action resides in the object."
Regarding the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth sūtras, these two are seen written together in the Tā-mūla manuscript without any distinguishing mark— [as noted by] Sampā.—
The activity of knowledge directed toward action is the fruit.
To the question "What is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)? he says:
"The means of valid cognition resides in the agent."
Karmasthā-prakaraṇa: Cognition that manifests the activity of the agent is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For instance, if an action is perceived as residing in the object (*karman*) or in the agent (*kartṛ*), the same applies to knowledge.
