To explain: one must admit some burning power (*dāhikā śakti*) inherent in fire, by whose operation pieces of wood are burnt; likewise, there exists some act of burning (*dāhakriyā*) inherent in the wood, by which those [pieces] are reduced to ashes.
In this same way, it should be understood elsewhere regarding both cognition and its object.
How does this [cognition] possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
For it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), and that which is the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*) is called an instrument.
And he says that its fruit is immediate:
"its fruit is that"— for when that [power] exists, the manifestation of objects is established.

Since the manifestation of the object as the result is established when that action—which resides in the agent and consists of the nature of valid cognition—is present, there is non-difference between the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) by virtue of both being contained within a single cognition; yet, due to their relationship as the established and the establisher, there is difference. Thus, the relation between the means of cognition and its result conforms to the uncontradicted *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects), which takes the form of both difference and non-difference. This immediate result has been stated as common to all means of valid cognition.
He states another immediate result:
"Or, the cessation of ignorance."
Others say that the fruit [of knowledge] is the cessation of the knower's ignorance regarding the object intended before the operation of the means of valid cognition; as they say:—

In reality, although there is identity [between the means and the result], there is a distinction: the manifestation of the object is oriented toward cognition, while the cessation of ignorance is oriented toward the object;
thus, the fruit of the means of knowledge is the direct and immediate removal of ignorance.
"In the case of the [soul] alone, there is pleasure and equanimity; for the rest, there is the cognition of taking up and abandoning" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.28). Thus [it is said].
To explain that which is separated [by an interval], he says:

"Or, among avagraha and the others, which possess the property of arising in succession, each preceding one is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and each succeeding one is the result (*phala*)."
39—of those whose nature is to arise from a collection—Tā. (variant: saṃmūrchana-dharmāṇām)
The forty-ninth and fortieth sūtras are seen written together in the Mūla manuscript without a dividing mark—[Editor’s Note].

Regarding avagraha, īhā, avāya, dhāraṇā, smṛti, pratyabhijñāna, ūha, anumāna, which arise in succession: that which is prior is to be understood as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and that which is subsequent is the result (phala).
For the self, possessing the transformation of avagraha, transforms into the result in the form of īhā; thus, with respect to the result of īhā, avagraha is the pramāṇa.
In this context as well, *īhā* (investigation) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and *avāya* (ascertainment) is the result;
furthermore, *avāya* is the means of valid cognition and *dhāraṇā* (retention) is the result.
This is because *īhā* and *dhāraṇā* have knowledge as their material cause, and thus they are to be inferred from their nature as knowledge.
From that, retention (*dhāraṇā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and memory (*smṛti*) is the result;
from that as well, memory is the means of valid cognition and recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the result;
from that too, recognition is the means of valid cognition and inference (*ūha*) is the result.

Furthermore, [the opponent holds that] ūha is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and inference (anumāna) is the result (phala); this is the distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result.
(39) The intention of the opponent is that because īhā consists of effort (ceṣṭā) and dhāraṇā consists of latent impressions (saṃskāra), they are not forms of knowledge (ajñānatva).
He states another result of knowledge, namely that it is the material cause of those two, or rather, that knowledge is the material cause [of them]:
"Or [the results] are the cognitions of abandonment and so forth."
Alternatively, the cognitions of avoidance, acquisition, or indifference are the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The presentation of multiple fruits is for the purpose of demonstrating that there is no contradiction in all of these being fruits, since the status of a "fruit" is relative to one's intention (*vaivakṣikatvāt*).
In comparison with that,
[the cognition] is the cognizer of the manifestation of the object and so forth.
— Because it has been examined—

[the Tattvasaṅgraha] states, for the purpose of examining the views of those who maintain that the result is both different and non-different from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "Different and non-different from the pramāṇa."
Because they consist of the nature of an instrument and the nature of an action, there is a distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*);

for if there were no distinction, the conventional usage of distinguishing between the means of valid cognition and its result would be untenable, and it would follow that either the means of valid cognition alone or the result alone would exist.

If it is argued that the designation "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) arises through exclusion from what is non-valid, and the designation "result" (*phala*) arises through exclusion from what is non-resultant, this is not so. If that were the case, then let there also be the designation "non-valid cognition" through exclusion from another valid cognition, and the designation "non-result" through exclusion from another result, because an entity is excluded from both heterogeneous and homogeneous things alike—just as [it is excluded] from other valid cognitions and results.
(Note: *anyapramāṇāt* corrected to *anyapramāṇaphalatvāt* based on the commentary).

Likewise, from another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is the transformation of that very self into the form of the means of knowledge, and its transformation into the nature of the result (*phala*); thus, with respect to a single cognizer, there is non-difference between the means of knowledge and the result.
If there were difference, however, such [non-difference] would be untenable, as in the case of a different self.

If it is argued that the determination of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) occurs through the proximity characterized by inherence (*samavāya*), such that wherever the means of knowledge inheres in a self, the fruit also inheres there, and thus there is no unwanted consequence for other selves—[we reply: no; because inherence is eternal and all-pervasive, it is without distinction across all selves just as it is in a specific self. Therefore, there can be no restriction of the relationship to a specific cognizer based on that [inherence]. Thus, it is established that the fruit is in some way both different from and non-different from the means of knowledge.

Just as the result belonging to a second self cannot be related to a means of knowledge residing in one self, so too let it not be the case for two [results] residing in one self; for since absolute difference is indistinguishable in both positions,
he defines the knower— [he] describes the knower— [as follows].
The cognizer (pramātā) is that which manifests itself and the other [object], and is subject to transformation (pariṇāmī).
Following this sūtra, the manuscript designated as Mū. contains the following: "Thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya in the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable teacher Hemacandra."
In the Saṃmūrchita manuscript, however, it reads: "The first section of the chapter:

That whose nature (*śīla*) is to manifest both itself (*svam*) and the external object (*param artham*) is 'that which manifests self and other' (*svaparābhāsī*), because it appears through being oriented toward itself and oriented toward the object, as evidenced by the cognition 'I know the jar,' wherein the object, the agent, and the action are perceived; for there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to deny either of these perceptions.
Nor is there a contradiction between its being a manifester of others and its being self-manifesting, just like a lamp."

For a lamp does not depend on anything else for its own illumination; by this, the views of those who maintain that [consciousness] is exclusively self-illuminating or exclusively illuminating others are refuted, [and it is established that] the Self, as the cognizer, is indeed both self-illuminated and the illuminator of others.
Likewise for the Buddhist: that which possesses transformation (pariṇāmī) as defined above exists;

for if the Self were immutable and eternal (kūṭasthanitya), then transformations such as joy, dejection, the experience of pleasure and pain, and so forth—characterized by engagement and withdrawal—could not occur.

Furthermore, if [the self] were subject to absolute destruction, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done; moreover, the worldly transactions well-known to every living being—such as memory, recognition, the recovery of deposited goods, and so forth—would collapse.
However, if the self is transformative, possessing the characteristics of arising, passing away, and persistence, everything becomes logically consistent.
As they say: "Just as the coiled state of a snake disappears immediately after [its straight state]," and so on.
Just as the state of straightness arises while the nature of being a snake persists,
so too for the Self, whose essential nature is eternal consciousness, there is neither a total disappearance of its form nor a persistence of every [prior] state.
However, its states characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, cease and those very same states arise again, while consciousness persists;
for if there were absolute destruction, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.

Furthermore, there would be no experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth for that which is of a single uniform nature; nor could agency and enjoyment belong to the person by depending upon its states.
Therefore, since the entity possessing the states is the true self, it is the agent alone who obtains the fruit thereof.
By these verses from the *Tattvasaṃgraha* (Kārikās 223–227), the doctrine of absolute permanence and impermanence is refuted;
the term "self" (ātman) excludes those who maintain the doctrine of non-self (anātmavāda);
and the idea that the self is the size of the body is not mentioned because it is irrelevant to the present context. Thus, the definition of the subject (pramātṛ) is well-established.
Just as the coiled state of a snake perishes absolutely, it vanishes immediately thereafter.
Just as the state of straightness arises while the nature of being a serpent persists,
so too for the Self, whose essential nature is eternal consciousness,
there is neither a total disappearance of its form nor a persistence of every [previous] form.
However, its states characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth cease and those very same states arise again, while consciousness persists;
for if there were absolute destruction, there would be the loss of what was done and the acquisition of what was not done.
Furthermore, there could be no experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth for that which is of a single uniform nature;

nor can agency and enjoyership belong to the person (puruṣa) when they are dependent upon a state [of being]. Therefore, because the possessor of the state is the reality itself, it is the agent alone who obtains the fruit thereof. (Tattvasaṃgraha, kārikās 223–227)
Because of the reality of the state—
because of the reality of each respective state— in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verse 227.
On account of its unity—
thus ends the first Āhnika of the first Adhyāya of the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* and its commentary composed by the venerable teacher Hemacandra.
Śreyas-tantram.
Now begins the second chapter.
Regarding the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) mentioned here—namely, perception (pratyakṣa) and non-perception (parokṣa)—perception has been defined.
Now he states the definition of indirect perception (parokṣa): "Indistinct [cognition] is indirect perception.
Here, the first and second sūtras are seen written together in the original manuscript (mūla-prati) without a dividing mark—[Editor’s Note:
because the general definition is restated while prescribing the specific definition, the term "determination of the correct meaning" (samyagarthanirṇayaḥ) carries over;
therefore, indistinct determination of the correct meaning is indirect valid cognition (parokṣapramāṇa).]
He states the classification:
"Recollection, recognition, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are its varieties."

The term "tad" (that) is a reference to something remote (*parokṣa*); therefore, these are varieties of the remote [means of knowledge] and not independent additional means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because that would entail the destruction of the established number of means of knowledge under discussion.

Now, one might ask: "Why are memory and the other [cognitions] not said to be independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? What is the point of this 'Dravidian’s eating of the *maṇḍaka* bean' logic?

Do not speak thus. For those [cognitions] such as memory, which are subsumed under the definition of the indirect (*parokṣa*), do not exist apart from the indirect means of valid cognition. Just as for the Buddhists, sensory cognition, mental cognition, self-reflexive awareness, and yogic cognition—which are all subsumed under the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—do not exceed the scope of direct perception, so too memory and the others, being implied by the definition of the indirect, do not oppose the established number of fundamental means of valid cognition.
There is a copulative compound (dvandva) of the five beginning with mindfulness (smṛti). Among these, he defines mindfulness (smṛti):
Memory is that which has the form "that" (tad) and is caused by the awakening of a latent impression (*vāsanā*).

A *vāsanā* is a residual trace (*saṃskāra*); its "awakening" (*udbodha*) is its activation, and memory is caused by—that is, dependent upon—that [awakening]. According to the statement, "Retention (*dhāraṇā*) should be understood as lasting for an incalculable or calculable time" (Gāthā 333), a latent impression, even if it persists for a long duration, is not the cause of memory when it is unawakened. However, when it has attained awakening through a collection of conditions such as the destruction-cum-subsidence of obstructions (*āvaraṇa-kṣayopaśama*) and a similar perception, it produces memory; thus it is said to be "caused by the awakening of a latent impression."

He states its specific characteristic: "The cognition characterized by the mental reflection 'that'—which, when expressing a generality, takes a neuter gender—as in 'that jar,' 'that cloth,' or 'that earring,' is memory (smṛti).
Retention (dhāraṇā) is the state of being oriented toward the generation of such memory."

Retention (dhāraṇā) should be understood as occurring when time is either uncountable or countable; this is stated as a general rule because, during the stage of practice (*abhyāsadaśā*) such as recitation (*guṇana*), the mental image of "that" [the object] is absent. (Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya, Gāthā 333). [Note: *anusmṛti* is the reading in the manuscript.]
The pond—
[as stated in] the Smṛti— is authoritative because it is non-contradictory, since we observe such worldly practices as searching for something that one has oneself buried.
But surely, since the object being experienced at the time of recollection is non-existent, how can memory, being without a basis (*nirālambanā*), be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

It is not so; for it is established that memory has a basis by virtue of the object having been previously experienced. Otherwise, even perception would result in invalidity, as it too would have as its object only what was previously experienced.
Furthermore, the illumination of its own object is no different for memory than it is for perception.

If it is argued that a destroyed object cannot be the producer of memory, and therefore, because it is not produced by the object, memory lacks validity—then have you been deceived into thinking that being produced by the object is the cause of non-contradiction even in other means of valid cognition? Do not be thus deluded. For just as a lamp, having its birth obtained through the power of its own causal complex, illuminates jars and other objects even though it is not produced by them, so too does cognition—which has its birth obtained through the power of the sense organs and the mind (internal organ) while depending upon the destruction and subsidence of obstructions—manifest the object.

To claim that "only that which does not fail to exhibit positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) is a cause, and only a cause can be an object [of valid cognition]" is mere idle chatter. This is because there is no disagreement regarding the validity of the knowledge of yogins, which has as its domain objects past and future and is not produced by those objects. Furthermore, if memory were invalid, an inferential argument (anumāna) would be deprived of its foundation, for it is impossible for inference to arise unless the pervasion (vyāpti) is apprehended by memory; indeed, it is established for all disputants that inference is preceded by the perception of the logical mark (liṅga) and the recollection of the relationship [between the mark and the probandum].
Therefore, it is proven that memory is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), since otherwise the validity of inference could not be accounted for.
If it is argued that its non-contradictoriness (*avisaṃvāditva*) is unestablished, he says:

"If you maintain that memory lacks validity even though it has an object because of the thing previously experienced, then why would direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) not also lack validity? For, by the same logic, that too would be without an object."

If the validity of cognition is accepted on the grounds that it is produced by an object already experienced, then even the cognition of water in a mirage would be valid, since it too is produced by an object.
Alternatively, if validity is held to consist in being produced by an object that is actually appearing [in consciousness], then inference would not be a valid means of knowledge.

For inference manifests a non-real universal (*sāmānya*), yet it is not produced by that [universal], because according to your own view, a universal is a non-entity; thus, the definition "whatever is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is necessarily produced by a non-entity" suffers from the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Furthermore, this is invalidated by the counter-example of self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), for that has itself as its object and is not produced by it. Moreover, if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not apprehended, there is no apprehension [of the definition], because such [unapprehended] would not be a means of valid cognition.
Thus [ends] the section on *mupā*.
Now, he defines recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*):

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the synthesis (*saṅkalana*) consisting of "this is that very same," "this is similar to that," "this is different from that," "this is the counter-correlative of that," and so forth; it arises from perception and memory.

Perception is direct sensory experience (*pratyakṣa*), and memory is recollection (*smṛti*); that which originates from these two is such [a synthesis], namely, recognition is a synthetic cognition whose causes are perception and memory.

He states its illustration: "This is that very same thing"—the neuter gender here is used for the sake of a general indication—such as "this is that very jar," "this is that very cloth," or "this is that very bowl";

"the *gavaya* is similar to that" (similar to a cow); "the buffalo is distinct from that" (distinct from a cow); "this is the counter-correlative of that," such as "this is smaller than that," "larger," "farther," or "nearer," and so forth—the inclusion of "and so forth" [refers to] "hairy," "buck-toothed," "dark-complexioned," "dwarf," or "large-eyed."
One who has a flat nose there should be identified as Caitra (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 143). A swan is that which separates milk from water; a bee is known by those with six feet;
and a seven-leafed tree is to be recognized by the wise as one with uneven leaves.

When one hears words such as "the gem shall be five-colored and called *mecaka*," or "there is a broad-chested young woman," or "the rhinoceros has a single horn," and subsequently perceives objects like Caitra or a swan that correspond exactly to those descriptions, one then confirms them as such; this too is called synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*), because there is no difference in its being produced from perception and memory.

Or, for example, when a northerner, censuring a camel, says, "Fie on this camel—its neck is exceedingly long and crooked, its lips hang down, it eats harsh and sharp thorns, its limbs are arranged in a loathsome manner; it is a wretch among animals," and a southerner, having heard this, travels to the northern region and, upon perceiving such a creature, realizes, "Surely this is the meaning of this word 'camel'"; that too is a synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanājñāna*) and a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), because it has both perception and memory as its causes.

In some cases, recognition arises even from two [causes] separately, such as the recognition "this is different from that," which arises from perception alone without recollection; or the recognition "this is different from that," which arises from recollection alone; or the recognition "this gavaya is similar to the cow staying in my house," and so forth. In this regard, the commentator has cited examples where there is causality by both [perception and recollection].—Sampādanakartā.
The synthesis of two objects by means of their unity, similarity, dissimilarity, and so forth, is *saṅkalanā*. [For example:
"One who is hairy, has protruding teeth, is dark-complexioned, short-statured, large-eyed, and has a flat nose—recognize him there as Caitra. (*Nyāyamañjarī*, p. 143).
The *payombubhedin* is the *haṃsa*; the *ṣaṭpada* is known as the *bhramara*.
The *saptaparṇa*, however, should be understood by the learned as having uneven leaves (*viṣamacchada*).
A gem that possesses five colors is called *mecaka*; likewise, a broad-chested young woman and even a rhinoceros (*gaṇḍaka*) with a single horn are proclaimed [as auspicious].
Thus says the *Satyārtha-dīpikā*.
The summary: here, "by the northerner" is very well [stated]—[the text reads] "neck"—Tā. (Commentary).
—*apasadam*—Mu.—*apaśabdam*—Ḍe.—inferior;
*Tātparya*, p. 198.

However, for those who maintain that there is a distinct means of valid cognition called analogy (*upamāna*) whose object is similarity, it would follow that there must be another distinct means of valid cognition whose object is dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*), as they have said:
"When [it is said]... (Tātparya-ṭīkā).
Analogy is the means of proving what is to be proven through similarity with a well-known object;
it is a means of establishing resemblance. What would be the proof [of its validity] through dissimilarity? It is the communication of the designator. (Laghīyastraya 3.10)
"This is small, large, distant, near, tall, or not so;

it is long"—such conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding an object present before one arises from relative dependence (*vyapekṣā*); this is another means of proof [for the existence of the mind]. (Laghīyastraya 3.12)
For since the operations of "small," "large," and so forth are relative,
mental cognition that is independent of the senses— being conceptual—
would result in being a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that "similarity" (*sādharmya*) will be treated as an incidental indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) or that a division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) will be made, then the author of the Sūtra would be unskilled, because the Sūtra would lack its defining characteristics.
As they say: "Those who know the Sūtras recognize a Sūtra as being concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in its application, free from redundancy, and irreproachable."
The connection with the components of the sūtra is as follows: "similarity (upamāna) is that which is non-repetitive and non-excessive";
the classification is that similarity is twofold: by way of commonality (sādharmya) and by way of difference (vaidharmya).
Those who know the sūtras recognize a sūtra as being concise in syllables, free from ambiguity, substantial, comprehensive in its application, free from filler words, and irreproachable;
it is devoid of superfluous statements, explanatory digressions, and indeclinable particles used merely for metrical padding.

[Objection: Is this not merely two cognitions—a memory [in the form] "that" and a perception [in the form] "this"? We do not perceive any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called recognition (pratyabhijñāna) distinct from these two.
[Reply: This is not correct, because it is impossible for an object that is the domain of recognition to be grasped by either memory or perception;
for the object of recognition is a substance (dravya) that possesses a single continuum of prior and posterior forms.

And that [object] is not within the range of memory, because memory has as its object only what has been previously experienced; as they say: "Memory arises with respect to merely what was previously cognized as 'that';
however, this recognition—'this is that very same thing'—is something distinct [from memory]."
Nor is it the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that [perception] functions only with respect to the present manifestation;
nor is there no cognition other than seeing and remembering, since another cognition occurring after seeing and remembering is experienced,
and it is not proper to deny what is being experienced, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
In the cognition "this is that very same thing," identity (*ekatva*) is the object; however, in the cognition "the *gavaya* is similar to a cow," it is similarity (*sādṛśya*).
As it has been said:
"The recollection 'that' arises merely with respect to what was previously cognized. (Tātparya-ṭīkā)

"But this recognition, 'This is that very same [thing],' is something additional; it exceeds the mere previously cognized object. (Tattvasaṃgraha, Verse 453). It is superior to the mere previously established [cognition].
Regarding the phrase "of that [perception]," it means that of that very perception there is a vivarta— a transformation, a modification, or a synonym, as the case may be.
—Regarding the phrase "knowledge of another"—[the commentary] says: "Now, some claim that this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*);
but this is not so, because its object is a present thing that is currently present."

"Do not forget that what is connected and present is apprehended by the eye and other [senses]" (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 4, Verse 84). Therefore, the identity of the past and the present is not within the range of perceptual cognition. If it is argued that "the sense organ, assisted by memory, produces a perception whose object is that identity, and thus its nature as perception is proclaimed," we say no; for a sense organ, whose function is restricted to its own specific object, does not operate upon another object even when a hundred auxiliary factors are assembled.
For the sense organ of sight does not operate toward an object such as fragrance—even when assisted by the memory of its scent—since that [fragrance] is not its proper domain;
and a single substance pervading both past and present states is not the domain of the sense organs.
Nor is it reasonable to claim that the sense organ, even when aided by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), has unity as its object, for the very reason already stated.
Furthermore, it would be more appropriate to say that the cognition of that [oneness] arises from the self alone, in dependence upon the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa);
for it is observed that from a self refined by dream-vidyās and the like, there arises a specific cognition even regarding other objects.
Now, one might object: just as the eye becomes possessed of excellence when refined by collyrium and so forth, so too will [the self], aided by memory, become directed toward the object of oneness.

This is not so, because the excellence of a sense faculty is perceived precisely through its not overstepping its own object, and not by means of grasping another object; as Bhaṭṭa has said: "And whatever excellence is observed, it occurs through the perception of distant or subtle [objects] and the like, without overstepping its own domain; it would not consist in the functioning of the ear with regard to color-form."
Thus it is established, according to *Ślokavārttika* Sūtra 2, verse 114,

that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to the difference in its object, and is included within the category of the non-evident (*parokṣa*); so say the Vaiśeṣikas and others.
That which is connected and present is perceived by the eye and other [senses] (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 4,
Verse 84); it is that which is associated with the sense organs such as the eye and serves as their auxiliary.
The meaning is that it is the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), fortune, or karma [residing] in one's own present objects, such as visible forms, which [produces results] in other objects, such as odors.
Because of the reason consisting in the non-engagement with other objects— [as stated in] the Ḍe manuscript,
"for even the eye, though refined, is not capable of grasping smell and so forth"— Ṭīkā.

Furthermore, whatever excellence is observed [in perception] results from not overstepping its own object; it may occur in the perception of distant or subtle things within its own domain, but never through the functioning of the ear with respect to color-form. (Ślokavārttika, Sūtra 2, Verse 114)

The excellence of the eye is manifested by its perception of objects that are distant or subtle, but not so for the sense of hearing, because it has no operation regarding the objects of form; for the auditory function does not extend to form due to the difference in their respective objects— this is the reason.
Nor is this [cognition] invalid, because it is free from contradiction;
for if invalidity were to follow from contradiction in some instances, then the invalidity of even direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) would be difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, if the oneness of the self and so forth, as determined by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), did not exist, the systematic distinction between bondage and liberation would be untenable.
For if there were only one [self], then both bondage and liberation would belong to that same one; knowing himself to be bound and suffering, he would strive for the sake of the bliss of liberation.
But if there were plurality, then one would be the sufferer and another the enjoyer of happiness; who then would strive, or for what purpose?

Therefore, since the entire empirical life—both seen and unseen—is rooted in unity, and since the life of that unity depends upon recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), recognition is established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Just as one might say, "He who was swift is this very same person."
And while [this] is the case—
[the text] says:
"Now he states the definition of *ūha*."

Inference (*ūha*) is the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on the signs of apprehension and non-apprehension. Here, "apprehension" (*upalambha*) is taken to mean any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in general, and not perception alone, because there is the possibility of using even an inferential means as a proof; for pervasion is not contradicted in the case of inferential objects, just as it is in the case of perceptible ones.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that which will be described hereafter; the knowledge of it is a specific kind of determinative cognition (*nirṇaya*) that grasps it, namely *ūha* (reasoning).

When the impermanence of sound is to be proven, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is indeed the means of proof (*sādhana*), which is itself to be inferred by means of its varying according to the difference in conditions (*pratyayabhedabheditva*). Furthermore, it will be explained that even smoke, when suspected of being vapor, serves as a means of proof for the fire that is to be inferred.
Nor should it be said that this apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises from perception alone;

for perception is incapable of performing such extensive operations as determining that "whatever smoke there may be, in any other place or at any other time, is the effect of fire alone and not of anything else," because it arises from the power of a proximate object and is non-discursive (*avicāraka*).
Nor does it arise from inference, because at the time of grasping pervasion, the knower would have to become like a yogi, which is impossible given the incapacity for such a burden.

Even if there is such capacity, does the inference under discussion itself grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*), or is it another inference? In that regard, if the understanding of pervasion arises from the inference under discussion, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*):
for the inference establishes its own nature only when the pervasion has been understood, and the understanding of pervasion occurs only upon the establishment of that inference’s nature.

If the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is derived from another inference, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that [second inference] must also have its own pervasion already grasped in order to grasp the pervasion of the primary inference.
And if the grasping of that [second] pervasion occurs through itself alone, then what wrong has the first one done that another inference must be sought?
If it is by means of yet another inference, then even in thousands of aeons, the grasping of pervasion would be impossible.
—[Regarding] the locus—[Devaṇṇa]:

Now, if indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is non-investigative, then the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising in its wake will grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*). If this is argued, it is not so; for if the pervasion is not grasped by the indeterminate perception, it cannot be grasped by the conceptual construction, since the object of a conceptual construction is the very object already grasped by the indeterminate perception.

Alternatively, if the conceptual construction has as its domain a different object independent of the object of the indeterminate perception, then is that [conceptual construction] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or not?
If it were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), one would have to tolerate another means of knowledge distinct from perception and inference;
however, if it were not a valid means of knowledge, then placing faith in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) through it would be like a eunuch longing for a son.

By this, the claim that "the understanding of the relation between cause and effect, or pervader and pervaded, arises from non-perception (*anupalambha*) and from the non-perception of the cause and the pervader" is refuted. This is because non-perception is a specific form of perception, and since the non-perception of the cause and the pervader function as logical marks (*liṅga*), that [cognition] produced by them is itself an inference. Furthermore, the defect in the apprehension of pervasion through perception and inference has already been stated.
— not [being] so, because of non-perception; by this, the effect [is established] from non-perception;
not from perception, that is, from direct perception.
It is not from inference;
here, "there is no smoke because of the absence of fire" is non-perception (anupalambha).
There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees;
the cognition of fire arises from the cognition of smoke— this is the sequence of those two.
"By means of perception and non-perception"—this connects with the five [types of inference].

"There is no jar here because of non-perception" means because of its own non-perception by direct observation (*svapratyakṣānupalambhāt*). For the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalambha*) indeed pervades the comprehension of the relationship between cause and effect and the pervaded and the pervader, characterized by the mental representation of smoke and fire. Therefore, even from that, the understanding of cause and effect occurs in the Buddhist system; however, while the understanding of the pervaded and the pervader arises from the non-perception of the pervader, the understanding of both [cause and effect] arises only from *ūha* (logical reasoning).
That cognition which arises from a mark (liṅga) is indeed inference; as for that which has been rejected [as such], it is simply not inference.

The Vaiśeṣikas, however, maintain that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through inferential-cum-eliminative conceptual knowledge (*ūhāpoha-vikalpa-jñāna*), which is the fruit of perception.

For them, if this fruit of perception is either perception or inference, then pervasion is not made its object; if it is something other than those two, it follows that it must be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that because the conceptualization of pervasion is a fruit, it is not proper to question its status as a means of valid cognition—this is not so, because there is no contradiction in its being a means of valid cognition since it serves as the cause for the fruit characterized by inference, just as the cognition of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa-jñāna*), though a fruit of sensory contact, is a means of valid cognition in relation to the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya-jñāna*).
For the result of perception is either perception or inference; in that regard,
"this is a jar" is perception, whereas "there is fire here because of smoke" is inference, according to the reasoning stated regarding non-apprehension.

For it has been stated that [this occurs] by way of having direct perception as its fruit; indeed, from the knowledge of the general [form], there arises the knowledge of the particular— [as stated in the] *Anu-* and *Mu-pā*.
The cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) and the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) constitute the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
However, the followers of Yoga (*yauga*) assert that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) arises from perception alone when accompanied by reasoning (*tarka*).

Even for them, if the apprehension of pervasion does not arise from perception alone but rather from perception aided by reasoning, then let the apprehension of pervasion proceed from reasoning itself.

What is gained by cleansing the reputation of this ascetic—either by [denying] direct perception or by charging it with the ingratitude of rejecting the apprehension of pervasion obtained through the grace of *tarka*?

Furthermore, if it is claimed that *tarka* is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and therefore the apprehension of pervasion is not desired from it, why then is it not a *pramāṇa*? For its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*), at least, exists here just as it does in other means of valid cognition.
Since the state of being an object [of inference] does not exist without the object characterized by pervasion (vyāpti),
therefore, inference (*ūha*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that is intent upon grasping a pervasion not grasped by other means of valid cognition.
Tarka (reductio ad absurdum) is the deduction of the pervader upon the acceptance of the pervaded.
They say that the pervader is that which does not reside in what is other than that [the subject], while the pervaded resides only in that;
the probandum is called the pervader, and the means of proof is called the pervaded.
In the case of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the application [of the reason], it is thus; in the case of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it is the reverse— namely,
"only when there is [the object]..."— for the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is dependent upon the object of cognition (*prameya*).
He defines pervasion (vyāpti):
"Pervasion is the existence of the pervader (vyāpaka) only when the pervaded (vyāpya) exists, or the existence of the pervaded only there [where the pervader exists]. (6)
Pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a property belonging to both that which pervades and that which is pervaded.

When it is intended as a property of the pervader, then—given that the pervader is the object to be known—it exists wherever the pervaded property exists; thus, pervasion is the inherent property of the pervader which consists in its presence everywhere where the pervaded is present.
Consequently, the cognition of the pervaded itself as being "pervaded" is dependent upon the existence of the pervader.

However, it is not restricted in this way—that the existence [of the pervader] occurs only when the pervaded exists—because that would entail the fallacy of the reason being absent; for even non-pervaders, such as corporeality (*mūrtatva*) and the like, exist therein.

Nor is it restricted such that [the pervader] exists only when the pervaded exists, because that would result in qualities such as "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) not being valid reasons, and it would render a reason "common" (*sādhāraṇa*), since eternality (*nityatva*) exists only among knowable objects (*prameya*), just as fire and so forth do.
The mountain possessing smoke and so forth [is inferred] as having fire.
Of the probandum, which has the form of fire,
[the cognition occurs] in smoke on the mountain and so forth.

[Objection: "But surely, smoke possesses both properties [of being pervaded and pervading]. Since there is no distinction between the two properties, how is there a cognition of being pervaded (*vyāptatā*)? It belongs to the *hetu* alone, not even to the *vyāpaka*. For they remember that the *hetu* alone is what is pervaded; and thus they say: 'The *hetu* is pervaded, and it is of three kinds' (Hetu 1). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And therefore..."—with reference to [the *vyāpaka*]—ḍe.

The cognition of the pervaded itself—i.e., the cognition of its very state as the pervaded (Tātparya)—is the cognition of its being pervaded by the pervader, which is the probandum (*sādhya*), acting as the agent; that is, the cognition of the pervasion of the reason (*hetu*) depends upon that [probandum]. (Muktāvalī)
Fire would be the probans even if it were non-pervasive, because the probans— such as corporeality— is present there on that mountain; for in this case,
the pervaded [probans] such as "being produced" simply does not exist, due to its deviation by lightning and the like.

In cases such as lightning and the like, pervasion exists even without impermanence or being produced immediately after an effort; thus, it would follow that a common pseudo-reason (*sādhāraṇahetvābhāsa*) would be a valid reason.

However, when pervasion is intended as the property of the pervaded (*vyāpyadharma*), then there is pervasion only when the pervaded—the indicator—exists precisely where the pervader—the object to be indicated—is present; that is, its existence is only where the pervader exists, and not even in the absence of the latter. Thus, there is no pervasion [if the indicator occurs] in the absence of the pervader.
In this case as well, it is not determined that "the pervaded exists only there," because that would entail the absence of the reason (*hetu*) since even what is non-pervaded might exist there;

nor is it determined that "the pervaded exists there only," because that would result in things that reside in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) being non-reasons, and common [reasons] would become valid reasons, since knowability (*prameyatva*) necessarily exists in eternal things such as mountains and the like.
The smoke that is the pervaded would not have the status of a reason;
for the state of being a reason exists only when there is pervasion,
yet such pervasion does not exist anywhere.
Since fire, though it is the pervader, is present there on that mountain,

the mention of the property of being both the pervaded and the pervader where the pervader exists is for the purpose of demonstrating that the cognition of the pervasion should not be of a single uniform form due to the equal status of these properties in both cases.

For instance: in the former case, the restriction is by way of excluding non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), while in the latter, it is by way of excluding connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*). How, then, could there be a single form for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in both cases?
As it has been said:
"In both [cases], namely, regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)."

When existence itself is the probans by virtue of being a pervading property, the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) necessarily exists in the mark (liṅga), and conversely, the mark exists only in the possessor of the mark.
"In the reversal of the rule, there is no connection between the mark (liṅga) and that which possesses the mark (liṅgin).
(6) "Reversal" means that the mark itself is treated as that which possesses the mark, or that when that which possesses the mark exists, the other [the mark] necessarily follows.
Now, he defines inference (anumāna), which comes next in the sequence:
Inference is the cognition of the probandum (sādhya) from the probans (sādhana). The definitions of the probans and the probandum will be stated hereafter.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*)—consisting of a correct determination of the object—derived from a means of proof (*sādhana*) that has either been perceived or taught; it is so called because "one infers by means of this. It is the subsequent discernment following the apprehension of the mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of its relationship [with the probandum], occurring once [the object] has come within the range of vision.
Because it was mentioned after [the definition of] inference for others, it is therefore "subsequent";
that [inference] is of two kinds: for oneself and for others.
That inference is of two kinds, distinguished as being for one's own sake (svārtha) and for the sake of others (parārtha);
that which is capable of removing one's own delusion is for one's own sake.
That which is capable of dispelling the delusion of others is for the sake of others (*parārtha*);
that by which one understands this for oneself is for one's own sake (*svārtha*).
This is for the sake of another (*parārtha*), by which another person attains understanding; therein he characterizes the purpose for oneself (*svārtha*) as follows:

the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) arises from the means of proof (*sādhana*) whose sole defining characteristic is its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum as determined by oneself.

The non-occurrence [of the probans] in the absence of the probandum is "inseparable connection with the probandum" (*sādhyāvinābhāva*). That which has as its sole characteristic this very inseparable connection with the probandum, as ascertained in its own nature, is "that which has as its sole characteristic the inseparable connection with the probandum as ascertained by itself. From such a means of proof (*sādhana*), that is, from the mark (*liṅga*), the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), is inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).

And here, a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not a factor for the cognition of an imperceptible object by way of mere suitability, as a seed is for a sprout, because fire is not cognized from smoke that has not been perceived; nor does it depend on a cognition of its own ascertainment, as a lamp does for a jar and so forth, because [an object] is not cognized even from a perceived [mark] if its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has not been ascertained. Therefore, the function of the logical mark is precisely the ascertainment [of the probandum] through its being inseparable from the imperceptible object; thus, the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) is included—[as in the phrase] "the ascertained [logical mark]" (*niścitaṃ sā...*).—Ḍe. edition.

—The capacity of smoke toward the cognition of fire is indeed a specific power (*śakti-viśeṣa*); however, for smoke that has been perceived leads to the inference of fire, whereas that which has not been perceived does not.
By this, it is made known that smoke is the indicator (*gamaka*) of that which possesses smoke only when its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been ascertained, and not otherwise.

Now, do not the Buddhist monks (bhikṣus) declare that the three characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*)—its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its existence in the similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*)—are intended for the purpose of refuting fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)?
For instance, they state that the first characteristic is the certain presence of the mark (*liṅga*) in the subject (*dharmī*) which is the object of inference;
here, by the word "presence" (*sattva*), fallacies such as visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) are excluded.

By the particle *eva*, the "unestablished in part of the subject" (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) is excluded; for example, in the argument "The elements, such as earth and so forth, are impermanent because they possess odor," among the four elements—earth and the others—which constitute the subject, the property of possessing odor exists in earth alone.
By placing the particle *eva* after the word "existence" (*sattva*), the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) property is excluded.
For if it were said that "existence" (sattva) must be in the inferable object (anumeya) alone, then "audibility" (śrāvaṇatva) itself would be the reason;
however, by the inclusion of the term "ascertained" (niścita), all cases of the "unestablished due to doubt" (sandigdhāsiddha) are excluded.
The second characteristic is that existence is ascertained in the similar instances (sapakṣa) alone.
Here too, by the inclusion of the term "existent" (sattva), the contradictory reason is excluded;

for that [contradictory] does not exist in the similar instances (sapakṣa). By the particle "only" (eva), the common inconclusive reason is excluded; for that does not reside in the similar instances alone, but rather in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa) as well.

By placing the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) before the mention of "existence in the subject" (*sattva*), it was stated that even a reason such as "being produced immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) can be a valid logical reason (*hetu*), despite not pervading the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). For if the restriction were placed afterwards, the meaning would be: "that which has existence *only* in the similar instances is a valid reason"; in that case, "being produced immediately after effort" would not be a valid reason, as it does not exist in all similar instances.

By the word "ascertained" (*niścita*), the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose concomitance is doubtful is excluded; for example, "someone is omniscient because he is a speaker. For being a speaker is doubtful in the similar instance (an omniscient person), whereas its non-existence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is certain; this is the third characteristic (*rūpa*).
In this context, by the inclusion of the term "non-existent" (*asat*), the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is excluded, for the contradictory reason exists in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

By the particle "only" (*eva*), the common reason (*sādhāraṇa*) that occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances is excluded; for when "being produced immediately after effort" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "impermanence" exists in some parts of the dissimilar instances, such as lightning, but does not exist in others, such as space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, by necessity, there is the exclusion [of the reason] from the absence of the property to be proven (*asattva*).

For if the restriction were placed on the former [term], the meaning would be this: "Only that which does not exist in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is a valid reason. In that case, since "being produced immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) does not exist even in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), it would not be a valid reason. Consequently, the phrase "ascertained" (*niścita*) was placed before; by this, the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason whose exclusion from the dissimilar instance is doubtful is excluded.

Thus, since it is precisely the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason that is capable of avoiding defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), it is proper to accept only that; so what is the use of having only a single characteristic?

For example, in the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is visible, like a jar," visibility in sound is unestablished (*asiddha*), because [the word] *sattva* (existence) was not placed at the beginning [of the reason].
—Only audibility—Ḍe: Just as when "impermanence" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "audibility" alone is the reason (*hetu*), yet it deviates (*vyabhicarati*) in the case of a pot;
thus, when there is doubt as to whether [the substance] is smoke or vapor, smoke and the like serve to establish fire.
By this statement regarding the "existence" [of the reason], even that which is common [to both similar and dissimilar instances] is excluded;
the connection is that it is "excluded.
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a pot."

The property of being produced immediately after an effort exists in a jar, but not in lightning; nevertheless, the status of "being produced immediately after an effort" as a logical reason is established because it exists in at least one part of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
This positive concomitance (*anvaya*), which consists in its observation in the similar instances, is what the Jaina states to the Mīmāṃsaka.
Since everything that is omniscient is included within the class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*),
[the argument] "the jar is impermanent because it is produced, like sound"—
wherein the property of being produced exists in sound but not in space and so forth— is [an example of a fallacy].
For example: "Sound is produced by effort because it is impermanent, like a jar"; [the reason] exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), just as in the case:
"This person is not omniscient because he is a speaker."

That is incorrect, because the avoidance of the three faults is established precisely through the ascertainment of the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). For inseparable connection is the state of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*);
and that is not possible for what is unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), or deviant (*vyabhicārin*).

However, since it is observed that even when the three conditions (*trairūpya*) are present, a reason (*hetu*) lacks probative force (*agamakatva*) if there is an absence of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), as in the case: "He is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Maitra, like other sons of Maitra"—if, in that instance, a restriction (*niyamavatī*) regarding exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not perceived, then it lacks probative force; therefore, since inseparable connection is the very nature of that [exclusion], even if the other two conditions are present, if the probative force toward the establishment of its own probandum is not admitted in the absence of that [inseparable connection], then that [inseparable connection] alone should be the primary definition (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, because it is established that [the reason] functions as a prover when it exists [in the subject] independently of any other two forms [of the logical mark], just as even for the proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins), means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are accepted because otherwise the establishment of what is desired and the refutation of what is undesired would be impossible.

Nor is there here the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) or presence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattva*); rather, the capacity to prove is established solely through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

[Objection: But if the property of being a feature of the subject were absent, then reasons such as "the palace is white because the crow is black" would also follow as valid. [Reply: Not so; for we accept that even those things which are not features of the subject can function as proofs by the power of invariable concomitance alone.

And since that [triple characteristic] does not exist here [in such cases], one must accept that inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) alone is the primary definition of a logical reason (*hetu*); for it is observed that a reason possesses probative power even when the triple characteristic (*trairūpya*) is absent,
whereas the triple characteristic cannot be the definition of a reason because it is under-inclusive (*avyāpaka*).

And likewise, in the celebrated proof "everything is momentary because it exists," the Buddhists indeed accept that existence (*sattva*), even though it is absent from the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), is a means of cognition;
as it has been said regarding the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*):
In the aforementioned inference,

the two characteristics consisting of presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and existence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*) would be absent if there were no exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) characterized by necessity.
Because exclusion from the counter-position is restricted [to the subject],
for the proponent of the emptiness of non-duality,

even the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not exist as a thesis (*pakṣa*) in his view; how then could there be the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)?
— Because of the consequence of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

In cases such as "He is dark-skinned because he is the son of Maitrī," where there is the property of being otherwise inexplicable (anyathānupapannatva), what is the use of the [other] three [conditions]?
"If that which cannot be established otherwise [than by the probandum] exists, what is the use of the three [other characteristics]?

By this, the Naiyāyika claim that a logical reason possesses five characteristics is also refuted, because those too are merely elaborations of *avinābhāva* (inseparable connection). To explain: the three forms previously mentioned, along with "having an uncontradicted object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and "having no counter-argument" (*asatpratipakṣatva*), constitute the five forms.

In this context, "having a sublated object" (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) refers to being employed immediately after the presentation of a thesis that is contradicted by perception or scripture. For example: "The composite substance of fire is not hot, because it is produced, like a jar," or "Wine may be drunk by a Brahmin, because it is a liquid substance, like milk.
Because these [theses] are negated, [the opposite] is "having an unsublated object" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*).

The state of having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatva*) consists in being sublated by a counter-reason (*pratipakṣahetu*). For example: "Sound is non-eternal, because its eternal properties are not perceived. Here, the counter-reason is: "Sound is eternal, because its non-eternal properties are not perceived.
Because this [counter-reason] is negated, there is the absence of a counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*).

In that regard, since the contradictory (*bādhita*) and the counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*) lack invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), both of these two forms are already subsumed by invariable concomitance alone;
as it has been said: "Because of the contradiction between invalidation (*bādhā*) and invariable concomitance" (Hetuprakaraṇa, Chapter 4).

Furthermore, since these two fallacies lack a subject in the form of a thesis (*pakṣa*) characterized by its own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*), these two defects are rendered purposeless by that very [absence of the thesis] itself; what is the point of stating them separately?
Thus it is established: [the definition] is "that which has the characteristic of being inseparable from the probandum" (sādhyāvinābhāvilakṣaṇa);
that is to say, the probandum (sādhya) is what is to be inferred (anumeya).
—*taddharma*— Ḍe.
*Tātparya*, p. 340.
—*asya tatpra*— Ḍe.
As for what they say:
these two are indeed fallacies of the *pakṣa* (the thesis);
therein, it characterizes inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

Inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is the rule of simultaneous or successive occurrence between two things that occur simultaneously or successively. Regarding simultaneous occurrences: it is the rule of simultaneous occurrence between form (*rūpa*) and taste (*rasa*) which depend on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīna*), as well as between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), such as "being a *śiṃśapā*" and "being a tree. Regarding successive occurrences: it is the rule of successive occurrence between the rising of the Pleiades (*kṛttikā*) and the rising of the Big Dipper (*śakaṭa*), as well as between cause and effect, such as smoke and fire. The rule of simultaneous occurrence for simultaneous things and the rule of successive occurrence for successive things—understood from the context as applying to the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)—is inseparable connection.
Regarding the probandum and the probans:
it has been stated that such an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva), when ascertained, is a factor for the comprehension of the probandum.
And from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does that certainty arise?
It cannot arise from perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that which is sensory has its operation restricted to objects present [to the senses].
As for the mind (*manas*), although it has all things as its object, its activity nevertheless occurs only with respect to objects already grasped by the senses.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that blind and deaf persons and others would not exist;
however, "cognizing all objects" is said only in the sense of having as its object everything within the range of all the sense-faculties, and not independently through yogic perception.
Let it be that the cognition of an inferable object occurs precisely from the apprehension of an inseparable relation (avinābhāva); what is the use of this wretched inference?

He says that if the certainty of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) were derived from inference, the aforementioned faults of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) would necessarily follow;

furthermore, there exists no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) capable of grasping such an object—this is indicated by the phrase "being certain for oneself" (*svaniścita*). Thus, [the certainty] is established as being certain for oneself.

In the same manner, with respect to external objects perceivable by the senses, it apprehends pleasure and so forth by means of the mind alone, because it grasps the objects of all the sense faculties,
such as fire and the like.
— Even the attainment [of certainty] from that— according to the Ḍe manuscript—

[is not possible], for if the ascertainment of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is achieved through inference, then what other inference must be considered for the ascertainment of the invariable concomitance of that very inference?
And for that too another, and so on, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

But there is a mutual dependence: the determination of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) arises from inference, and the emergence of inference occurs only when invariable concomitance is determined;
therefore, its determination arises from *ūha* (reflective reasoning).
The certainty of that invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) arises from reasoning (ūha), which has been previously defined; thus,
the means of proof (sādhana) has both been characterized and examined.
Now he analyzes that:
"The means of proof is fivefold: intrinsic nature, cause, effect, inherence in the same object, and the contradictory. (12)
There are five types of proof: the four—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—are proofs for affirmation, while the contradictory (*virodhi*) is a proof for negation.
Regarding essential nature as a proof, for example, when the impermanence of sound is to be proven, "producedness" or "audibility" may be used.
Now, since audibility is an over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, how can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) be established?
We reply that it is by the force of the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in the case of the opposite [of existence] that [the probans] is [established], just as in the case of existence itself.

Furthermore, existence alone is not the reason (*hetu*), because if it were, specific properties such as "having an origin" (*utpattimattva*), "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), "occurring immediately after an effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*), and "varying according to the difference in conditions" (*pratyayabhedabheditva*) would result in being non-reasons.
Moreover, what indeed is this so-called "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatva*)?
If "being present" (vartamānatva) belongs only to the subject (*pakṣa*), then that is equally true of "existence" (*sattva*) when proving that everything is momentary.

If the subject, which possesses the property to be proven, is also considered a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), then what is this prejudice here? If only that which is other than the subject is a similar instance, then in the argument "diamond is scratchable by iron because it is earthy, like wood," the quality of being earthy would also lead to the conclusion that diamond is scratchable by iron.

If it is argued that [the reason] is not [a valid probans] because of the absence of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), then let this alone be the definition of a logical reason (*hetu*).

If it is further objected that this would result in even that which is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) becoming a means of proof, let it be so provided that there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). For instance, the rising of the *kṛttikā* constellation is seen to be indicative of the rising of the cart (the Pleiades), and a consistent instruction is seen to be indicative of the existence of an omniscient being.
However, the blackness of a crow does not indicate the whiteness of a palace, as it is not impossible otherwise; thus, due to its lack of necessity, it is not a true indicator.
Likewise, since visual perceptibility in a jar is possible even without impermanence in sound,
audibility and the like— though they are "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reasons— do not deviate from impermanence.
Now, if impermanence is to be proven of sound on the grounds of its being produced, would it not follow that impermanence applies to the substance as well, just as it does to its modes?

This is not so, because it is precisely the impermanence of the synonyms that is to be proven. Do you perhaps forget that even what is not explicitly stated becomes the probandum (sādhya) if it is made the object of one's intention? [Objection: But if there is identity between "being produced" (kṛtakatva) and "impermanence" (anityatva), then it follows that the probandum is already established just like the probans (sādhana), and the probans would likewise be a probandum just like the probandum. [Reply: This is true; however, the formal argument (prayoga) is for the purpose of dispelling delusion.

As it has been said: "Regarding permanence, which is the opposite of impermanence, the objection is: 'How could sound, which was previously inaudible by nature, become audible through utterance later? This subverting proof [of contradiction] establishes impermanence because audibility is incompatible with permanence; existence consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)."
And since that [reasoning] is applicable only to the position of impermanence, audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) also results in being a property of existence (*sattva*),
because its occurrence is established through the non-arising of the constellation Rohiṇī when the rising of the constellation Kṛttikā is observed.

Someone might argue: "There exists a person who perceives all things directly, because otherwise the non-contradictory knowledge of astrology would be inexplicable. However, in this inference—"Sound is impermanent because it is visible"—visibility is established even without the impermanence of sound, as it occurs in jars and other objects; thus, being established elsewhere, it does not prove the impermanence of sound.
(Smaṃ visma—Ḍe)
Even for that which has a beginning, there is no end; yet, for one who through delusion perceives it as such,
the relationship of probandum and probans regarding the impermanence of a single entity would not be subject to fault.

Just as fire is [inferred] from smoke that is doubted to be vapor or the form of a mosquito-wing, or the rising of specific clouds is [inferred] from rain— how is it that this [reason], though well-known even to children, cowherds, and women, is not perceived even by a subtle-seeing logician?
For indeed, everyone who seeks a result proceeds to act upon seeing a specific cause.

If it is argued that this specific feature must be known—that which is non-deviant—and that activity proceeds solely from the certainty of causality; let that be a certainty regarding a specific logical mark (*liṅga*) produced by perception. However, regarding the future result, we perceive no basis other than inference.
Since every cause would become a non-cause due to occasional deviation, there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the effect itself would likewise be so.

If it is argued that [the eye] is not [the cause of the cognition] because tears and so forth are not its effects, there is no fault here either: whatever does not arise from something is not the cause of that thing.
For just as something is designated as an effect with reference to a certain cause, so too is something designated as a cause with reference to a certain effect.

Just as there is no status of being an effect with respect to that which does not produce it, likewise there is no status of being a cause with respect to that which is not produced by it; thus, there is no distinction between these two cases.

Moreover, for the proponent of logic (nyāyavādin) who desires the inference of color through the inference of a single causal complex consisting of taste and so forth, the causality of the cause is indeed accepted; as he says: "The instrument... [fragmentary manuscript reading].
Maśavarti—
O friend, this smoke indicates fire;
rain is imminent due to the rising of specific clouds.
Regarding rain that is about to fall,
the Sage said: "The cause is unimpaired."
From direct perception— according to the manuscript reading *mu*—
causes do not necessarily possess their effects; rather,
it is the effect that serves as the indicator.
As they say:
"The cognition of color and so forth, which depend on the same causal complex, occurs through taste;
just as fire is known from smoke, so too is fire known as that which effects the transformation of fuel and acts as a burner."

"This taste possesses a specific causal complex (*vaiśiṣṭyasāmagrī*), because its possession of that specific quality would otherwise be inexplicable. From this reason, there arises the knowledge of the specific causal complex; and from that, the knowledge of [the cause's] capacity to produce color and so forth.

This occurs through the inference of a property of the cause (*hetudharma*), just as [fire is inferred] from smoke which is a transformation of fuel. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.10). Here, "cause" (*hetu*) means the causal factor (*kāraṇa*); its "property" (*dharma*) is the capacity to produce color and so forth; the "inference" (*anumāna*) of that is its determination (*pariccheda*) by means of a logical mark (*liṅga*).
Nor do we claim that anything whatsoever is a cause;

rather, [we ask] how it is known that for a particular thing there is no obstruction of its power by mantras and the like, nor any deficiency of other causes? To this we reply: there certainly exists a distinction between that which possesses qualities and that which is otherwise.
However, that thorough knowledge belongs even to those who gather dust,
as they say: "It is a cooperative cause."
And even for those such as Haladhara, there is the totality [of these sounds], whose unimpeded nature shatters mountain caves with the onset of deep thundering.

"Clouds whose lofty forms are reddened by contact with streaks of lightning, and which possess a dark luster like that of a bee, a buffalo-horn, a serpent, or a tamāla tree—such clouds never fail to bring rain in this world. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 129; Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya, 20; Nyāyamañjarī, p. 126).
An effect [is inferred] as follows: from a specific swelling of a river in relation to rain, from smoke in relation to fire, and from breath and so forth in relation to consciousness.
If it is asked, "How is the specific nature of that swelling known?"—on this point, the Naiyāyikas have stated what they say:
"Possessing large, turbid water characterized by the presence of whirlpools and eddies..."

Is it not possible to recognize even this extraordinary flood of the river, marked by masses of foam bursting from the violent impact of the waves and crowded with thick moss, fruits, and young grass being carried along?
As it is said in the *Nyāyamañjarī* (p. 130): "The determination that smoke, breath, and so forth are also effects is not difficult," as they have stated:
The [sequence] beginning with *prāṇa*—how is it known? As it was said: "In the *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*."
The water was turbid and vast, possessing whirlpools and eddies, marked by masses of foam bursting forth from the violent impact of formidable waves—
*sphuṭaḥ phena* (D).
Is it not possible to discern even a particular flood of a river, crowded with abundant moss, fruits, and young grass, as it flows along? (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 130)
It cannot be established—
[as] he said:
"Smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of an effect."
The nature of an effect is its occurrence when the cause is present, or its non-occurrence when the cause is absent;

if it were to exist even in the absence of that [cause], it would transcend the state of having a cause. (Pramāṇavārttika 1.35) For if an effect were to exist even in the absence of its cause, it would either be causeless or have something other than its [intended] cause as its cause.
If there were no cause, there would be either perpetual existence or perpetual non-existence.

If there were another cause, then since it would arise from something other than what is observed, it would not be produced by that which is observed; and since it would arise from the observed even in the absence of others, it would not have another as its cause—thus it would simply be causeless.
Regarding this, it has been said: "That which is perceived to arise from something else does not possess the nature of smoke, because of the difference in its causes."
And it has been stated that smoke has an external cause;
moreover, [the alternative would be] causelessness.
One might imagine that the cause of this [fire] is other than fire,
or that it is something else entirely.
If the head of Śakra has the nature of fire, then it is simply fire;
but if it does not have the nature of fire, how could there be smoke there from an anthill? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.37)

Thus, the effect—such as breath and so forth—which is impossible without consciousness, leads to the inference of that consciousness, just as audibility leads to the inference of impermanence; for, by virtue of a subverting proof in the case of the contrary, the pervasion (vyāpti) of this [breath] is established just like that of existence (sattva), as has already been largely stated.
Therefore, although breath and so forth are "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) reasons, they do not deviate from consciousness.
Furthermore, positive concomitance (anvaya) is not the defining characteristic of a logical reason, because in its absence there would be no fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa).

That which is contradictory (*viruddha*) is indeed [present] only in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), while that which is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) is present even in the counter-example. When omniscience is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the very absence of negative concomitance (*vyatirekābhāva*) in the case of "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*) is the cause for its status as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), not doubt regarding positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus, even according to the proponents of logic (*nyāyavādin*), these two are declared to be fallacies of the reason precisely due to the absence of negative concomitance. Furthermore, even the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason would not be inconclusive if it were certain that it is absent in the absence of the property to be proven; for, in the absence of any other alternative, it would establish the property to be proven.

Furthermore, if positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were the [sole] form [of a valid reason], then just as a reason that subsists in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is non-informative because it lacks negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) to some extent, so too would a reason that subsists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) be non-informative due to its lack of positive concomitance to some extent.

As it has been said: "If the form of the reason is asserted to be positive concomitance, just like negative concomitance, then it would not be present in both the similar and dissimilar instances; rather, it would be like that which is absent from both."
