If it is argued that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) consists in existence only in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and not merely existence in the similar instances, then let it be so; however, this would amount to accepting our own position, namely that it is indeed negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For we have also established that the logical reason (*hetu*) is characterized solely by "the impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*);
thus, it is not only in the similar instances but also in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*).

If form (rūpa) is asserted to be a positive concomitance (anvaya) of the reason just as its negative concomitance (vyatireka) is, then it would not be both [present] in the similar class (sapakṣa), just as it is not both [present] in the dissimilar class (asapakṣa); for in the similar class, there is either presence or absence of that [reason].
Likewise, when one object is perceived—whether it be seen or unseen—the means of proof (sādhana) which inheres in that same substrate is established by the probandum (sādhya).

This constitutes "inherence in a single object" (*ekārthasamavāyitva*), as in the case of color and taste residing in a single fruit. Examples include the rising of a cart and the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation; the rising of the moon and the swelling of the ocean; rain and the agitation of ants carrying their eggs; and the burning of a betel vine and the withering of its leaves. In these cases, the taste inheres in the same object as the color, or the color inheres in the same object as the taste; for a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not possible between two things that exist simultaneously.
Dependent on inherence (samavāya):
"This fruit possesses a specific color because it possesses a specific taste;
this portion of the sky will have the rising of the constellation Śakaṭa because it possesses the rising of the Kṛttikās."
This time possesses an increase of the ocean because of the rising of the moon; likewise, in what follows, time is the subject (dharmin)— [possessing] a form that has entered [into it].
If it is argued that the cause which produces an effect at the same time is what is inferred, then the effect would not be the object of inference;

for if the cause is inferred, the effect is already inferred by implication, since there can be no status as a producer in the absence of that which is produced. [To this we reply: Alas, in that case, it would follow—which you do not desire—that the cause is the inferential indicator (*anumāpaka*) of the effect.

However, in the cases of the rising of the constellation Kṛttikā and the appearance of the cart, the relationship of probandum and probans exists according to their respective invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

As it has been said: "But when there is a co-inherence in a single object, just as [the presence] of certain things [indicates others], so those are the indicators; therefore, the cart is not an indicator from the rising of the Kṛttikās. The same should be stated regarding other means of proof as well."
Now, one might ask: why is the inherence of "producedness" and "impermanence" in a single object not accepted? It is not so, because those two are identical, as it has been said:
"The nature of the cause is known from the form of the effect."
And of what nature is that?
It is inferred as the producer of an effect characterized by taste which occurs at the same time,
because when the rising of the constellation Śakaṭa is perceived, the rising of Kṛttikā is also perceived, and thus its cognition does not arise through inference.
Inherence in a single object, however, is such that those things which possess it are themselves the indicators; thus, the cart is not the indicator because of the rising of the Kṛttikā star.
Existence depends on a beginning and an end, while being produced is impermanence.

"The cause is one and the two probanda are not based on a single locus. Thus, the four means of proof—essential nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth—function as proofs for affirmation; however, they function as proofs for negation only in relation to a contradictory [object], for it is that [contradictory] which, by its own presence, establishes the negation of the other, since otherwise contradiction would not be established.

The word "ca" (and) indicates that because these—namely, essential nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*kāraṇa*), effect (*kārya*), and pervader (*vyāpaka*)—establish their own probandum (*sādhya*) by being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapanna*), for that very reason they themselves do not exist in the absence of that [probandum]. Therefore, he states that their non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is also a means of establishing non-existence.
Among those, non-perception of essential nature is as follows: "There is no jar here, because of the non-perception of that which is capable of being seen.
Non-perception of a cause is as follows: "There is no smoke here, due to the absence of fire."
Non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*) is, for example: "There are no causes of smoke here whose capacity is unimpeded, because of the absence of smoke.
Non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) is, for example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because of the absence of trees.
[In this case], those that co-inhere in the same object (*ekārthasamavāyin*) are the pervaders.
Precisely because it cannot be otherwise [than the probandum],

[the reason] is the absence of smoke, or [it is] the pervader— [the pervasion being established] through contradiction; for that which is contradictory to the object of negation, as well as its effect, cause, and pervader, and the effect of that which is contradictory, [constitute the contradictory reason].

For example: "there is no sensation of cold," "the causes of cold do not possess unimpeded capacity," "there are no specific instances of horripilation," and "there is no sensation of frost"—these constitute various forms of formal argument (*prayoga*) based on the effect (*kārya*), such as [the inference] from fire or smoke.
As for the effect: ḍe.

Having defined and analyzed the means of proof (sādhana), he states the definition of the probandum (sādhya): "The probandum is that which is intended to be proven, is unestablished, and is not sublated; it is the subject (pakṣa).
That which is intended to be established is "that which is desired to be proven" (*siṣādhayiṣita*).

By this, there is an exclusion of that which is not intended to be established from being a "probandum" (*sādhya*); for example, for a Vaiśeṣika, the statement "sound is eternal" [is a probandum], whereas "sound is a quality of space" is not a probandum for the Vaiśeṣika even though it is accepted by him because it is stated in his treatise, since at that time it is not intended to be established.

Furthermore, a subject (*pakṣa*) is considered "intended" even if not explicitly stated; for example, in the argument "The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another (*parārtha*), because they are composite, like beds, seats, and other [objects]," the term "for the sake of another" means "for the sake of a self" (*ātmartha*).

Similarly, in the argument "Earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent cause (*buddhimatkāraṇapūrvaka*), because they are effects," [the intended subject] is "preceded by an incorporeal and omniscient [cause]. Thus, "for the sake of another" refers to the intellect (*buddhi*)—[as noted in Ḍe].

—Previously, by the statement "the unestablished" (asiddha), it is meant that an object which is the domain of non-apprehension, doubt, or error is the *sādhya* (that which is to be proven), not that which is already established, such as [the argument] "sound is audible.
For the *nyāya* (logical method) does not operate upon what is unperceived or already determined; *Nyāyabhāṣya* 1.1.1.
1.1 Thus he said, "This is indeed for the entire assembly."
By the term "uncontradicted" (*abādhyam*), he states that what is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition should not be the probandum (*sādhya*);
this is the definition of the probandum,
and "the thesis" (*pakṣa*) is merely another name for the probandum itself.
He demonstrates the contradiction that is to be excluded by the apprehension of what is non-sublated:
"Contradictions consist of perception, inference, scripture, worldly consensus, one's own words, and common understanding."
Perception and the other means of knowledge are "sublating" (bādhā) because they sublate by establishing objects contrary to [the thesis].

Among these, sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*) is as follows: "Fire is not hot," "Honey is not sweet," "The opening jasmine bud does not have fragrance," "A jar is not visible to the eye," "Sound is not audible," "External objects do not exist," and so forth.
Sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*) is, for example: "The palm of the hand has hair," or "Sound is eternal.
In these cases, there is sublation by inference through non-perception (*anupalambha*) and through the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*).
Sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*) is, for example: "Dharma does not bring about happiness after death."

That dharma bestows happiness in the next world is established by all the scriptures. As for the contradiction with worldly consensus, such as [the claim] that "a human skull is pure," it is well known in the world that human skulls and the like are impure.
Contradiction by one's own statement is, for example, "My mother is barren.
Contradiction by common cognition is, for example, "The moon is not the moon.
Here, the fact that the moon is denotable by the word "moon" is established by common cognition; thus, there is contradiction by common cognition.
"Because it is produced" is the logical reason (*hetu*) for the probandum (*sādhya*).
Because it arises from various tastes, like a combination of many flavors;
because it is a part of the creeper, like a leaf;
and because it is absolutely distinct from form, like wind.

Because it does not appear in its actual state, that which exists does not exist even though it does not appear in its actual state, just as cognition [does not exist] because it is a part of the body like an arm,
or because it possesses limbs similar to those of a woman in the forest.
The moon, which is denoted by the word "candra," is not [necessarily] the lunar disc (śaśin) because it has risen in the sky, like the sun.
Here, there is a doubt as to whether the probandum (sādhya) is the property (dharma) or the collection of both the property and the locus (dharmin); therefore, to exclude this doubt, he says:
"The probandum is the locus qualified by the property to be proven," though in some cases it is the property alone.

"The probandum" (sādhya) means that which is denoted by the word *sādhya* and expressed by the word *pakṣa*; to the question "What is it?", he replies: it is the locus (*dharmin*), such as sound, as qualified by the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*), such as impermanence.
This property of being denotable by the term "probandum" (sādhya) is relative to the time of formal application (prayoga).
However, at the time of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), the property itself is expressed by the word "probandum," for otherwise the pervasion could not be established;
indeed, it is impossible to establish a pervasion such as "every mountain possessing smoke is possessed of fire" upon the mere sight of smoke, because that would contradict valid cognition (pramāṇa).
15— Regarding the dependence [on other factors]— in order to define the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), he says:
The subject (dharmin) is established by means of valid cognition (pramāṇasiddha).
A subject becomes established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception (pratyakṣa) and so forth, as in the case: "This place possesses fire."
For here, the locus (*deśa*) is established by perception;

by this [statement], he refutes the Buddhist position that "the entire operation of inference and the object of inference (*anumeya*) proceeds according to the principle of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) as they have ascended into the intellect, and does not depend on external existence or non-existence.

For this conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*) cannot establish a property-bearer if it has not apprehended an objective support (*ālambana*), whether internal or external; because if that [support] were unreal, it would be impossible for the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) which are based upon it to be real, since such a cognition could not establish a real entity even through a mediated succession.
Therefore, a mountain or the like, once established by another conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) and assuming the status of an object, attains the state of being the subject (*dharmin*);
and this being so, it is entirely logical that what is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should serve as the subject.
The means of proof and the object to be proven— the manifestation of the object of knowledge.
That subject is the substratum of those two [properties] which belong to that conceptual cognition of them.
Non-conceptual [cognition] has an attained object; its conceptualization also has an attained object— thus,
even through such a succession of characteristics, it is non-conceptual.
He states the refutation regarding the status of conceptual construction as an object: "Even though established by the intellect..."
A subject (*dharmin*) is not established exclusively by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, a subject may also be established by conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*).
By the word "also" (*api*), he shows that a subject may be established by both valid cognition and conceptual cognition.

In that regard, when the subject (*dharmin*) is established by cognition, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)— whether existence or non-existence— is established by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example, "the omniscient one exists" or "the sixth element does not exist"— here the subject is established because otherwise, the non-contradictory knowledge of astrology would be inexplicable.
Since that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived, [it follows that it does not exist].

Now, if the subject (*dharmin*) is not directly present, then because properties of both existence and non-existence would be unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive, they could not serve as the objects of inference; how, then, can existence and non-existence be the probanda?
To this, he says:
When the reasons are unestablished, there exists no property of an entity that is deviant and dependent on both [sides] with respect to the subject (dharmin).
"The reason possesses both properties;
how can that existence, which is a contradictory property of non-existence, be established? (Pramāṇavārttika 1.192–3). Thus, "contradictory property"—Mu.
The contradictory [position] is that non-existence (adharma) is the subject;
[the reply is: no, for omniscience is not thus, because in mental perception only a subject in the form of a positive entity (bhāvarūpa) is apprehended.

Nor is inference useless because its existence is already established by the establishment of that [object], for even if someone—out of sheer audacity or some other reason—does not accept it despite having done so, inference remains effective against such a person. Furthermore, there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) resulting from the possibility of the existence of things like a donkey’s horn through mental cognition, because such mental cognition is a pseudo-perception (mānasapratyakṣābhāsa), as its object is a thing whose existence has been sublated by a contrary cognition.

If it is asked, "In that case, how can the sixth element (the self) and so forth possess the status of a subject (*dharmin*)? [The answer is: Because at the time of the formal application of the subject, no subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) arises, the possibility of its existence is established. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) and the like simply because a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) is absent; for, since there is a well-ascertained absence of any subverting means of knowledge, there is a certainty of existence—just as in the case of pleasure and so forth—and thus doubt is untenable therein. [To this, the opponent replies: "Not so. — *Ḍe*.
The existence of the subject [is established] by means of the objects.
The subject (dharmin) established for both [parties] is like existence (sattva) and pleasure (sukha) etc., as in the case: "Sound is impermanent."

For it is not possible for those of limited vision to ascertain through perception all sounds as delimited by specific directions, locations, and times; thus, the fact that sound is established as an object of valid cognition by both [the proponent and the opponent] allows its properties, such as impermanence, to be proven by the cognizers.
By the cognizers.
What is established by those who perceive directions indeterminately [as being] in a determinate direction and place?
It is "having accomplished" (prasādhya)— thus [says] the Tātparya.
[Objection: But surely the example (dṛṣṭānta) is also recognized as a constituent part of inference;
so why are only the probandum (sādhya) and the probans (sādhana) stated to be the constituents of inference, and not the example? [The author] says:
"The example is not a constituent part of inference."
Regarding the eighteenth and nineteenth sūtras, they are seen written together in the *Mūla* manuscript without any distinguishing mark;
here, even for us, the unity of these two appears very clear—[Sampādaka].
An example, whose definition will be stated later, is not a constituent part—that is, a cause—of inference.
Why is this? He says:
Because the establishment of that [object] occurs through the mere means of proof (sādhana)—

since inference, which is characterized by the comprehension of the probandum, exists through a means of proof defined by the "inseparability from the probandum" (sādhyānyathānupapatti) even when devoid of an example— the example is not a constituent part of inference.

For would that [perception] be useful for the comprehension of the probandum (*sādhya*), or for the apprehension of the inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), or for the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)?
First, it cannot be the first position, because the comprehension of the probandum is established from the reason (*hetu*) as already described.
Nor can it be the second, because the apprehension of the inseparable relation arises precisely from the sublation (*bādhaka*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
Furthermore, how could an example consisting of a single individual instance convey the pervasion (vyāpti) in its entirety?
To establish the pervasion regarding other individual instances, another example would have to be sought.

Furthermore, because it is impossible to ascertain the pervasion in its entirety due to its nature as a particular manifestation (*vyakti*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if one required further and further examples.

Nor is the third [alternative] tenable; for one who has grasped the relationship [between the probans and the probandum] remembers the pervasion from the mere perception of the means of proof (*sādhana*), whereas one who has not grasped the relationship does not remember it even in the presence of an example, since remembrance is preceded by prior apprehension.
An illustration of a present cause.
In every man, there being [a woman].
He states the definition of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) as follows:
"It is the locus for the observation of pervasion (*vyāpti*)."

*Sa* (that)" refers to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "The characterized" (*lakṣya*) is the pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Demonstration" (*darśana*) is the manifestation of that which has been characterized; its "ground" (*bhūmi*) means its basis (*āśraya*). This is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Now, if the example is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of inference, for what purpose is it defined?

It is said: in the context of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), because an exception-based example (*āpavādika udāharaṇa*) will be permitted in accordance with the requirements of comprehension,
and because that [example] consists in the statement of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), the definition of an illustration is established.

Furthermore, for some cognizer, the realization of internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*) occurs by the power of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) observed in an example; thus, the definition of an example is not untenable even in the section on inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*). (20) [Śiṣya]
Because the example is intended to be inferred at the point of its introduction.
He states its division:
"It is twofold, by way of similarity and dissimilarity.

In the *Tātparya-ṭīkā*, the *Mūla-bhāṣya*, the *Saṃgraha-bhāṣya*, and in the palm-leaf manuscript of the sūtra along with its commentary, that example does not exist; rather, it is of two kinds: by similarity through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and by dissimilarity through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
He analyzes the example by similarity: "An example by similarity is that which possesses the property to be proven as necessitated by the proving property. (22)

An example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is that which possesses the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*), being connected with the means of proof (*sādhana-dharma*) rather than occurring by mere chance (*kākatālīya*);
for example, when sound is to be proven as impermanent by virtue of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), a jar or the like serves as the example.
Dharma is indeed the means of accomplishment (sādhana),
while dharma is that which is to be accomplished (sādhya)— Ḍe.

He explains the example by dissimilarity (vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta): An example by dissimilarity is that which possesses the cessation of the probans (sādhana-dharma) necessitated by the cessation of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma).
Thus ends the second daily lesson of the first chapter in the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* composed by the venerable teacher Hemacandra.
The first chapter is completed. — Tā — Mū.
Thus... the second daily lesson.
First Chapter—The *Saṃmūrchita* [Commentary]:

A counter-example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is that which possesses the exclusion of the probans (*sādhanadharmanivṛtti*) as necessitated by the exclusion of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharmanivṛtti*), and not merely any exclusion of the probans at random;
for example, when sound is to be proven as impermanent by virtue of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), space (*ākāśa*) and so forth serve as the counter-example.
Thus ends the second lesson of the first chapter of the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* and its commentary, composed by the venerable teacher Hemacandra.
Now begins the second chapter.

Inference for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*), characterized in the first chapter, has now been completed; he now defines inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), which follows in due order:
"That which arises from the statement of the means of proof as previously described is [inference] for the sake of others."
The first and second sūtras are seen written together in the Tā-mū manuscript without any distinguishing mark,
as it is said: "The statement of that means of proof (*sādhana*) which has as its sole characteristic an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) as determined by oneself."

"Abhidhāna" (designation) is that by which something is designated or communicated to another; it is speech (*vacana*). That from which the correct determination of the meaning arises is "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*); the meaning is that it is the cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) which depends upon instruction from another.
As it has been said:
Now, they say that speech is inference for the sake of others; how is that so? He says:
"Speech [is so called] by way of metaphor.

For speech, being insentient, is not the direct cause of the fruit of valid cognition; thus, it does not possess the status of a primary means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, by virtue of being the cause of inference in its primary sense, it attains the designation of "inference" through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). This metaphorical usage here consists in applying the name of the effect to the cause: from the statement of the aforementioned proof, a recollection (*smṛti*) of that [object] arises; from that recollection, inference arises. Therefore, the statement of the aforementioned proof is the cause of inference through a causal chain. Upon that cause—the speech—the metaphorical attribution (*samāropa*) of the effect—inference—is made.
Therefore, due to superimposition (*samāropa*), the word "inference" (*anumāna*) is used for the statement as its cause;
or else, it is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the term "inference"—the cause—to the statement which is the effect produced by inference.
The meaning is that the statement is an inference only figuratively, not in a primary sense.
And here, with respect to being denotable by the term "inference" (anumāna), figurative usage (upacāra) proceeds when there is a sublation of the primary meaning, along with a purpose and a cause.

In this context, the primary meaning is the determination of a correct object, which is the direct fruit of valid cognition; this is the primary meaning of the word "inference for others" (parārthānumāna), which stands in grammatical apposition with the word "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa). There is a sublation of that [primary meaning] because it is impossible for a verbal statement to be a [direct] determination.

The purpose [of this discussion] is as follows: the technical usage in the treatise that "the members of inference, such as the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth, are the [means of proof]" is merely conventional; for such usage would be untenable with respect to a determination (*nirṇaya*) which is essentially partless.
However, the underlying cause (*nimitta*) for this usage is that the statement serves as the cause for an inference whose nature is determination.

The metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the primary meaning—[in the case of] the word "fire" used [metaphorically] for a young brahmin boy (*māṇavaka*), as in "the fire is a boy"—is as follows: the primary meaning is the quality of burning; the purpose (*prayojana*) is the cognition of him as someone to be avoided; and the basis (*nimitta*) for the application of the word is his capacity to cause distress (*upatāpakatva*).
In the case of inference for others,
the previously mentioned [process] applies to the engagement.
That is twofold:
that inference for others, which consists of speech, is twofold, meaning it has two modes.
He states the distinction between the three types:
"Likewise, due to the distinction between 'it being possible' and 'its being otherwise impossible'."
Likewise, there is one mode: that the establishment of the probans occurs only when the probandum exists;
and a second mode: that it is impossible [for the probans to exist] otherwise, namely, in the absence of the probandum.

"Just as this mountain possesses fire because the presence of smoke is established, or otherwise the presence of smoke would be untenable"—this much alone constitutes the distinction of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), and it is not ultimate; he indicates this by means of the word "distinction" (*bheda*).
Only when there is possession of fire— this is what [the author] says: "etadevāha" (he says this very thing).
There is no difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of these two. That is to say,

regarding the intended meaning— defined as "that which a word aims at is its meaning"— there is no distinction or difference between these two modes of application, namely *tathopapatti* (logical consistency) and *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-inexplicability).
This is what is meant: the denotable object (*abhidheya*) of a word is one thing, while its manifestable purpose (*prayojana*) is another.

In that regard, the capacity to denote (*vācakatva*) differs depending on the denotable object, but the manifestable [purpose] is non-different. When positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is stated, there is an understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and when negative concomitance is stated, there is an understanding of positive concomitance; thus, in both cases, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the probans (*sādhana*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) is manifested.
And it is not the case that wherever there is a difference in the denotable object, there must also be a difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

The point is that there is no difference in the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*) between these two sentences— "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day" and "Fat Devadatta eats at night"— and therefore they should not be distinguished even by way of their intended meaning (*tātparya*).
(This passage is not found in manuscript *ḍe*).
The meaning is that the *tātparya* (purport) of a word is that which is its "other" (*para*) object;
that is, the object of this word which is "other," meaning superior (*prakṛṣṭa*).— Tātparyaṭīkā.

The meaning of the sūtra is that affirmation is to be stated through "being otherwise impossible" (anyathānupapatti), whereas negation is [stated] through "not being otherwise possible" (anyathānupapatti)— this is the remainder [of the sense].
He states the result of the non-difference of the intended meaning:
"For this very reason, there is no employment of both."

Precisely because there is no difference in the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of these two, it is not proper to employ both "presence in similar cases" (*tathopapatti*) and "absence in dissimilar cases" (*anyathānupapatti*) simultaneously. For the reason (*hetu*) is employed through both presence in similar cases and absence in dissimilar cases for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*);
and since the demonstration of pervasion is accomplished by one alone, the employment of both is redundant.
As it has been said:

"The formal application [of a reason] may occur either through the logical possibility of the reason itself or otherwise; in either case, the proof of the probandum shall be established. (Nyāyabhūṣaṇa 17)

Now, one might object: "If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason has been demonstrated by a single application (*prayoga*), then a second application is useless; likewise, let there be no application of the thesis (*pratijñā*) either, since it would be fruitless—for no one understands any meaning from the thesis alone. If that were so, there would be no disagreement at all. To this he says: "In some cases, the meaning... (Tātparya).
Since the meaning is understood from the mere statement of the proposition,
the proposition is nevertheless stated for the purpose of indicating the subject matter.

The presentation (*upadarśana*)—that is, the imposition (*āropaṇa*) upon the cognition of another—of that which provides the object (*viṣayaprada*), namely the reason (*hetu*) which is sought for the sake of establishing its own probandum (*svasādhya*) through either *tathopapatti* (logical possibility) or *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-untenability); for that purpose, the proposition (*pratijñā*) must again be employed—this is the remainder [of the sentence].
(*svasādha*—Ḍe.)

The meaning is this: when a discerning person utters speech for the purpose of communicating with another, they should inform that other person of only that which the latter desires to know; for in that case, by expressing what is desired to be known, the other is informed. Indeed, one who, being asked about horses, speaks of wild oxen (*gavaya*), does not have speech worthy of the questioner’s attention.
And how can one whose words are not to be heeded be called a teacher?

For example, when a trainee (śaikṣa) was told by a monk, "O trainee, bring alms-food," and instead of saying, "I shall do so," he merely exerted himself for that purpose, the monk became angry with him, saying: "Ah, you mere semblance of a disciple, you scum of a monk! Do you hold us in contempt? Thus he spoke.

Thus, for one who desires to understand that sound is impermanent, if one says anything at all—whether "because it is produced," or "whatever is produced is impermanent," or "because production is established in that very way," or "because production cannot be otherwise"—all of this is disregarded by him, as he perceives it to be an initial, irrelevant statement. Consequently, being inattentive, he is unable to understand; thus [the proof] is like food obtained by begging. (Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, p. 104)
"I am going for the sake of alms-food"— thus speaking— she...
Censuring the definition of sound for the sake of the one being instructed.

If it is argued that, at the outset, one must first be attentive to the statement, "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot; and sound is produced," which—by the very force of its meaning—necessitates the ascertainment of the impermanence of sound, and thus attention is required here; we say no, because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
For when there is attentiveness (*avadhāna*), there is the ascertainment of the object as it truly is; and from that [ascertainment], attentiveness [arises].
Now, the assembly and the respondent do not act as authorities for the proponent such that they would strive to establish a connection with his speech;
for if that were the case, they would have no need for the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, since the ascertainment of the meaning would occur simply from the non-statement of those [reasons].

When the statement "sound is impermanent" is made in response to an inquiry, and the doubt arises as to "why?", there follows [the reason] either because "being produced" is established in that very way, or because "being produced" is otherwise impossible; this is what is meant by the statement that the thesis (pratijñā) serves the purpose of indicating the object [of proof].
— because of the determination of the meaning—
the proponent, who has been established as an authority by those two, [is refuted].
Even though the proponent has established himself as a valid speaker, there are still the assembly and the opponent.
By that word, the proponent states its verbal expression:

"Now, when it is said, 'Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar; and sound is produced,' it is understood from this that sound is impermanent, because this is obtained through the force of the implication (*sāmarthya*); nevertheless, there is the consequence of redundancy (*punaruktatva*) in stating that [again], for the restatement by one's own words of what has already been established by the sense of the matter is redundancy" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.14).

And he said: "Abandoning the passion for the Ḍiṇḍika [doctrine], close your eyes and consider for a moment whether conviction might arise by this much alone; if it does, what is the use of the expansion of the world? Thus he spoke regarding the cause. (Hetupariṇāma, verse 1)
By implication, *ḍiṇḍika* refers to a specific type of red-colored mouse;
likewise, having abandoned the "redness" (*rāga*), that is, the redness residing in the eyes, one makes the eyes clear— this is the meaning (Mu-ṭīkā).
For the *ḍiṇḍikas* indeed engage in dispute when the first name is not written, having discarded [the previous claim]: "By what was said by me, [it is] thus"— ḍe॰— pra॰— ḍe॰.

Even though the existence of impermanence is understood— that is, it is being cognized— it is nonetheless established [by the example] in order to dispel doubt regarding the locus of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), just as the application of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra) occurs in the case of the factual base (dharmin).

The property to be proven (*sādhya*) alone is the predicate; its locus is the subject, and there is doubt regarding that [locus]. For the purpose of dispelling that doubt—even when it is stated that "whatever is produced is impermanent"—there remains doubt concerning the subject: "Is the sound impermanent, or is it a jar? Therefore, for the sake of removing that [doubt], the statement of the *sādhya* (the probandum) is appropriate, even though it is already implied, just like the statement that summarizes the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*) in order to make known the proving property (*sādhanadharma*) within the subject of the *sādhya*.

For just as the statement "sound is produced" (the formulation of the property of the subject) is employed— even though the locus [of the probans] is already understood through the observation of the probans pervaded by the probandum— in order to demonstrate its necessary connection with a specific subject, so too the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is indeed appropriate for the purpose of making known the connection of the probandum with a specific subject; that is,
the subject qualified by the property to be proven.
For instance: [the definition of the subject] is, in general, the substratum of the property to be proven—
[as stated in the *Jñānaśrīmitranibandhāvali*].

Surely, disputants disagree regarding the formal argument (*prayoga*); for instance, the Sāṅkhyas hold that inference consists of three members— proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*udāharaṇa*)—
the Mīmāṃsakas hold it to have four members with the addition of the application (*upanaya*),
and the Naiyāyikas hold it to have five members with the addition of the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Thus, regarding such a disagreement, he states what the formulation of the inference is like:
"This much is the formulation for a discerning person.

This alone constitutes [the proof]: namely, a formulation (*prayoga*) consisting of a reason (*sādhana*) and a proposition (*pratijñā*) that is logically established either through *tathopapatti* (possibility only in that way) or *anyathānupapatti* (impossibility otherwise), intended for the sake of making it understood by a discerning, wise person. It is neither more than this, as the Sāṅkhyas and others claim, nor less than this, as the Buddhists claim—that "for the wise, only the reason (*hetu*) need be stated" (Pramāṇavārttika 1.28).
As they say:
"For those who do not understand that [subject], the existence of the probandum and the existence of the cause are [established] by means of an example."

"Surely those who act for the sake of others out of compassion must awaken others by some means or another; they should not cause a collapse of their intelligence by proposing an unreal state of affairs. Why, then, is such a laborious formal argument employed?"—anticipating this objection, he demonstrates the second sequence of formal arguments as well: "The awakening of others... (ḍe॰).
The refutation of others— ḍe॰:
the destruction of their conviction— mu॰.
— ...the five members— proposition, reason, example, application, and conclusion— are [to be employed] according to the requirements of the person to be enlightened.

The "one to be enlightened" (bodhya) is the disciple; "conformity with him" (anurodha) is the dependence upon the commitment to bring about his enlightenment. For that reason, all five [members] beginning with the proposition (pratijñā) must be employed, and these are designated by the term "members" (avayava), as Akṣapāda stated: "The proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion are the members" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.32).

1.32 By the word "also" (*api*), it should be understood that the five purifications of the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the other members must also be employed in accordance with the requirements of the subject to be known (*bodhya*).
As the venerable feet of the holy Bhadrabāhusvāmin stated:
"In some cases [the proof] has five members, or it is tenfold; in every respect, it is not prohibited. (Daśavaikālika-niryukti 50).
Regarding that, he states the definition of the proposition (*pratijñā*):

The statement of the probandum is the thesis (*pratijñā*). The "probandum" (*sādhya*) is the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by the property (*dharma*) one desires to prove. It is called a "statement" (*nirdeśa*) because it is expressed by means of it; thus, the "statement of the probandum" is the thesis, since it is by means of this that [the matter] is proposed as a thesis. For example: "This location possesses fire."
He defines the reason (hetu): A statement of the means (sādhanavacana) ending in a case-ending that manifests its status as a means is the reason.
The fifth or third case-ending that manifests the state of being a means (*sādhanatva*) is "that which ends in such an ending"; the statement of the means, defined as above, is the "reason" (*hetu*),
and the first word [of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding [the application of] the term "reason" to things such as smoke.

The second [type of probans] is for the purpose of refuting a reason that is under-extended; it is of two kinds, namely by "being established in that way" (*tathopapatti*) and by "not being possible otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*). For example: [the probans is] "because smoke is established in that way," or "because smoke is not possible otherwise.
The statement of a reason that is not pervaded by that [conclusion] is its being a reason; in the statement of the reason— ḍe— ḍe.
He defines the example:
"The statement of an illustration is the example" (13).

An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is that which possesses the characteristics already described; the statement that establishes it is the illustration (*udāharaṇa*). This too is of two kinds based on the distinction between examples: a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is one that possesses the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) as being concomitant with the proving property (*sādhana-dharma*); the statement of that is the similar illustration (*sādharmya-udāharaṇa*), such as: "Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, just like the kitchen area."

A counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is that which possesses the cessation of the probans (*sādhana-dharma*) necessitated by the cessation of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*); the statement of such an example is the "counter-example illustration" (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*), as for instance: "Whatever is devoid of fire is devoid of smoke, just like a body of water.
He now states the definition of the application (*upanaya*):

The application (*upanaya*) is the subsumption of the probans (*sādhana*) under the subject (*dharmin*). That which is the subsumption of the probans-property, having been extended to the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), back onto the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), is the application; it is verbal in form, as in "and this [subject] possesses smoke. This is so because by means of it (*anena*) the property is subsumed (*upasaṃhriyate*) or brought near (*upanīyate*).
Of that which is expanded and diffused— Ḍe.

The definition of the application (*upanaya*)— which consists in the presentation of the probans-property upon the subject under discussion— is as follows; it then defines the conclusion (*nigamana*):

The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) upon the subject (*dharmin*). It is called a "conclusion" because by means of it, the meaning of the preceding members [of the syllogism] is brought to a final resolution. For example: "Therefore, it possesses fire."
The purpose is determined:
these five members, which are in the form of parts of a sentence, establish the state of being inseparable.

Since these very five [members] are pure—because none of the five members are suspected of having superimposed defects—and since each is capable of producing its own respective cognition regarding the object of meaning free from faults, one should employ exactly five purifications in the form of refutations for each specific defect suspected in the thesis and the other members. Thus, this ten-membered inferential statement should be employed according to the requirements of the person to be enlightened.
The meaning characterized by the means of proof (sādhana) is that which is invariably concomitant (avinābhāvī) with the probandum; "regarding oneness"—
this refers to the defects of these [reasons], which are suspected, doubted, or superimposed.
Those for whom the definition has been stated here in this treatise are capable [of attaining the goal]; those who lack that definition are well known as mere semblances thereof.

Just as in the absence of the general definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), doubt, error, and non-apprehension constitute fallacious cognitions (*pramāṇābhāsa*); as in the absence of the definitions of doubt and so forth, there are fallacies of doubt and so forth; as in the absence of the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is the fallacy of perception; and as for those [cognitions] included within the indirect (*parokṣa*)—such as memory and the rest—in the absence of their respective individual definitions, there are their respective fallacies, and so on;
in the same way, it is easily understood that when reasons (*hetu*) lack their own specific definitions, they possess the status of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
However, since the fixed number of fallacious reasons and the definition of each individual instance are not easily grasped, he states the following for the purpose of defining them:
That which has been stated therein— [the commentary on] the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*—
is the supreme manifestation;
it is easily performed, meaning its realization is easy to accomplish.
The three fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)— the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—
are called *hetvābhāsa* because they appear to be reasons while actually being non-reasons (*ahetu*). These include the unestablished and the others.

Although these are indeed defects of the proof (*sādhana*)—since they do not exist when the proof is flawless—they were nonetheless designated as such by the former masters through metaphorical application (*upacāra*) to the reason (*hetu*) which expresses the proof. Therefore, we too, not disregarding the consensus established by them, describe them specifically as defects of the reason;
the phrase "the three former masters" is used for the purpose of excluding other numbers.
By this, there is an exclusion of the *kālātīta* (mistimed) and *prakaraṇasama* (neutralized by counter-argument) [fallacies].
Among those, the *kālātīta* is included within the faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*).

For its definition is: "That which is employed immediately after the statement of a reason that is sublated by perception or scripture is called *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed). For example: "The composite whole consisting of light is not hot, because it is produced, like a jar."

The *prakaraṇasama* (the "neutralized" reason), however, is simply not possible; for there is no possibility of another inference being employed when an inference characterized as described above has been stated and remains unrefuted.

As for the example cited—when one person says, "Sound is impermanent because it is one or the other of the subject (*pakṣa*) or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)," and a second person replies, "Sound is permanent because it is one or the other of the subject or the similar instance"—that is utterly untenable.
For what sane person, whether a proponent or a respondent, would utter such an incoherent statement in an assembly consisting of four members?
(16) "The time has passed" means it has elapsed.
—*dharmidharmini*—Ḍe;
—*ṣite cānu*—Tā;
*dī caivaṃ*—Ḍe.
Regarding that, he states the definition of the unestablished (*asiddha*):

"That which is neither non-existent nor of ascertained existence, and which is not otherwise impossible" (is the unestablished). When there is non-establishment or doubt regarding existence (*sattva*), it is the unestablished (*asiddha*).

The meaning is that when a reason (*hetu*) does not exist and is "otherwise impossible" (*anyathānupapanna*), it is unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the non-establishment of its existence; this is what is meant by the "unestablished fallacy of the reason" (*svarūpāsiddha*).

One should not think that the reason "because sound is visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*) is unestablished merely because it is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*); therefore, he says: "it is otherwise impossible."

This [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it lacks the definition of a reason, which consists in the impossibility of its existence otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*); it is not unestablished due to a lack of "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).

For "property-of-the-subject" is not the defining characteristic of a reason, since—as has already been largely stated—it is possible for something to function as a reason by the force of "impossibility otherwise," even in the absence of that [property].
Bhaṭṭa also says:

Anticipating the objection that "even if [the presence of the reason] in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is unestablished, the reason is nonetheless established by the fact of its being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) alone— as in such cases as 'there has been rain upon the mountain because the river's flooding is otherwise impossible'— he says:

Furthermore, the inference of a son’s Brahminhood based on the Brahminhood of his parents—as in "this son is a Brahmin because his parents are Brahmins"—is well-known to all the world; it does not depend upon the presence of the logical reason (*pakṣadharma*) [in the subject]. Thus.

Likewise, when the existence [of the reason] is uncertain—that is, when its existence is doubted—it is not "otherwise impossible" (*anyathānupapanna*); thus, even when there is doubt regarding its existence, the fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is "unestablished," meaning it is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).

For example, a line of smoke that is itself being doubted as to whether it is actually vapor or the like, yet is presented for the purpose of proving fire; or, for instance, the property of having qualities perceived everywhere, when used to prove the omnipresence of the self (*ātman*), despite the self being established, because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) [to establish such a property].
For example: "The self is omnipresent because its qualities are perceived everywhere"— here,
the possession of those qualities is doubtful.
He states the divisions of the unestablished (asiddha):
"This division [arises] from the distinction between the proponent, the opponent, and both" (18).

The proponent (*vādī*) is one who stands on the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), while the opponent (*prativādī*) is one who stands on the rejoinder position (*uttarapakṣa*); both together constitute the proponent and the opponent. From their distinction, there arises the distinction of the unestablished (*asiddha*). Among these, that which is unestablished for the proponent (*vādyasiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is subject to transformation because it possesses origination."

This [reason] is unestablished for the Sāṅkhya himself as a proponent, because in his system the possession of origination is not admitted; for according to his tenet, "the non-existent does not originate, nor does the existent perish, since origination and destruction consist in manifestation and disappearance. Furthermore, regarding the statement "trees are sentient because they die when all their bark is stripped away," the death characterized by the cessation of consciousness, the sense-faculties, and the life-force is unestablished for the Buddhist opponent with respect to trees.
The unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*) has already been mentioned as "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*).
Likewise, the doubtful-unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*) should also be understood as being threefold, based on the distinction between the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*).
— And from the end of the mind— ḍe;
it is not only unestablished in its own nature (svarūpāsiddha).
"Now, other fallacies of the reason (hetvābhāsa), such as the unestablished subject (viśeṣyāsiddha) and so forth, are accepted by some; why have they not been mentioned?
To this he says: "The unestablished subject and others are included within these very [categories].

Among these very [types of reasons] which are unestablished for both the proponent and the opponent, the cases of the unestablished qualification (*viśeṣyāsiddha*) and so forth are illustrated therein.
An example of the unestablished qualification is as follows: "Sound is impermanent because it is visible while possessing generality."
The unestablished by qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because, while being visible, it possesses generality and particularity.
The unestablished by partial presence (*bhāgāsiddha*) is, for example: "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort.
The unestablished by locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) is, for example: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) exists because of its transformation into the universe."

An example of [the reason] being unestablished with respect to a portion of the locus (*āśrayaikadeśāsiddha*) is: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*), the Spirit (*puruṣa*), and God (*īśvara*) are eternal because they are unproduced.

An example of [the reason] being unestablished due to a redundant qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣyāsiddha*) is: "Sound is impermanent because, while being produced, it possesses generality (*sāmānyavat*). An example of [the reason] being unestablished due to a redundant qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*) is: "Sound is impermanent because, while possessing generality, it is produced."

The unestablished reason (*asiddha*) with a doubtful predicate (*sandigdhaviśeṣya*) is, for example: "Kapila is still possessed of passion and so forth, because, while being a human being, he has not yet produced the knowledge of reality.

The unestablished reason with a doubtful qualifier (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇa*) is, for example: "Kapila is still possessed of passion and so forth, because, while being devoid of the knowledge of reality at all times, he is a human being," and so on.

These varieties of the unestablished reason, when intended as being unestablished for one or the other of the two parties, become either unestablished for the proponent (*vādyasiddha*) or unestablished for the opponent (*prativādyasiddha*).
When they are intended to be unestablished for both disputants, they are "unestablished for both" (ubhayāsiddha).
[This is] according to the rule for words such as *āhitāgni* in Pāṇini’s Sūtra 2.2.37.
153 The self is delimited.
In one part, or a single portion, [the reason] is unestablished; because "being produced immediately after effort" is absent in thundering,
the generality [of the reason] is excluded for the Naiyāyika.

One might object that the qualification "provided it possesses generality" (*sāmānyavattve sati*) is intended to exclude *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (destruction). This is not so; for the Buddhist and the Mīmāṃsaka stand as the proponent and the opponent respectively, and in their view, non-existence (*abhāva*) does not exist at all.
Therefore, in order to exclude [the category of] stones and the like, it was stated "provided it is a person" (*puruṣatve sati*).
He now states the definition of the contradictory (*viruddha*):

A contradictory [reason] is one whose restriction is inverted, such that it is established in a manner other than [the intended one]; because its restriction is inverted, it is established even without the probandum (sādhya). 20.

The "contrary" (*viparīta*) is that whose rule (*niyama*), or inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), is the reverse of what was stated; its demonstration is as follows: "it is established otherwise. For example: "Sound is eternal because it is a product," and "The eyes and so forth are for the sake of another because they are composite, like beds, seats, and other [composite] objects. Here, when the probandum (*sādhya*) is "being for the sake of a non-composite [subject]," the compositeness of the eyes and so forth is contradictory (*viruddha*).

Likewise, in the case of "The earth and so forth are preceded by an intelligent agent because they are products," when the probandum is "being preceded by a creator who is bodiless and omniscient," the property of being a product is "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite.

The objects [of inference] are for oneself because they possess an inseparable connection with the probandum, whereas [the objects of inference] for others lack an inseparable connection with what is contradictory to the probandum.
Non-existence as a composite [is not established],
because this [reason] proves only that which is a composite for the sake of another.
By this, those other contradictory [reasons] cited by others are also subsumed;

for example, when there is a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there are four varieties, such as that which pervades both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), e.g., "Sound is eternal because it is a product."

A reason that pervades the subject (pakṣavyāpaka) but occurs in only one part of the counter-subject (vipakṣaikadeśavṛtti) is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because, while possessing generality, it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves.
A reason that occurs in one part of the subject but pervades the counter-subject (pakṣaikadeśavṛtti-vipakṣavyāpaka) is, for example: "Earth is both eternal and non-eternal, because it is produced.
A reason that occurs in one part of both the subject and the counter-subject (pakṣavipakṣaikadeśavṛtti) is, for example: "Sound is eternal, because it follows immediately upon effort."

When there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there are four types of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*): that which pervades both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), such as "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*);

and that which pervades the subject but occurs in only a portion of the dissimilar instances, such as "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is perceptible by an external sense organ" (*bāhyendriyagrāhyatvāt*).

That which exists in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) but pervades the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāpaka*) is, for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space because it is not composed of atoms.

That which exists in one part of both the subject and the dissimilar instances (*pakṣavipakṣaikadeśavṛtti*) is, for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space because it follows immediately after effort.

In these four cases, there is the fault of being contradictory (*viruddhatā*); however, in the four cases where [the reason] exists in one part of the subject, there is a combination of both faults, namely, the unestablished (*asiddhatā*) and the contradictory (*viruddhatā*).
For the property of being an effect (kāryatva) is observed in the subject, sound, as well as in the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa), such as impermanent things like jars; thus,
the reason exists in impermanent things like jars, but does not exist in [impermanent] things such as dyads (dvyaṇuka) or pleasure and pain.

In the case of earth in its form as an atom (*paramāṇu*), "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) does not exist, whereas it does exist in its form as an effect (*kārya*); thus, [the reason] exists in only one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛttitā*). Regarding sound, the word "place" (*deśa*) refers to lightning, which is not produced by effort (*aprayatnānantarīyaka*); since "being produced by effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) does not exist there, it exists in only one part of the subject.
Furthermore, because no other specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is possible apart from sound, there is an absence of similar instances (*sapakṣābhāva*).
Conjunction and the like are general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*);

while external-sense-perceptibility exists in cases such as conjunction with space, it does not exist in [qualities] such as magnitude (*mahattva*), and since the sounds of clouds and so forth lack the nature of words (*apadātmatva*), there is the fault of the reason residing in only a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛttitā*). In the case of conjunction and the like, there is indeed the absence of the nature of a word.

In the counter-example (vipakṣa), such as conjunction (saṃyoga) and so forth, there is the property of being immediately following upon effort (prayatnānantarīyakatva); however, this does not exist in magnitude (mahattva).
Because it exists in only one part of the subject (pakṣaikadeśe vidyamānatvāt)—[the text here contains a corruption: "tā vetyu" should likely be "tāvat" or similar]—it is [an inconclusive reason].
— [The teacher] states the definition of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) [reason]:
when the rule [of concomitance] is unestablished or doubtful, that which can be accounted for otherwise is the inconclusive.

Not only does the term "niyama" mean "non-existence without" (avinābhāva) when the probandum exists; rather, when that [non-existence without] is unestablished, it is "inconclusive" (anaikāntika). For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*). Knowability exists even in eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*), etc.
In the case of doubt, for example: "Someone is not omniscient, or possesses passion and so forth, because he is a speaker.

For the property of being a speaker is not established as being contradictory with either omniscience or freedom from passion, both of which are beyond the reach of perception; nor is speech the effect of passion and so forth. Thus, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is doubtful.
Furthermore, whatever other varieties of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) fallacy have been cited by others are all included within the definition already stated.

An example of [the reason] pervading all three positions (*pakṣatrayavyāpaka*) is: "Sound is impermanent, because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*). An example of [the reason] pervading the subject and the similar class (*sapakṣa*), but occurring in only one part of the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is: "This is a cow, because it has horns. An example of [the reason] pervading the subject and the dissimilar class, but occurring in only one part of the similar class is: "This is not a cow, because it has horns. An example of [the reason] pervading the subject, but occurring in only one part of both the similar and dissimilar classes is: "Sound is impermanent, because it is perceptible" (*pratyakṣatvāt*).

A reason that resides in one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśavṛtti*), pervades both the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), is as follows: "Space, time, direction, self, and mind are not substances because they lack momentary specific qualities (*kṣaṇikaviśeṣaguṇarahitatvāt*). 2. Because it is delimited by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

the state of possessing horns does not exist in horses and the like, whereas it does exist in buffaloes and the like; thus, [the reason] "because of possessing horns" has the property of occurring in only a portion of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣaikadeśavṛttitva*).
Having seen a goat, one says that [the property] exists in buffaloes and the like, but does not exist in horses and the like;
whereas dyads and so forth are not perceptible, pots and the like are perceptible.
Eternity and generality are perceptible, but space is not;

the self and space are endowed with non-momentary specific qualities such as pleasure, sound, and so forth, whereas the counter-examples— earth and the rest— possess specific qualities that are momentary, namely odor in earth and viscidity in water.
Space is formless, while earth is formed;

earth in the form of atoms is not perceptible, but earth in its manifested form is perceptible—this is one part of the thesis (*pakṣaikadeśa*). There is an absence of perceptibility in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), such as water, fire, and binary compounds (*dvyaṇuka*); yet there is perceptibility in eternal entities such as universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.

There are eight fallacies of the example based on similarity and eight based on dissimilarity (sādharmya-vaidharmya). Since the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is of two kinds—by way of similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—there are eight fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) for each, appearing as if they were valid examples.
