When it is to be proven that sound is eternal because it is formless, action, atoms, and a jar are deficient in the probandum, the probans, and both respectively. In this formulation— "Sound is eternal because it is formless"— action and the others are deficient in the probandum and so forth, according to their respective order.
In that context, "like action" (*karmavat*) is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because action is impermanent;
"like an atom" (*paramāṇuvat*) is deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*), because atoms possess form (*mūrtatvāt*);
and "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*) is deficient in both the probandum and the probans, because a jar is both impermanent and possesses form.
Thus, there are three fallacious examples of similarity (sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).
All three [are] sā°—mu—pā°.
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), atoms, motion, and space are examples that lack the exclusion of the property to be proven (*sādhyāvyatirekin*);

for in this very same argument— "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal"— atoms, motion, and space are fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) because they do not exclude the property to be proven, the probans, or both.

That which is not eternal is also not formless, as for example an atom (*paramāṇu*); this is a pseudo-example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) because it lacks the exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyāvyatirekī*), since atoms are eternal. "As for example action (*karman*)" is one where the probans is not excluded (*sādhanāvyāvṛtta*), because action is formless. "As for example space (*ākāśa*)" is one where both are not excluded (*ubhayāvyāvṛtta*), because space is both eternal and formless. Thus, there are exactly three types of pseudo-examples of dissimilarity.

Likewise—from the statement [of passion], there is passion; from passion, the properties of mortality and limited knowledge; [in these cases] the positive and negative concomitances with the probandum and so forth are doubtful, as in the case of people on the street and the like.

25— There are three fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa) characterized by doubtful positive concomitance (anvaya) of the probandum, the probans, and both; and there are likewise three characterized by doubtful negative concomitance (vyatireka) of the probandum, the probans, and both.
Who are they? He says: street-urchins and so forth.
In what respect are they [examples]?
In the case of passion (rāga), and in the cases of being subject to death and limited knowledge (maraṇadharmakatva and kiñcijjñatva).
He asks "Why? and says: [Because of] speech and passion.

In that regard, [the fallacy of] the concomitance of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) being doubtful is as follows: a particular person intended [as the subject] is passionate because he speaks, like a man on the street.
[The fallacy of] the concomitance of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) being doubtful is as follows: this person is subject to death because he is passionate, like a man on the street.
An example of doubtful positive concomitance of both properties (*sandigdhobhayadharmānvaya*) is: "This person possesses some knowledge because he has passion, like a man in the street.

In these cases, since the mental states of others are difficult to ascertain, the presence of both passion and some knowledge in the man in the street—the instance of similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*)—is doubtful.
Similarly, an example of doubtful negative concomitance of the probandum (*sandigdhasādhyavyatireka*) is: "He has passion because he speaks, like a man in the street."
An example of doubtful exclusion of the probans (*sandigdhasādhanavyatireka*) is: "This person is subject to death because he possesses passion, like a man on the street.
An example of doubtful exclusion of both [the probandum and the probans] (*sandigdhobhayavyatireka*) is: "This person is a knower of something because he possesses passion, like a man on the street.

In these cases, as in the previous ones, because the mental states of others are difficult to ascertain, the absence of passion and the state of being a knower of something in the man on the street—the instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*)—is doubtful.
Of the two things to be proven, according to their respective order.
Whoever is not possessed of passion is also not a speaker;
since it is ascertained that there is an absence of speech in a person on the street by some means such as corporeality, the state of being passionate is doubted [in that case].
A Jaina says this to a Sāṅkhya who denies death:
Likewise, in the [logical] applications—
there are inverted positive and negative concomitances.
A reversed positive concomitance (*viparītānvaya*) and a reversed negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*) constitute fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

Among these, an example of reversed positive concomitance is as follows: when one ought to say, "Whatever is produced is impermanent," one says instead, "Whatever is impermanent is produced, like a pot."

An inverted negative concomitance (*viparītavyatireka*) is as follows: when one ought to state that "in the absence of impermanence, producedness certainly does not exist," one instead says, "in the absence of producedness, impermanence certainly does not exist, as in the case of space.
Thus, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) consists in the affirmation of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by way of restating the property that serves as the proof (*sādhanadharma*);
whereas negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) consists in the affirmation of the exclusion of the property that serves as the proof by way of restating the exclusion of the property to be proven.
The state of being otherwise regarding those two is their contrariety, as it has been said: "the state of being otherwise... [Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa].

"From the restatement of the probandum, there is the rule of the contrary positive concomitance of the mark; [in the case of] anvaya-viparyaya, [there is] the absence of the reason, while the probandum is non-existent in the case of the reversal of vyatireka. (26)
He says:
"In this context, the positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) have not been demonstrated."
These two—wherein the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not demonstrated and wherein the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not demonstrated—are fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*).

These arise from the failure to present valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and not merely from the non-employment of words expressing repetition (*vīpsā*) or universal determination (*sarvāvadhāraṇa*); for even when such words are present, those two [concomitances] remain unestablished if there is no valid means of knowledge.

There are eight fallacious examples based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): those deficient in the probandum (*sādhya-vikala*), deficient in the probans (*sādhana-vikala*), and deficient in both; those where the positive concomitance of the probandum is doubtful (*sandigdha-sādhya-anvaya*), where the positive concomitance of the probans is doubtful (*sandigdha-sādhana-anvaya*), and where the positive concomitance of both is doubtful (*sandigdha-ubhaya-anvaya*); that with inverted positive concomitance (*viparīta-anvaya*); and that with unshown positive concomitance (*apradarśita-anvaya*). Likewise, there are exactly eight fallacious examples based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*): those from which the probandum is not excluded (*sādhya-avyāvṛtta*), from which the probans is not excluded (*sādhana-avyāvṛtta*), and from which both are not excluded (*ubhaya-avyāvṛtta*); those where the exclusion of the probandum is doubtful (*sandigdha-sādhya-vyāvṛtti*), where the exclusion of the probans is doubtful (*sandigdha-sādhana-vyāvṛtti*), and where the exclusion of both is doubtful (*sandigdha-ubhaya-vyāvṛtti*); that with inverted negative concomitance (*viparīta-vyatireka*); and that with unshown negative concomitance (*apradarśita-vyatireka*).
These pertain to the inferential cognition known as *ūha*, which apprehends pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Whatever is produced,
whatever is produced—
all that which is produced is indeed impermanent.
Regarding positive and negative concomitance—[the commentary] says:
"O Goddess, [regarding] the two...

Now, it may be argued that some have also mentioned non-concomitance and lack of negative concomitance as fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), such as: "This person possesses passion and so forth, because he speaks."

In this regard, although there is coexistence (*sāhitya*) of passion and speech in the self within the similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), and although there is simultaneous cessation (*saha-nivṛtti*) in a piece of stone within the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Why, then, are these two—non-concomitance and non-exclusion—not mentioned here? It is said: because they do not differ from those [already mentioned] preceding them, there are exactly eight fallacious instances (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) for each of the similar and dissimilar types.
As they say:

"Due to the absence of a relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for the probans; thus, there are eight [fallacies] of the non-exclusive (*avyatirekin*)."

"These [reasons] do not indicate the state of being 'otherwise impossible' (nānyathānupapannatva) in any way. (27) Inference for the sake of others has been concluded; now, he defines refutation (dūṣaṇa), which is inseparable from it:
"Refutation is the pointing out of defects in the proof (sādhana)."

Regarding the defects of the proof (*sādhana*), namely the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth, which were mentioned previously: that by means of which these are "brought to light" (*udbhāvyante*) or revealed is called "bringing to light" (*udbhāvana*). A statement that brings to light the defects of the proof is a "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*).
Since the term "unreal" (*abhūta*) will be mentioned later, it is established here that a refutation consists in the bringing to light of a real defect (*bhūtadoṣa*).

Regarding the defects of real [objections] (*bhūtadoṣa*): since the definition of a fallacious objection (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) is easily understood from the definition of a valid objection (*dūṣaṇa*), he states its definition merely for the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between them.
Fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) are rejoinders (*jātyuttara*) that consist in the pointing out of non-existent faults.
They are fallacious refutations because they are the propounding of defects in a proof that do not exist; although they are not actual refutations, they appear as such. 29.
And those are "futile rejoinders" (jātyuttara);
the word *jāti* signifies similarity; "futile rejoinders" are those similar to a valid reply (*uttara*), because they are employed in the place of a reply.
Sophistical refutations (*jātyuttara*) are answers resembling [the original] argument;
they are called *jātyuttara* because they are answers based on similarity (*jāti*).

When a valid reason (*samyag-hetu*) or a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is employed by a proponent, it is impossible to enumerate exhaustively the counter-arguments (*pratyavasthāna*), which are essentially reflections of the reason itself, because they are infinite and their specific defects do not immediately appear. Nevertheless, following the direction shown by Akṣapāda, twenty-four types are demonstrated according to the distinctions of counter-argument based on similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth: namely, by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), augmentation (*utkarṣa*), diminution (*apakarṣa*), the commendable (*varṇya*), the non-commendable (*avarṇya*), the alternative (*vikalpa*), the attainment of the probandum (*sādhyaprāpti*), non-attainment (*aprāpti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), non-arising (*anutpatti*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), the topic under discussion (*prakaraṇa*), the non-reason (*ahetu*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*), occurrence (*upapatti*), perception (*upalabdhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), permanence (*nitya*), impermanence (*anitya*), and the effect (*kārya*). These are presented as being of similar form.
This is the term *saṃjñā*—
"that which has a form similar to its effect" (kāryasarūpa)—
and the counter-position established there through similarity is the *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity) fallacy.

For example, when the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar" has been stated using a formulation based on similarity (*sādharmya*), one objects by means of a formulation based on similarity alone: "Sound is permanent because it is partless, like space;

and there is no specific reason why sound is impermanent due to its similarity to a jar through being produced, rather than permanent due to its similarity to space through being partless. This objection based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is the fallacy known as *vaidharmyasama*.

For example, in the very same argument—"Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—that same counter-reason is employed by way of dissimilarity: "Sound is permanent because it is partless; for that which has parts, such as a jar, is seen to be impermanent. Yet there is no specific reason to conclude that sound is impermanent due to its similarity to a jar (in being produced) rather than permanent due to its dissimilarity to it (in being partless). These two types of opposition based on exaggeration and depreciation constitute the fallacies of *utkarṣasama* and *apakarṣasama*.

In that very same application, one employs the sophistical refutation known as *utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition) by attributing some property of the example to the subject of the thesis: "If sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar, then let it also be corporeal, just like a jar;

if it is not corporeal, then let it not be impermanent either, like a jar. Thus, one attributes the addition of another property (*dharmāntarotkarṣa*) to the sound. Conversely, *apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction) proceeds thus: "A jar is produced and yet is observed to be non-audible; let sound be so too."
If [the opponent argues], "Let it not be impermanent like a jar," and thereby removes the property of audibility from sound—
this is the *varṇyāvarṇyasama* (balancing the similar and dissimilar) futile rejoinder. Here,
that which is to be established is the *varṇya*, and its opposite is the *avarṇya*.

These two, the "equal to the subject" (*varṇyasama*) and the "equal to the non-subject" (*avarṇyasama*), are sophistical refutations (*jāti*) that function by reversing the properties of the probandum and the example—namely, [arguing] that "the property of sound, such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), is not like the property of a jar; and the property of a jar is not like the property of sound.
(5–6) The sophistical refutation called "equal to the alternative" (*vikalpasamā jātiḥ*) is an objection based on the variation of other properties.

For example: "Just as some things that are produced are seen to be soft, such as a bed of woolen blankets (*rāṅkavaśayyā*), while others are hard, such as an axe, so too some produced things will be impermanent, such as a jar, while others will be permanent, such as sound. (7)
The *sādhyasamā* (balancing the probandum) fallacy consists in an opposition based on establishing an equality with the probandum;
for example: "If, as the jar is, so is the sound, then it follows that as the sound is, so is the jar;
and since the sound is the probandum (*sādhya*), the jar must also be the probandum."
And thus, the example would not be something to be proven for that which is to be proven;

if it were not so, even then, because of the difference in nature, it would all the more fail to be an example. This is the "balancing by attainment and non-attainment" (prāptyaprāptisama) sophistical refutation, which consists of an opposition based on the alternatives of attainment and non-attainment.
For instance, as for this "producedness" which you have put forward as a proof: does it establish [the probandum] by reaching it or without reaching it?
If it reaches it, then meeting occurs only between two things that both exist, not between one that exists and one that does not;
and since both exist, what is the proven and what is the proof? 9
"But it is improper for [the probans] not to attain the status of a means of proof, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
This is the fallacy of "balancing the consequence" (prasaṅgasama), which consists in an objection by way of pointing out an over-extension:
for example, "If 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) is the means of proof for impermanence, then what is the means of proof for 'being produced' itself?"

If it is asked, "What is the proof for that [proof]?"—the *pratidṛṣṭāntasamā* (counter-example-equivalent) fallacy consists in an opposition by means of a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*). For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, like a pot," the proponent of the fallacy says: "Just as a pot is seen to be impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort, so too is the counter-example, space (*ākāśa*), seen to follow immediately upon effort, since it is perceived immediately after the effort of digging a well."
This is not merely an indication of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because it is a counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) by way of a different method.
The "balancing through non-arising" (*anutpattisama*) is a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) consisting of a counter-objection based on non-arising;
for example: "Since the subject (*dharmin*) called 'sound' has not yet arisen, where could the property (*dharma*) of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) reside?"
Thus, because of the absence of a reason, there is no proof for impermanence.

(13) That same *jāti* (futile rejoinder), whether it be "balancing the homogeneous" (*sādharmyasama*) or "balancing the heterogeneous" (*vaidharmyasama*), which was previously illustrated, becomes the *jāti* "balancing the doubt" (*saṃśayasama*) when it is concluded with a doubt, as follows:

"Is sound impermanent because of its similarity to a jar through its being produced, or is it permanent because of its dissimilarity to that [jar] or its similarity to space through its being partless? (14)
When that same *jāti*—whether it be *sādharmyasama* or *vaidharmyasama*—is employed with the intention of raising a second alternative, it becomes *prakaraṇasama*.

In the very same application, such as "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a pot," one might state: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*)"; the difference between them should be understood as consisting merely in the distinction of the manner of presentation.
(15) The *jāti* called *ahetusama* is the opposition to a reason based on its impossibility across the three periods of time.
Just as the cause is the means of proof, would it exist prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneously with that which is to be proven?
If it exists prior; since that which is to be proven does not yet exist, for what would it be the means of proof?
Now, if the means of proof (*sādhana*) comes later, then the probandum (*sādhya*) must come first; and if that [probandum] is already established beforehand, what is the use of a means of proof?

Or, if the probandum and the means of proof are simultaneous, then—like the left and right horns of a cow—the relationship of probandum and means of proof would not exist at all. This is the *jāti* (futile rejoinder) called *arthāpattisamā*, which consists in an opposition based on an implied necessity (*arthāpatti*).

If sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of being produced— which is a property shared with what is impermanent— it follows by implication that it must be permanent because it possesses the property of being eternal— which is a property shared with what is eternal—

and since it indeed shares the property of being partless with eternal things such as space, this is merely a different mode of raising an objection. (17) An opposition based on establishing non-distinction is the futility called *aviśeṣasama*.

Just as if one were to accept that sound and a jar share a single property, such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), then because they possess this common property and thus lack distinction, it would follow by logical necessity that all things likewise lack distinction; this is the *upapattisama* fallacy, which is an objection based on reasoning.
For example: if the impermanence of sound is established by the reasoning of its being produced, why does its permanence not also follow from the reasoning of its being partless (*niravayavatva*)?

The intended meaning is that because both sides are equally possible, the argument results in indecision (*anadhyavasāya*); thus, this is merely a difference in the method of objection (*udbhāvana-prakāra-bheda*).
(19) *Upalabdhisama* (the "equal-to-perception" sophistical refutation) is an opposition based on perception.

For example, when it is argued, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," one objects: "Indeed, following immediately upon effort is not the proof for impermanence; for that alone is called a 'proof' by which the probandum cannot be perceived in its absence."
Furthermore, impermanence is perceived even in lightning and the like without being preceded by effort;
likewise, it occurs in some cases of sound produced by trees being shattered by the force of the wind.
This counter-argument based on non-perception is the fallacy known as *anupalabdhisama* (balancing the non-perception).

Just as when that very reason—being produced immediately after effort—is put forward, the proponent of the *jāti* (fallacious rejoinder) says: "Sound is not an effect of effort; it exists even prior to its utterance, but it is not perceived because of its connection with an obstruction.

If it is argued, "Even though the obstruction is not perceived, since [the sound] is not perceived, the sound simply does not exist," [the reply is]: No, for even when the obstruction is not perceived, the non-perception [of the sound] still occurs;
and from the non-perception of the non-perception of the obstruction, there follows the non-existence [of the obstruction].
And because an obscuration is perceived in the absence of that [sound], its existence follows;

therefore, just as in the case of a root, a nail, or water hidden by earth, the non-perception of sound prior to its utterance is caused solely by the perception of an obscuration. Thus, since it does not have the effort [of utterance] as its effect, sound is eternal.

This is the *nityasamā* (balancing the eternal) fallacy, which establishes the eternity of sound by means of an alternative between the permanence and impermanence of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

For example, when the proposition "sound is impermanent" has been stated, the proponent of the *jāti* (fallacy) analyzes it as follows: "Is this impermanence that is predicated of sound itself impermanent or permanent?
If it is impermanent, then it must necessarily pass away; thus, because impermanence passes away, sound would be permanent.

On the other hand, if impermanence is indeed permanent, then since a property (*dharma*) cannot exist without a substratum (*āśraya*), the sound which serves as its substratum must also be permanent; for if that [sound] were impermanent, it would be impossible for its property to be permanent. Thus, in both cases, sound is permanent. (22)
The fallacy of "balancing the non-eternal" (*anityasama*) is an objection raised by establishing the non-eternality of all things.

For example, if it is argued that sound is non-eternal because it possesses a similarity with a pot—which is non-eternal—then since there is some degree of similarity between a pot and all other entities, those too would have to be non-eternal.
If, on the other hand, other entities are not non-eternal despite having such a similarity, then let sound likewise not be non-eternal.
This fallacy (*jāti*) is distinct from the "balancing the non-difference" (*aviśeṣasama*), because it first establishes mere impermanence and then brings forth a specific distinction.
The fallacy of "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*) is an opposition based on the presentation of the diversity of effects produced by effort.

For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it follows immediately upon effort," the proponent of the genus (*jāti*) says: "Effort is observed to have two forms: some thing that was previously non-existent is produced by it, as in the case of a jar and the like; and some thing that already exists is manifested through the removal of an obstruction and so forth, as in the case of a wooden peg hidden within the earth. Thus, due to this diversity in the effects of effort, there arises a doubt as to whether sound is manifested or produced by effort. This is the *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) fallacy. It is distinguished from *saṃśayasama* (balancing the doubt) because of the difference in the method of producing the doubt. 24.

The Jaina offers the following reply: "The property of being partless (*niravayavatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*); furthermore, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the existence of] cognition. In this case as well, [the opponent] renders the example inconclusive by introducing a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) between the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) and the property of the example."

The *varṇyasamā* sophistical refutation (*jāti*) occurs when, by means of the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*), one seeks to demonstrate the equality of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) which is not itself the property to be proved; thus, it would follow that the example lacks the status of being an example. The *avarṇyasamā* sophistical refutation occurs when, by relying on an example that is not the property to be proved, it follows that the means of proof (*sādhana*) itself becomes something that is not the property to be proved. And as for the [text] "gha—mu—pā"— [Note: The final fragment appears to be a scribal or editorial notation.]

Likewise, the example [cited] against the Jaina is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because he indeed accepts both the eternality and non-eternality of "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*); thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is also unestablished (*asiddha*). This is the formal presentation (*udbhāvana*). — Tattvārtha-prabhā.
When that has first been accomplished—[the manuscript reads] "ḍe"—the manifestation [is achieved]; [the manuscript reads] "pra"—[the manuscript reads] "ḍe".
Here, the answer is exactly as previously stated.

If [it is argued that] "it is indeed so," [then] the answer here is: because it is differentiated by differences in cognition, the fact that the intended sound does not follow immediately upon effort (*aprayatnānantarīyakatva*) is already established. By means of the effort toward the substance, the intended sound is produced (*janyate*) and not merely manifested (*vyajyate*).
—Indeed, it is not so;

for in the case of impermanence, which has a perishable nature, the conceptualization of "permanent" or "impermanent" is simply not possible. Otherwise, let the "producedness" of producedness itself be questioned. Against the Jaina, there is no probandum; against the Naiyāyika, the pervasion of sound’s producedness by impermanence is not observed, due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Thus, although the varieties of *jāti* (futilities) are infinite due to the different types of conceptual constructions regarding the objects of their manifestation, these twenty-four varieties of *jāti* have been shown here with the intention of providing unmixed examples. As for the refutation of all *jāti*s, it consists precisely in the examination of the definition of inference—namely, that [the probans] cannot be otherwise established; for when the reason (*hetu*) possesses its unimpaired definition, such showers of dust (objections) have no power to prevail.

Furthermore, because the relationship between being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and following immediately after an effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*) is firmly established, the non-perception of sound is not caused by an obstruction or the like, but is indeed caused by its impermanence (*anityatva*). When an opponent employs a futile rejoinder (*jāti*), one must state the correct answer; one should not respond perversely by means of futile rejoinders themselves, as that would lead to a state of total incoherence. — *Kṣaṇahetuparī* — Ḍe. edition.
Moreover, because it lacks the quality of being a correct rejoinder, even *chala* (quibble) is indeed called a *jātyuttara* (futile rejoinder).
For it has been stated that there are infinite *jātyuttaras* due to the differences in the methods of their manifestation;
among these, *chala* is the obstruction of an opponent's speech by means of establishing an alternative interpretation of the meaning as they speak.
That [quibble] is threefold: quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*), quibble regarding generality (*sāmānyacchala*), and quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāracchala*).
Among these, *vākchala* is the denial of a meaning other than that intended by the speaker when a common term has been employed, by imagining a different meaning.

For example, when it is said, "This boy has nine blankets" (*navakambalo 'yaṃ māṇavakaḥ*) with the intention of expressing "new," another person attributes the sense of the numeral nine and denies it, asking: "How can he have nine blankets?"

*Sāmānyacchala* (quibble regarding the general) is the refutation of a general property by attributing to it the status of a logical reason (*hetu*), even when that property is introduced merely as a possibility.

For example, in the context of praising a Brahmin, someone says: "Oh, how truly endowed with learning and conduct is this Brahmin! To which another person, a quibbler, replies: "It is possible for a Brahmin to possess the perfection of learning and conduct.

The quibbler then objects by superimposing upon *brāhmaṇatva* (the state of being a Brahmin) the status of a logical reason: "If the perfection of learning and conduct exists in a Brahmin, then it would also exist in a *vrātya*; for a *vrātya* is indeed a Brahmin."
Quibble regarding metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*) is the opposition raised by denying the primary sense when a metaphorical application is made;
for example, when it is said, "The platforms are crying out," another person objects: "How can inanimate platforms cry out? It is the people standing on the platforms who are crying out.
In all three types of quibble, the resolution should be understood as simply an investigation into the semantic power of words as established in the linguistic usage of the elders.
And indeed thus
— ḍe — .
—The statement of proofs, refutations, and so forth generally occurs in debate; therefore, he states the definition of debate:
"Debate (*vāda*) is the presentation of proof and refutation in the presence of an audience and others, for the purpose of preserving the truth."
The proof (*sādhana*) of the proponent for the sake of establishing his own position, and the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) of the opponent for the sake of negating that [proof]; likewise,
the proof of the opponent for the sake of establishing his own position, and the refutation of the proponent for the sake of negating that [proof].

Thus, for one who speaks in this manner, there is the presentation of proof and refutation; and for the opponent as well, there is the presentation of proof and refutation. How is it that the speaking—that is, the verbal expression—of both the proponent and the opponent constitutes *vāda* (debate)? He explains: "In the presence of the *prāśnikas* and others.
The *prāśnikas* are the members of the assembly (*sabhyas*), who are experts in their own and others' systems, of noble birth, desired by both sides, and patient.
Those who are experts in the paths of debate and are impartial like a scale are called "assessors" (*prāśnika*);
such is their definition.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the chairman (*sabhāpati*) and the plaintiff and defendant (*vādiprativādin*) are also encompassed. This is the four-limbed discourse (*caturaṅgā kathā*), for if even one of these limbs is deficient, the status of being a formal discourse (*kathātva*) is untenable.

For neither are the proponent and the opponent able to pursue the path of establishing their own positions and refuting those of the other without a presiding judge who possesses the aforementioned characteristics—being impartial, viewing all with an equal eye, and capable of maintaining the system of justice and injustice by protecting the castes and stages of life—and nor can the common folk, who follow others blindly and are swept away by the chatter of ignorant people who are eloquent only in fragments of ill-taught sophistry, ever attain the true path; therefore, he states its purpose: "for the sake of preserving the truth."

By the word *tattva* (reality), the ascertainment of reality as it revolves within the hearts of virtuous people is intended; its protection [is required] from the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa-kalpanā*) produced by those who are poorly educated.

Regarding the phrase "in the protection of those two"—[those who are] knowledgeable in their own system and the systems of others, born of noble lineage (*kulaja*), desired by both sides, and patient.
"Those who are proficient in the paths of debate and are impartial like a scale are called judges"—
thus it is said. [But] surely, the preservation of truth is the purpose of *jalpa* or *vitaṇḍā*.

As for the statement— "Sophistry (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the purpose of protecting the determination of truth (*tattva-adhyavasāya*), just as the pruning of thorny branches is for the purpose of protecting the growth of seeds" (Nyāyasūtra 4.2.50)— it is not so, because debate (*vāda*) also serves to protect truth by virtue of its possession of points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
Furthermore, its status as a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) is not unestablished;

for debate (vāda) consists of the employment of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and reasoning (tarka) for proof and refutation, is not contrary to established tenets (siddhānta), and is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism], involving the adoption of a position and its counter-position (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.1).

Thus, in the definition of *vāda* (disputation), by the phrase "not contrary to established tenets" (*siddhāntāviruddha*), the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) is permitted; and by the phrase "endowed with the five members" (*pañcāvayavopapanna*), the two points of defeat consisting of deficiency and excess, as well as the five types of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), are permitted—making eight points of defeat in total. Since these [eight] serve as indicators for other points of defeat, *jalpa* (wrangling) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) are not considered forms of discourse [in this context], because *vāda* alone serves the purpose of preserving the truth. [Objection: But is it not the case that *jalpa* is defined as "the employment of means and refutation through the use of quibbles (*chala*), futile rejoinders (*jāti*), and points of defeat, as previously described" (*Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.2)?
That which lacks the establishment of a counter-position is cavil (vitaṇḍā); Nyāyasūtra 1.2.2.

3. Thus, because of the difference in their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*), *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) are indeed types of discourse (*kathā*). [Response: No; for *vitaṇḍā*, which is devoid of the establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣasthāpanāhīnā*), cannot logically be considered a discourse.

For how can a caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*), who does not accept nor establish his own position but merely refutes the opponent's position with whatever arguments he pleases, be one whose words are worthy of attention?

As for *jalpa*, although it attains the status of discourse because both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) have the possibility of establishing proofs and offering refutations, nevertheless, it is not a different thing from *vāda* (discussion), since its purpose is fulfilled by *vāda* alone.

If it is argued that [the *vāda*] is not fulfilled because of its association with a greater abundance of *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*, we say no. This is because the employment of *chala* and *jāti* constitutes fallacious refutations (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*) and thus should not be employed;
furthermore, since *nigrahasthānas* are not prohibited even in *vāda*, such things as pinching, slapping, or gagging—though improper forms of defeat—are certainly not utilized even in *jalpa*.
And there is no contradiction in the use of appropriate *nigrahasthānas* even in *vāda*.
Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between debate (*vāda*) and wrangling (*jalpa*).

However, purposes such as the desire for gain, honor, and fame—which are secondary to the primary fruit characterized by the preservation of the determination of reality—cannot be prevented even in debate, because they are attributes of the person; thus, [wrangling] is not inferior. (Vādavidhi-vṛtti, Ḍe manuscript)
The suffix *ikaṇ* is applied [to form *prāyojanika*] by [Pāṇini 4.3.117]: *prayojanam*. *Haimaśabda-anuśāsana* 6.4.117.
— nor is there any [independent] self-nature even in relation to its own [cause]; and that which is "something" (kiñcit) is its discourse (vāda).

Indeed, the employment of quibbles (*chala*) and futile rejoinders (*jāti*), which follow the specific nature of the grass [of the opponent's argument], does not occur in formal debate (*vāda*) because they are fallacious replies; however, since their use is permitted in contentious discourse (*jalpa*), there is a distinction between *vāda* and *jalpa*.
As it has been said: "How else could those whose mouths are set in motion by fragments of ill-taught, fallacious reasoning—those pseudo-scholars arrogant in their sophistry—be defeated?
For the world follows like a flock of sheep, led astray by them onto a false path."
"The compassionate Sage spoke of deception and the like [only] so that [beings] would not go [to lower realms]," thus it is said.
Not so, for it is improper to refute an opponent through fallacious rejoinders; indeed, great-souled ones do not seek victory, fame, or wealth by unrighteous means. (Nyāyamañjarī, p. 11)

If it is argued that, upon seeing a powerful opponent, one might fear the destruction of the Dharma if that opponent were defeated; or, due to a failure of ingenuity (*pratibhā*), being unable to perceive the correct reply, one might scatter "bad replies" like dust—thinking that uncertainty is better than certain defeat, and thus incurs no fault—this is not so. For this application of a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) as a rebuttal lacks the capacity to establish a different type of discourse (*kathāntara*).
Even in a formal debate (*vāda*), if one should somehow employ a bad reply in accordance with the substance, place, time, and circumstances, would a different type of discourse thereby ensue? No.
Therefore, it is established that debate (*vāda*) alone, by means of the exclusion of frivolous talk (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), attains the status of the primary form of discourse.
[Those whose mouths are made to chatter by fragments of ill-taught, fallacious reasoning...]
Otherwise, how could those who are "scholars" in the grand display of caviling (vitaṇḍā) be defeated?
Deceived by them, the world follows like a flock of sheep along a wrong path, devoid of [the knowledge of] quibbles and other such fallacies.
"The compassionate Sage spoke of fallacies and the like [only] so that [the opponent] would not succeed," thus [it is said]. (Nyāyamañjarī, p.
11). If there were victory for that opponent—this [is the sense]. (Tātparyaṭīkā)
Since a debate concludes with victory or defeat, he states the definition of victory and defeat: "Victory is the establishment of one's own position. (31)
Whether for the proponent (*vādin*) or the opponent (*prativādin*), victory is the establishment of one's own position (*svapakṣasiddhi*).
And that [establishment] occurs through the avoidance of faults in the proof of one's own position and the exposure of faults in the proof of the opponent's position.

Even without stating a proof for one's own position, the opponent wins over the proponent by exposing the contradiction in the proponent's proof; for by the very act of exposing the contradiction, one has effectively stated a proof for one's own position.
As it has been said: "The other [opponent] defeats the proponent by bringing forward a contradictory reason";
the meaning is that this occurs through both the presentation of a rebuttal and the presentation of an objection, not through either one separately.
Defeat consists in the non-establishment of the contradictory reason (viruddhahetu).
Whether for the proponent or the opponent, that which constitutes the non-establishment of one's own position is defeat;
and this occurs either through the statement of fallacious proofs (*sādhanābhāsa*) or, even when the proof is correct, through the failure to refute the objections raised by the opponent.
Now, if non-establishment constitutes defeat, then what kind of "defeat" (nigraha) is that? For it is said that a debate ends in defeat; thus he says:
"That defeat belongs to both the proponent and the opponent.
The thirty-third and thirty-fourth sūtras have been written together in the Saṃmūrchana manuscript:

"That defeat itself is the *nigraha* (defeat) of the proponent and the opponent, not execution, imprisonment, and so forth; or rather, that very defeat, consisting in the non-establishment of one's own position, is called *nigraha* because it is the cause of defeat, and nothing else. As others have said: "Misapprehension and non-apprehension are the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). (Nyāyasūtra 1.2.19).
