There he says:
It is not merely a lack of comprehension; rather,

"wrong practice" (*vipratipatti*) refers to a perverted, contemptible, and censurable form of practice— namely, the cognition of a fallacious proof as a valid proof, and the cognition of a fallacious refutation as a valid refutation.

Non-comprehension (*apratipatti*), however, is the failure to initiate action regarding a subject that ought to be initiated; and this consists in not providing a refutation against a proof (*sādhana*) or not offering a rebuttal against a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). Non-comprehension is thus the non-performance of these two tasks.
For a proponent is defeated in two ways: either by failing to comprehend what must be done, or by comprehending it erroneously.
Misapprehension and non-apprehension are not merely misapprehension and non-apprehension that constitute grounds for defeat; rather, it is the failure to establish one's own position.

Since the status of misapprehension and non-apprehension as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) has been refuted, he begins by refuting the status as points of defeat of their various subdivisions as well.

And these are twenty-two, namely: 1. Loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), 2. Shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), 3. Contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), 4. Abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), 5. Shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), 6. Irrelevancy (*arthāntara*), 7. Meaninglessness (*nirarthaka*), 8. Non-comprehension of the meaning (*avijñātārtha*), 9. Incoherence (*apārthaka*), 10. Untimeliness (*aprāptakāla*), 11. Deficiency (*nyūna*), 12. Redundancy (*adhika*), 13. Repetition (*punarukta*), 14. Failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), 15. Ignorance (*ajñāna*), 16. Lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), 17. Evasion (*vikṣepa*), 18. Admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), 19. Neglecting what ought to be censured (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), 20. Censuring what ought not to be censured (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), 21. Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and 22. Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
In this context, non-reproduction, ignorance, lack of ingenuity, distraction, and overlooking what ought to be questioned are types of non-apprehension (*apratipatti*);
the remaining varieties are types of misconception (*vipratipatti*).

Among these, the definition of the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) is as follows: "The admission of a property belonging to the counter-example in one's own example is the abandonment of the thesis" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.2).
Thus [ends] the Sūtra.

The commentary of the author of this [text] is as follows: "When one, being countered by a property contrary to the property to be proven, admits a property of the counter-example (pratidṛṣṭānta) in one's own example (svadṛṣṭānta), one abandons the thesis; this is 'abandonment of the thesis' (pratijñāhāni)."

For example, when it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," the opponent objects: "Since the universal (sāmānya) is seen to be perceptible by the senses yet eternal, why should sound not be likewise? Thus, even while recognizing the fallacious nature of the reason he himself has employed, he fails to conclude the debate and instead abandons his proposition (*pratijñātyāga*). He says, "If the universal is perceptible and eternal, then let the jar also be eternal.
Indeed, by attributing eternality to the example used as a means of proof (*sādhana*), he abandons his entire thesis up to its conclusion (*nigamana*).
And it is said that by abandoning the thesis (*pakṣa*), one abandons the proposition (*pratijñā*), because the thesis is the locus of the proposition; thus [it is stated] in the *Nyāyabhāṣya* 5.2.2.

This is entirely inconsistent, because it constitutes a direct abandonment of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); since the property (*dharma*) is abandoned in that very [example], there follows by implication the abandonment of the reason (*hetu*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*), for if the example is invalid, those too are invalid. Thus, it results in nothing but the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), and so it remains entirely inconsistent.

The author of the Vārttika, however, explains: "It is both seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and situated at the end (*anta*), thus it is *dṛṣṭānta*"; *svadṛṣṭānta* means one's own position (*svapakṣa*), and *pratidṛṣṭānta* means the opposing position (*pratipakṣa*).

By admitting the property of the counter-position into one's own position, one abandons the thesis; for instance: "If the universal is perceptible by the senses and eternal, then let sound be so as well" (Nyāyavārttika 5.2.2).

This explanation as well is incoherent, because it is impossible to determine that the abandonment of a thesis (*pratijñāhāni*) occurs only in this specific manner. Indeed, the abandonment of a thesis does not consist solely in one who admits the property of the opponent's position into their own position; for we observe that someone may, after having proposed something as the probandum (*sādhya*), propose its opposite due to causes such as being overwhelmed by insults and the like, natural timidity in an assembly, or distraction of mind. Thus, it is established that human error can arise from many causes.
The property of the commonality of the counter-example is permanence; this is "admission of the property" (*dharmābhyanujñā*). — Vātsyāyana.

In the *Vātsyāyanabhāṣya*, however, it is stated: "When an opponent has countered with a property contrary to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), one abandons the thesis (*pratijñā*) by admitting the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one's own example; this is the 'abandonment of the thesis' (*pratijñāhāni*). The illustration is as follows: When it has been argued that "sound is non-eternal because it is perceptible by the senses, like a jar," another person objects: "Perceptibility is observed in the universal (*sāmānya*), which is eternal; why then is sound not likewise [eternal]? When thus countered, he says: "If the universal is perceptible and eternal, then let the jar be eternal as well."
Indeed, this proponent, by implying the eternality of the example, abandons the very thesis up to its conclusion;
and it is said that "by abandoning the thesis, he abandons the proposition," because the thesis is the locus of the proposition—
*Nyāyabhāṣya* 5.1.39.
2.2-mu-ṭi:
He has been cross-examined by the opponent.
The proponent [states]: "Because of the inconclusiveness of the reason adduced..."
prasañjana— °ḍe° prasajjayan— mu° the accepted position (pakṣa).
Regarding that loss of the thesis,
[it occurs] when the example— [the phrase "dṛṣṭānte sādhutve" in the manuscript]— is not established.

In the *Nyāyavārttika*, however, it is stated: "That which is seen and established at the end is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*); and since it is both one's own (*sva*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), by the term 'one's own example' (*svadṛṣṭānta*), the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is denoted.

And by the term 'counter-example' (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) is denoted; and since it is both a counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), this is what is meant."

When one accepts as one's own position that very property which belongs to the opponent's position—just as when the proponent of the second position (the Naiyāyika) has countered with the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and [the Mīmāṃsaka] replies: "If it is observed that a universal is both perceptible by the senses and eternal, then let sound be likewise"—[this is called *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*].
(Nyāyavārttika 5.2.19)

2—The conclusion (*anta*) is the summary; therein resides one position, which is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). That is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and that is the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*)—Ḍe.
Because it serves as a cause—

[variant reading: "because it is the state of being a cause"]— when the opponent has refuted the matter asserted in the thesis, for one who then declares another property to be proven regarding that very same subject (*dharmin*), there occurs the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "shifting the thesis" (*pratijñāntara*).

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and an objection regarding deviation (vyabhicāra) has been raised on the grounds of the universal (sāmānya) being likewise [perceptible], if one should say: "It is correct that the universal is perceptible and eternal, for it is all-pervading (sarvagata), whereas sound is not all-pervading"—this person, having previously asserted the proposition "sound is impermanent," now makes a different proposition, namely "sound is not all-pervading," and thus becomes defeated by a change of proposition (pratijñāntara).
This too, like the abandonment of a proposition (pratijñāhāni), is not tenable, since that [abandonment] also admits of multiple causes.
Furthermore, how is this [fallacy] distinct from *pratijñāhāni* (relinquishing the proposition), since the abandonment of the thesis is indistinguishable in both cases?

For just as there is an abandonment of the thesis by admitting the property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) into one’s own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*), so too is there an abandonment of the thesis through a change of proposition (*pratijñāntara*).

And just as a change of proposition is formulated for the sake of establishing one’s own position, so too—under the influence of delusion—is there an admission that "let sound also be eternal" for the sake of establishing the non-eternality of sound. And just as this contradicts one who is not deluded, so too does a change of proposition.

Furthermore, if there were a distinction [in the fallacies] based on a distinction in their defining characteristics (*nimitta*), there would be the undesirable consequence of other points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) being included as well;
and if those were to be subsumed under it, then "shifting the proposition" (*pratijñāntara*) would also have to be subsumed under "abandoning the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*).
(2) *Pūrva-prati*—Ḍe.

—When the opponent, even though he has not yet formulated a refutation of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*), says out of apprehension, "But sound is all-pervading," then that other proposition [is introduced] due to the necessity of another cause; [thus it is said: "that sound... —Ḍe.
— Annuṣaṅgaḥ— Ḍe:
Contradiction between the proposition and the reason is "contradiction of the proposition" (pratijñāvirodha), Nyāyasūtra 5.2.4.

There is a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) called "contradiction" (virodha), as in the case: "Substance is distinct from its qualities, because no object other than [the qualities] such as color is perceived.

This is a contradiction between the proposition (pratijñā) and the reason (hetu): if substance is distinct from its qualities, how can there be a non-perception of any object other than color and the rest? Conversely, if there is a non-perception of any object other than color and the rest, how can substance be distinct from its qualities? Thus, he is defeated because he has stated something that contradicts his own proposition.

This is inconsistent because, once the thesis has been refuted by the reason as being a thesis, this would either be stated as a "rejection of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*) due to its being of a different nature, or it would be a fault of the reason characterized as "contradiction" (*viruddhatā*), rather than a fault of the thesis. When the opponent has refuted the proof of one's position, if one denies the very thesis out of an inability to rescue it, that constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "renunciation of the thesis" (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*).

For example, when it has been stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses," and the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*) has been pointed out on the basis of the universal (*sāmānya*), if he should say, "Who says that sound is impermanent?"—then he is defeated due to the abandonment of his proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).

This too does not differ from the loss of the proposition (*pratijñā-hāni*), because there is no distinction here either in the abandonment of the proposition, since the inconclusiveness of the reason (*hetu*) has been perceived.
(4) Thus [ends] *Prati*—*Ḍe*.
When a reason has been stated without qualification and is refuted, stating a qualification for that reason constitutes the point of defeat called *hetvantara* (a different reason).

For instance, when that very same argument has been invalidated by showing the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the general property—such as by adding the qualification "provided it possesses a genus" (*jātimattve sati*)—one who employs such a qualification is defeated by means of a different reason.

This too is an over-extension (*atiprasṛta*), because when a general example has been stated and is refuted— whether in the application (*upanaya*) or the conclusion (*nigamana*)— if one then desires a specific [example], another distinct example would also result as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), since the objections and resolutions there would be identical.
This is the "different reason" (*hetvantara*).
The point of defeat called "irrelevant" (arthāntara) occurs when one states a different matter that is not relevant to the subject at hand;
for example, [stating] the reason: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."
Regarding the term "hetu" (reason): it is a derivative word formed from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*.

Having introduced the categories of speech units—namely nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), particles (*nipāta*), and prefixes (*upasarga*)—one who proceeds to explain nouns and the others is refuted by means of a different meaning.
Is this "shifting to another matter" (*arthāntara*) a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) applicable when a capable proof or refutation has been stated, or when an incapable one has been stated?
It is not [a point of defeat] when [the proponent] is capable, because even if he dances after having established his own thesis, there is no fault, just as in the world.
Furthermore, would it serve to defeat the opponent even when he is incapable, whether the opponent's position is established or not?
In the first case, his defeat arises precisely from the establishment of that position, and not from this [supposed] ground of defeat.

Therefore, even in the second case, there is no defeat (nigraha), because the establishment of the thesis (pakṣasiddhi) is absent for both [parties]. This is "irrelevance" (arthāntara) regarding the subject matter at hand—[the term] *pada* is indeed [the word] *nāma*. 6. Tātparya-ṭīkā.
The name of the conviction—
another alternative, another meaning— the very establishment of it.

A "meaningless" (nirarthaka) point of defeat occurs when there is merely the employment of a sequence of phonemes devoid of a denotable meaning, distinct from other [types of defeat]; for example: "Sound is impermanent because *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* have *ga-ja-ḍa-da-ba*, like *gha-jha-ḍha-dha-bha-va-dha*."
Furthermore, would this [fallacious argument] lead to defeat because it is entirely devoid of meaning, or because it is useless for establishing the probandum (*sādhya*)?

Regarding these two alternatives, the first is untenable, because a word that is entirely devoid of meaning is impossible; for even the specification of a sequence of phonemes possesses meaningfulness by virtue of its referent (*anukārya*). As for the second alternative, however, every instance of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would become meaningless, since there would be no distinction in their lack of utility for establishing the probandum.

If a distinction were made based on even a slight difference, then even the making of a *khāṭ* sound, the clapping of hands, or the slapping of the armpits—which are useless for the proof (*sādhya*)—would entail being a separate point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
[Regarding the reading *bhede vā* in the variant *ḍe*, and *ṣaṭkṛta* in the variants *mu* and *pā*:

That statement of proof or statement of refutation which, even though stated three times, cannot be understood by the assembly and the opponent, constitutes the point of defeat called "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha*).

On this point, the following is said: Even if a statement has been uttered three times by the proponent, it may not be understood by the assembly and the opponent either because of their dull-wittedness, because of its cryptic expression, or because of rapid pronunciation.

In the first case, this would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) even for a proponent of a valid proof, since it is possible that the assembly and the opponent might fail to understand it due to their dull-wittedness.

In the second case, however, the same consequence would follow even when using written statements, as it is observed that even highly intelligent members of the assembly and the opponent may fail to understand a statement due to its cryptic expression.

Now, even if this [point] is not understood by both [the proponent and the opponent], the proponent explains it; let him explain his own hidden presentation himself. However, if he does not explain it, there is simply an absence of victory for him, not a defeat (*nigraha*), because the other's position has not been established.
Even in the case of rapid pronunciation, some understanding of these two [points] is indeed possible, since [the audience] knows both systems of tenets (*siddhānta*).

But regarding that which is useless for the proof and is merely the proponent's idle chatter, their lack of understanding is not "non-understanding of the meaning" (*avijñātārtha*), as it is like the mere recitation of a sequence of syllables.
Therefore, this [fault] is not distinct from the "meaningless" (nirarthaka), as its meaning remains uncomprehended;
it consists in the utterance of words whose meanings are obscure,
even when the means for establishing the point are present.
The consequence of being unintelligible refers to riddles and the like, as well as messages written on leaves.
The proponent of the thesis (*sādhyavādin*),
who knows the established tenets (*siddhānta*)— thus [in the manuscript] *ḍe*—
then, anticipating the objection that "the definition of the uncomprehended is merely the disputant's idle chatter," the proponent of the defeat (*nigrahavādin*) speaks as follows.
The genitive case is not used in the sense of the agent— [as in the phrase] "not known"—

because the employment of a collection of words that are disconnected in terms of preceding and following parts constitutes the point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) called "the meaningless" (*apārthaka*), wherein the meaning of the sentence is not established.
For example, "ten pomegranates, six cakes," and so forth—
this also does not differ from the meaningless.
For just as there is meaninglessness of the phonemes in [the string] "gajaḍadaba" and so on, so too is there meaninglessness of the words here.

If, however, word-meaninglessness (*padanairarthakya*) is a distinct point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is different from syllable-meaninglessness (*varṇanairarthakya*), then sentence-meaninglessness (*vākyanairarthakya*) would also have to be a distinct point of defeat, as it too is different from those two; for sentences that are not employed with a proper sequence of prior and posterior parts are also observed in many ways, such as: "In the plantain tree there is a conch, and in the drum there is a plantain; in that drum there is a very great palace; that palace of the conch, drum, and plantain became like the river Gaṅgā [flowing] out of its mind.
And so forth.
Because it is useless for the purpose of what is to be proven, due to the meaninglessness of both phonemes and words:
there is a conch in a plantain tree, and a plantain tree in a drum; and in that drum, there is a very great celestial palace.
That palace, with its conchs, drums, and plantain trees, became like the mad Gaṅgā;

yet, if the meaninglessness of words implies the meaninglessness of sentences because the sentence consists of a collection of words, then the meaninglessness of syllables would imply the meaninglessness of words, since a word consists of a collection of syllables, given that syllables are everywhere devoid of meaning. If it is argued that this consequence applies to the word as well; then, because the word is itself meaningless, it follows by extension that the sentence—which consists of a collection of such words—is also meaningless.

Since a word possesses meaning, it [is meaningful] in relation to its word-meaning; likewise, let that [meaningfulness] belong to a phoneme as well in relation to the phoneme-meaning, just like a stem or a suffix. Indeed, neither a stem alone nor a suffix alone constitutes a word, yet there is no lack of meaning in these two;
for if they were meaningless due to the absence of a manifested meaning, then that same [charge of meaninglessness] would apply to the word as well.

For just as the meaning of the base (prakṛti) is manifested by the suffix (pratyaya) and the meaning of the suffix is manifested by the base, since neither of them is used in isolation, so too in expressions such as "Devadatta stands," the meaning of the word ending in a suffix beginning with *ti* is manifested by the word ending in a suffix beginning with *sti*, and thus it is not used alone.
The meaningfulness of a word that depends on another word is the same for a suffix that depends on its base, and for a phoneme within a base that depends on that [suffix]. 9.
In the case of "ten pomegranates, six cakes," however, the meaninglessness belongs to the words alone and not to the sentence, because no verb is heard; yet,
[it is argued] that even such a sentence possesses meaning through its connection with another [sentence].
Furthermore, regarding the base and the suffix:

when a syllogism of inference (*anumānavākya*) is employed by transposing its members (*avayava*), thereby violating the sequence of the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*), it constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "untimely" (*aprāptakāla*). This is because, in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), just as in one's own realization, the sequence is also a constituent factor in generating understanding in another.
This too is untenable, because for discerning listeners, the comprehension of meaning is observed even without a fixed order of the members [of the syllogism].

Now, one might argue that just as from hearing a corrupt word (*apaśabda*) there arises a recollection of the correct word, and from that the cognition of the meaning—so that the cognition of the meaning ultimately derives from the word itself through a causal chain—likewise, from the transposition of the members such as the proposition (*pratijñā*), there arises a recollection of their proper order, and from that the cognition of the sentence-meaning, but not directly from the transposition itself. This too is without substance, because no such cognition ever occurs.

If it is argued: "Because that very object for which comprehension arises from a word once uttered is its denoter and no other, otherwise one could just as well say that from a corrupt word (*apaśabda*), from its sequence, and from the transgression [of grammatical rules], there is recollection and from that the comprehension of the meaning—thus the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of words would be useless"; we reply: not so, because this merely results in an undesired consequence for the proponent, and because grammatical analysis is observed even in the case of corrupt words.

If there were a fixed rule that from a *saṃskṛta* word [the cognition of] dharma arises and from another [word] adharma arises, then the performance of other means for dharma and adharma would be useless, and there would follow the contingency of no fixed determination regarding dharma and adharma, since that word is perceived in both the non-dharmic and the dharmic cases.

Or, even if the cognition of meaning occurs through that sequence, nevertheless, the cognition of meaning remains sequential; therefore, a sentence by which that sequence is transposed is "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*), and not "out-of-order" (*aprāptakāla*).
(As stated in the Nyāyabhāṣya: *yathāpi śabdā*—ḍe—)
For those who advocate gradualism, there is both dharma and adharma— [in the case of] the unrighteous, [there is] the righteous— [and vice versa].

It is also incorrect to claim that when a five-membered syllogism is to be employed, the absence of even one of those members constitutes the point of defeat called "deficiency" (*nyūna*), because the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible in the absence of the proof (*sādhana*), and because all five members—starting with the proposition (*pratijñā*)—are proofs; for it has been stated that the establishment of the probandum occurs even without the employment of the five members, whereas it does not occur without the employment of the proposition and the reason alone. Therefore, only the deficiency of those [essential members] constitutes the point of defeat called "deficiency. 11

When an object has already been established by means of a single reason or example, for one to state another reason or another example constitutes the point of defeat called "redundancy" (*adhika*), because it is a useless statement.
This too is incorrect; for if the thesis is established from such a statement, defeat is impossible.
Furthermore, how can you accept the convergence of multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃplava*) in this manner?
Or, if [the additional reason] is accepted, it would lead to further defeat;

yet there is no defeat because the purposes of strengthening the understanding, providing corroboration, and establishing proof exist. This is the same in other cases as well: even when an object has been established by one reason or one example, a second reason or example is not useless, because its purpose exists.
Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, since, as with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is possible for something to become free from expectancy in a particular instance.

And how could there be the statement of the suffix *-ka* in its own sense (*svārthika*) regarding "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth—namely, that statement of "whatever is produced, that is impermanent" within the pervasion (*vyāpti*)? Furthermore, if the meaning is already understood from the mere use of the words in the *vṛtti*, would not the employment of the full sentence be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) due to being redundant? If it is argued that even such [redundancy] is not [a defeat] because it serves as a specific means for comprehension, then why would the statement of multiple reasons or examples—which serve as means for that comprehension—not be a ground for defeat?
However, the statement of that which is meaningless is a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) precisely because of its meaninglessness, and not because of redundancy (ādhikya).
[This is stated] in the passage "from two kinds of sentences" (*vākyāt*),
referring to one joined with another reason (*hetvantara*).
— Or it is understood as "more than" (adhika)— Ḍe;
— the word "vṛtti" [in the commentary] means "produced" (kṛtaka) and "impermanent" (anitya)— Ḍe.
The restatement of either the word or its meaning is the point of defeat known as "repetition" (*punarukta*), except in the case of a restatement for the sake of clarification (*anuvāda*).
"Repetition of the word" (*śabdapunarukta*) occurs when that very same word is uttered again, such as: "Sound is impermanent; sound is impermanent."

Redundancy of meaning (*arthapunarukta*), however, occurs where that same meaning which was first expressed by one word is stated again by another synonym, as for example: "Sound is impermanent, perishable, [and] noise. But in the case of restatement (*anuvāda*), such redundancy is not a fault; as it is said: "The conclusion (*nigamana*) is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the adducing of the reason" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.39).

1.39 Thus, in this case, it is only semantic tautology (*arthapunarukta*) that is untenable, not verbal tautology (*śabdapunarukta*), because the latter is impossible even when there is identity of words provided there is a difference in meaning—as in: "When the master laughs, she laughs; when he cries out loudly, she weeps excessively; when he runs forward with his loincloth tied and perspiration breaking out, she runs after him."

"One who praises what is endowed with virtues and free from faults, yet censures and reviles it; one who makes a machine, purchased for a mere fragment of wealth, dance and dance"—as stated in *Vādanyāya*, p. 111, and so forth.
Therefore, the members of the assembly (*sabhyāḥ*) should be addressed by those very words or by other words that express a clear meaning.

However, the expression of words that do not convey that [already established] meaning—whether once or repeatedly—is *nirarthaka* (meaningless), but it is not *punarukta* (redundant). Furthermore, regarding what is called *punarukta*, namely the verbal restatement by its own word of what has already been implied by the sense—as when it is said, "When there are no clouds, rain does not occur," which implies by implication that "when they exist, it does occur"—if this is stated explicitly, it becomes *punarukta*. For when words are employed for the purpose of conveying a meaning, once that meaning is already understood, what is the use of those words? This too is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) because it is useless insofar as it conveys a meaning already grasped, and not otherwise.
And thus, this would not differ from the meaningless;
as it was said: "Where... (ḍe);
"...spoken" (ḍe).
When the mistress laughs, she laughs; when she cries out loudly, she weeps excessively; when he has girded his loins, she runs and rushes about, perspiring profusely.
He reviles and censures one who is endowed with virtues and free from faults;
yet he dances and dances for one who is possessed of faults—a machine purchased for a mere fragment of wealth. —*Vādanyāya*, p. 111.
Regarding the subject (*viśeṣya*):

when the opponent fails to restate that which has been understood by the assembly and has been stated three times by the proponent, that constitutes the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "non-reproduction" (*ananubhāṣaṇa*). For, if one does not restate [the argument], on what basis could one state a refutation?
In this regard, does "non-reproduction" refer to the failure to restate everything said by the proponent, or only to that which is indispensable for the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*)?
Among these, the first position is untenable; for even one who does not repeat everything stated by the opponent can still utter a refutation without contradiction.

For example, when it is said, "Everything is impermanent because of existence," one might state the very reason and point out its contradictory nature, supporting this by arguing that "existence is impossible because purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is entirely contradicted in the extreme view of momentary destruction.
Since the opponent's reason is thus refuted by that much alone, what is the use of repeating anything else?

Therefore, it should be understood that non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) consists precisely in the failure to restate that [statement] without which the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) is impossible.

Now, if one is unable to refute [the argument] in this way because of a lack of specific knowledge regarding the meaning of the treatise, then such a person is rejected solely due to the failure to grasp the rejoinder (*uttarāpratipatti*), and not on account of non-reproduction. (14) Or rather, that which is inseparable from effort... [Tātparyaṭīkā]

Furthermore, even when the meaning of the proponent's statement has been understood by the assembly, the opponent's lack of comprehension regarding it constitutes the point of defeat known as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*). This applies whether [the statement] follows immediately upon an effort or not.
Thus, even if the opponent is part of the assembly, his failure to understand the meaning of the disputant's words results in the defeat called ignorance.

For how could one who has not understood the subject matter of the reply provide that reply? Nor is this merely a case of non-reproduction (ananubhāṣaṇa), since we observe an inability to reproduce even when the matter is known;

this too is incorrect, because it would entail the loss of distinction between the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) such as "abandonment of the thesis" (pratijñāhāni) and others, as ignorance itself would be possible in those cases as well.

If those [points] were merely subdivisions of that [inability to respond], it would follow that there is no fixed determination of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because there would be a multiplicity of points of defeat based on the various distinctions such as not understanding half of what was stated by the opponent. [Commentary on the distinction:
Even when the opponent's position has been grasped and restated, the failure to find a response to it is the point of defeat called "lack of ingenuity" (*apratibhā*).
This too does not differ from ignorance (ajñāna). 16.
Distraction (vikṣepa) is the interruption of the discussion due to preoccupation with other tasks; Nyāyasūtra 5.2.16.

The nineteenth point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) occurs when one, having determined that the matter one intends to prove is impossible to establish, interrupts the debate—saying things such as, "This duty of mine is being neglected," or "My throat is choked by a cold"—and by thus interrupting the debate through distraction, one is defeated.
This too is not a separate point from "lack of understanding" (*ajñāna*). (17)
—[The opponent] does not differ from himself.

[Sva-... pā-]. When one, without having removed a fault alleged against one's own position, applies that very same fault back against the opposing position, it constitutes the point of defeat called *matānujñā* (admission of the opponent's view).

When it is said, "You are a thief because you are a man, like a well-known thief," one who replies, "You too are a thief because you are a man," is defeated by the *matānujñā* (concession of the opponent's position), as he thereby accepts the fault of thievery attributed to himself by the other. This [rejoinder] does not differ from ignorance (*ajñāna*), or else there is the fallacy of the reason being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*) here. For he, having seen the inconclusiveness of his own reason, says: "This fault is equal even in your position; since you too are a man, [your reason] is indeed inconclusive. Thus he merely points out the inconclusiveness [of the original argument]. 18.
— by one's own [fault]—
the non-rebuttal of one who has reached a point of defeat (nigrahaprāpta) constitutes the ground for defeat called "overlooking the censurable" (paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa).

"One who should be questioned" (*paryanuyojya*) means one who must necessarily be urged on account of the occurrence of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), such that he should be told: "This point of defeat has come upon you; therefore, you are defeated. He who overlooks such a person and does not defeat him is himself defeated by "overlooking the one who should be questioned" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*).

When questioned by the assembly, "Whose defeat is this?", this [fault] should be pointed out; however, the opponent himself should not disclose his own fault by saying, "I am worthy of defeat, yet I was overlooked by you.
This too does not differ from [the fault of] ignorance (*ajñāna*). 19.

The application of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) where there is no point of defeat constitutes "objection against one who should not be objected to" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), according to Nyāyasūtra 5.2.22.
This is indeed a point of defeat.

If one should say of a speaker who has stated [his case] correctly, who is not negligent, and who is not deserving of defeat, "You have been defeated," that person alone is defeated by the manifestation of a non-existent fault;
this too does not differ from ignorance.
20 — *sthānābhiyo* — mu — pā.

"Deviation from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*), a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), occurs when, having accepted a tenet, one proceeds with a discussion without restriction [regarding that tenet]; Nyāyasūtra 5.2.23.

He who, having first accepted a certain tenet (*siddhānta*) and initiated a debate, asserts something contrary to that tenet in order to prove the point he intends to establish or to censure his opponent, is defeated by the fallacy of "contradiction of one's own tenet" (*apasiddhānta*). This too is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) only when the opponent has established a counter-position, and not otherwise. (21)

And the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and so forth, as described in Nyāyasūtra 5.2.24, are points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

In this case as well, it is logical that defeat (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*) occurs because the counter-position is established by the adducing of a contradictory reason (*viruddhahetu*); however, when the opponent has already established the counter-position by adducing [a reason] such as the unestablished (*asiddha*), it is appropriate [to declare defeat], and not otherwise. (22.34) Having thus examined the grounds for defeat taught by Akṣapāda, the grounds for defeat according to the Buddhist scriptures are now examined:
Nor is there [a fault] in the statement of what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*), nor in the pointing out of a fault (*doṣodbhāvana*).
Nāsādha-tā-mū-ityācāryaśrīhemacandraviracitāyāṃ pramāṇamīmāṃsāyāṃ dvitīyasyādhyāyasya kiyanti sūtrāṇi.
Homage to the son of Śrīvāmā.
May there always be auspiciousness for the scribe and the reader. — Chaitra Saṃvat Mūla.
Failure to establish one's own position is indeed defeat, and not merely the failure to state a member of the proof or the failure to point out a fault;

as Dharmakīrti has said: "The non-statement of a member of the proof and the non-pointing-out of a fault are the points of defeat for both [parties]; anything else is not logical, and thus it is not accepted."
*Vādanyāya*, Chapter 1:

"The statement of what is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) constitute the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for both parties; any other [point of defeat] is not logical, and thus it is not accepted. — *Vādanyāya*, Chapter 1.

For in this case, when either the proponent or the opponent—whether establishing their own position or not—defeats the other either by failing to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) or by failing to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*), [the following occurs]:
in the first alternative, since he is already defeated by the very fact that his own position is not established, the pointing out of the other fault is useless.

In the second alternative, even if there is the pointing out of the failure to state a member of the proof and so forth, there is victory for neither party, because the establishment of the position is absent for both.
Furthermore, regarding its explanation:

"The means of proof (*sādhana*) is the establishment (*siddhi*); its constituent part (*aṅga*) is the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*). The non-statement of that—whether it be silence or some random speech—is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent. Or, the constituent part of the means of proof, namely the three-featured logical mark, is the justification (*samarthana*), which consists in the presentation of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the counter-position (*vipakṣa*). The non-statement of that is a point of defeat for the proponent. This applies equally even to one who maintains the use of the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-prayoga*), for he too could say: "The Buddhist proponent is defeated because he fails to state the five-membered syllogism, which is a constituent part of the establishment."

Now, one might argue that there is no defeat even if these two are not stated, because the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the conclusion (*nigamana*) are understood through the power of the restatement of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmopasaṃhāra*), and because stating what is already understood would entail redundancy; furthermore, even when those two are employed, the probandum is not established without the employment of the reason (*hetu*). This too is incorrect, because by this same logic, the restatement of the property in the subject would also necessarily fail to be stated.

Now, if it is argued that even though it is understood through implication, the statement of the application of the property to the subject—namely, "whatever exists is momentary, like a jar, and sound exists"—is for the purpose of excluding the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddha*) due to its not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*); then why should there not also be the statement of the conclusion (*nigamana*), which, although understood by implication, serves to remove doubt regarding the locus of the probandum and demonstrates that the proposition, the reason, the example, and the application have a single common purpose?

For the coherence of the thesis and the other members cannot be established without demonstrating that they share a single objective, just as it would not be the case for a thesis and other members directed toward different subjects.

If you argue that once the probandum is established by the thesis, the statement of the reason and so forth would be useless—otherwise, they would not be limbs of the proof—then, by parity of reasoning, for you as well, once the probandum is established by the reason, the example would be useless; otherwise, it would not be a limb of the proof. Thus, the situation is the same.

Now, it might be argued that the example (dṛṣṭānta) is not useless because its purpose is to demonstrate the pervasion (vyāpti) between the probandum and the probans, since a reason is non-probative if that [pervasion] is not demonstrated therein. This too is incorrect, because it would follow that reasons such as "existence" (sattva) would be non-probative when proving the impermanence of all things, due to the impossibility of an example [for "all"]. Alternatively, if existence and the like were probative by virtue of their exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa), then every reason would likewise have to be probative in that same way, and thus the example would be entirely useless.
Furthermore, while establishing the reason through its exclusion from the counter-example, how could one possibly reject the thesis (pratijñā)?
And if that [proposition] is not stated, where would the reason or the probandum reside?

If it is argued that they reside in the very object of the proposition as it is being understood, then there should likewise be a justification for the reason as it is being understood, and not for the one already stated.

Or, if you say that even the reason, though already understood, is stated for the sake of comprehension by those of dull intellect, then why is there dissatisfaction with stating the proposition as well?

—Even so, [in the case of] defeat—[there is] the application of the reason [based on] the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the non-property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*). —Mu. —By means of the reason, [the application is] established. —Tā.
— even though such words— O Lord, words— O Lord—
even though it is the nature of the eyes— O Lord.
—*kārthapratiprada*—Mu;
*kārthapratijñāprada*—Ḍe.

Furthermore, regarding this other explanation of the phrase "not a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅga*): "When the reason is stated by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is redundant because it is already understood; and when there is an application by way of dissimilarity, the statement of similarity is redundant for the same reason. Therefore, it is not a member of the proof. This too is incorrect, because would the defeat (*nigraha*) belong to the proponent who establishes his own position through the power of a correct proof, or to one who fails to establish it?
In the first case, he is not defeated merely by the censure of an excess of words that does not obstruct the establishment of the thesis (*sādhya*), because there is no contradiction. [Objection:

But in that case, would he not also incur defeat from engaging in activities such as reciting plays? [Reply: This is true; however, just as in the world, there is no fault even for one who dances after having established his own thesis, otherwise, even a proponent of a true proof would incur defeat due to chewing betel, frowning, making grunting sounds, clapping hands, and so forth.

Now, if he is defeated because he fails to establish his own position, one must ask: in this case as well, is the opponent’s censure of the proponent’s excessive speech intended to be a point of defeat (*nigraha*) when the opponent has established his own position, or when he has not?

In the first case, since the proponent is already defeated by the very failure to establish his own position, pointing out the excess of speech is useless; for even if that excess exists, victory is impossible without the establishment of one’s position.

In the second case, however, there would follow the consequence of either a simultaneous defeat or a simultaneous victory for both the proponent and the opponent, since there is no difference between them regarding the absence of the establishment of their respective positions.
Is it not the case that victory and defeat are not based on the establishment or non-establishment of one's own position, since they are based on knowledge and ignorance?
For the proponent must state a valid proof after having understood it, and the opponent must state a refutation.

In that regard, when the meaning is understood from the statement of similarity or the statement of dissimilarity, if both are stated by the proponent, he suffers defeat because the opponent points out in the assembly that his statement lacks the constituent parts of a valid proof, thereby establishing the proponent’s ignorance of the valid proof.

Furthermore, the claim that victory for the opponent would result from his certain knowledge of the refutation [of the proponent's argument] is also charming only when left unexamined; for, would that opponent point out the fault of "excess of speech" (vacanādhikya) against one who is either a speaker of a valid proof (*satsādhana*) or a speaker of a fallacious proof (*sādhanābhāsa*)?
In the first case, how could the proponent have a lack of knowledge regarding the correct proof, given that there is an absence of even the knowledge regarding the extent of that speech?
In the second case, however, no knowledge of refutation is established for the opponent, because he has not pointed out the fallacious nature of the proof.

If it is argued that he is a "knower of refutations" because he recognizes the fault of redundancy in the statement, then he is likewise not a "knower of refutations" because he fails to recognize fallacious arguments (*sādhanābhāsa*); thus, he would not necessarily defeat the proponent, since he is unable to prevent the opponent's defeat characterized by the failure to point out such faults. Furthermore, if the victory of the respondent were established merely by pointing out the fault of redundancy, then the pointing out of fallacious arguments would be useless. But if, in this way, his defeat is established through the failure to point out fallacious arguments, how could the pointing out of redundancy lead to his victory?

Now, if the opponent wins by pointing out either a redundancy of statements or a fallacious proof, how could the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) lead to defeat when there is a statement of similarity (sādharmya), or the statement of similarity lead to defeat when there is a statement of dissimilarity?

And how would the adoption of a thesis and a counter-thesis by the proponent and the opponent not be rendered useless, given that it is possible for one or even both parties to simultaneously possess knowledge or lack knowledge of the capacity of their respective proofs? Indeed, in an investigation into whether sound and so forth are eternal or non-eternal, the knowledge of the capacity of a proof by one side and the lack of such knowledge by the other cannot be the basis for victory or defeat.
Furthermore, if both the proponent and the opponent simultaneously lack knowledge of the capacity of their proofs, whose victory or defeat would there be, since there is no distinction between them?

If it is argued that [the fault] belongs to no one, then neither victory nor defeat would accrue to anyone. For, in that case, it would be established that the proponent of the proof (sādhana-vādin) merely lacks knowledge of the proof’s efficacy because he has committed the error of excessive speech, while the opponent merely knows of the existence of that fault because he has pointed out the defect of excessive speech.

Indeed, one who knows a fault of something does not necessarily know its quality as well; for instance, even when one perceives the power of a poisonous substance to cause death from some source, the perception of its power to eliminate leprosy does not arise.
Therefore, it is not possible to establish victory and defeat based on whether one knows or does not know that capacity [of the reason], because that would entail the aforementioned defects.
However, those two are faultless when based on the establishment or non-establishment of one's own position, since there is no futility in adopting a thesis and its counter-thesis.

For if the establishment of someone's own position from some source were well-ascertained, then due to the absence of such establishment for the other, the consequence of simultaneous victory and defeat for both would follow.
From the statement of similarity, the object—
[as noted by Ḍe]—
is not necessarily won; [as noted by Ḍe]— not exclusively so.
— The radiance of manifestation arises— O Goddess,
how does it triumph?— O Goddess, the foundation of this...— O Goddess.
— only in the mere [cognition], [the state of] knowledge—
[the state of] object-perception—
accomplished, certain— O Goddess.

Regarding the explanation of the phrase "non-pointing out of a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*): if it is taken as an absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), "non-pointing out of a fault" would merely mean the absence of pointing out a fault; however, if it is taken as an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), then the pointing out of fallacious faults (*doṣābhāsa*) or other actual faults by the opponent constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This [latter view] is indeed accepted by the proponent when he employs a proof that is free from faults, provided that the proponent establishes his own position and not otherwise;
as for the fault of "excessive speech," that has already been refuted previously.

For just as the use of five members in a formal argument constitutes a point of defeat due to redundancy, so too would there be deficiency in the use of three members, since there is no difference [in the logical requirement];

for all five—the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*)—are indeed members of the inference, according to the *Nyāyasūtra* (1.1.32): "The members (*avayava*) are the proposition, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion."

Because of this statement, if even one among those [required members] is not mentioned, the fault known as "deficiency" (nyūnatā) necessarily follows; for [the Nyāyasūtra states]: "That which is deficient by even one [member] is 'deficient' (nyūna)" (Nyāyasūtra 5.2.12).
Because of this statement, there is no cause other than the stated cause for the determination of victory or defeat; so, enough of this digression.

This fourfold debate previously described sometimes requires the support of a written document (*patra*); therefore, its definition must necessarily be stated here, because the support of such a document cannot lead to victory if its nature is not understood, nor can an opponent's document be refuted if its nature is not understood. Thus he says:
Sixfold prosperity.
Sixfold prosperity.
May there be auspiciousness and great glory.
They say: "Śrī-tā-."
Thus ends the first daily lesson (āhnika) of the second chapter of the *Pramāṇamīmāṃsā* and its commentary, composed by the venerable teacher Śrī Hemacandra.
